name: ATSAMV71Q21B-AABT
title: SAM V71 Arm Cortex-M7 microcontroller, 300 MHz, 2048 KB Flash, 384 KB SRAM, Ethernet AVB, high-speed USB, two CAN-FD, Media LB, AEC-Q100 Grade 2 LQFP144
summary: ATSAMV71Q21B-AABT is the 144-pin, 2048 KB Flash, revision B member of the SAM V71 family, qualified to AEC-Q100 Grade 2 (-40 °C to +105 °C) in a 20 x 20 mm LQFP144. Its Cortex-M7 runs at up to 300 MHz with 16 KB instruction and data caches, a double-precision FPU and tightly coupled memory carved from 384 KB of multi-port SRAM. Around it sit a 10/100 Ethernet MAC with AVB, a 480 Mbps USB device/host port, two CAN-FD controllers, Media LB, an image sensor interface, QSPI with execute-in-place, an external bus, two 12-bit analog front ends, a 2-channel DAC and up to 114 I/O lines. The Grade 2 parts run from a single 3.0 V to 3.6 V supply through an on-chip core regulator.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M7, up to 300 MHz, FPU (single and double precision), 16 KB I-cache + 16 KB D-cache with ECC
2048 KB (density code 21), 512-byte pages, 128-bit unique ID, 512-byte user signature
384 KB multi-port SRAM (up to 128 KB ITCM + 128 KB DTCM), plus 1 KB backup SRAM
16 KB with SAM-BA boot (UART0, USB) and IAP routines
3.0 V to 3.6 V single supply (AEC-Q100 Grade 2 devices); 1.7 V to 3.6 V for industrial devices
LQFP144, 20 x 20 mm, 0.5 mm pitch (package code AA), tape and reel
114 I/O lines on PIOA to PIOE (144-pin devices)
Ethernet 10/100 MII/RMII with AVB, USB 2.0 high speed 480 Mbps, 2 x CAN-FD, Media LB, 3 x USART, 5 x UART, 3 x TWIHS, 2 x SPI, QSPI, SSC, 2 x I2SC, HSMCI
2 x 12-bit AFEC (24 channels on 144 pins), dual S&H up to 1.7 Msps; 2-channel 12-bit DAC, 1 Msps; analog comparator; temperature sensor
Backup mode down to 1.1 μA typical with RTC, RTT and wakeup logic; Wait mode wake in under 10 μs

notes: In the USB column HS stands for high speed and FS for full speed.

An order code is built as ATSAM, the series (V71, V70, E70, S70), the pin count letter (J = 64, N = 100, Q = 144), the Flash density (19 = 512 KB, 20 = 1024 KB, 21 = 2048 KB), the device variant (A = revision A, legacy; B = revision B, current), a hyphen, the package type (A = LQFP, AA = LQFP for Grade 2 parts, C = LFBGA/TFBGA, CF = UFBGA/VFBGA, M = QFN), the temperature range (N = industrial, B = Grade 2, both -40 to +105 °C) and T for tape and reel where it applies.
ATSAMV71Q21B-AABT is the 144-pin, 2048 KB Flash, revision B device in the Grade 2 (AEC-Q100) LQFP144 package, -40 °C to +105 °C, on tape and reel.

columns: reset state (signal, dir, PU, PD, HiZ, ST)
notes: (1) WKUPx works when the PIO controller has the line set as an input.
(2) This extra function is chosen in the parallel capture mode of the PIO controller.
(3) PIODCEN1/PIODCx takes priority over WKUPx (PIO parallel capture mode).
(4) See the slow clock generator of the supply controller (SUPC).
(5) This extra function is chosen in the I/O lines section of the external bus interface, whatever the PIO setting; the PIO line still needs its pull-up or pull-down set as required.
(6) The analog input takes priority over WKUPx; the analog input is chosen in the EBI I/O lines section, and WKUPx works when the PIO controller has the line set as an input.
(7) The analog input takes priority over RTCOUTx; the analog input is chosen in the EBI I/O lines section, RTCOUTx in the RTC waveform generation section.
(8) The analog input takes priority over WKUPx; the analog input is chosen in the EBI I/O lines section, PIODCEN2 in the PIO parallel capture mode.
(9) Set by CCFG_SYSIO in the bus matrix.
(10) See the main crystal oscillator of the clock generator; the choice does not depend on the PIO setting, and the PIO lines must be set to match XINxx (input) and XOUTxx (output).
(11) DAC0 is connected when DACC_CHER.CH0 is set, DAC1 when DACC_CHER.CH1 is set.

Reset state: PIO means the line comes out of reset as a static I/O (its PIO_PSR bit resets low); a signal name means the line comes out of reset driving that peripheral function (its PIO_PSR bit resets high), as on the memory address lines. I or O gives the direction, PU or PD the pull-up or pull-down enabled, ST a Schmitt trigger enabled, HiZ high impedance.

notes: (1) VDDIN needs a ceramic capacitor of 4.7 µF (±20%) or more to the nearest GND pin; it is required, and it cuts the start-up current and improves transient response and noise rejection.

(2) The regulator is stable only with a 1 µF (±20%) capacitor from VDDOUT to the nearest GND pin; solid tantalum or multilayer ceramic both suit. A further 100 nF from VDDOUT to the nearest GND pin lowers output noise and improves load-transient response.

(3) Once the threshold is crossed the internal reset follows in under 200 µs and stays asserted until the power-on reset is active.

circuits.title: 16-bit parallel programming interface
circuits.description: Connection to a gang programmer in fast Flash programming mode: TST, PGMEN0 (PD10) and PGMEN1 (PD11) tied to VDDIO, the four handshake lines NCMD, RDY, NOE and NVALID on PA3, PA4, PA5 and PA21, the mode bits MODE[3:0] on PB0 to PB3, the 16-bit data bus on PA7 to PA14 and PD0 to PD7, and an external clock on XIN (PB9) with the oscillator in bypass. VDDCORE, VDDIO, VDDPLL and GND are supplied.

circuits.title: Separate backup supply powering scheme
circuits.description: The main supply feeds VDDIO, VDDUTMII and VDDIN, each node decoupled to ground; a separate supply feeds VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC with its own decoupling, and the regulator output VDDOUT is left unconnected. In Backup mode only VDDIO needs to stay present.
notes: USB needs a main supply of 3.0 V or more, MediaLB 2.7 V or more, and the ADC, DAC and analog comparator 2.0 V or more; with main supply and VDDIN above 3 V every peripheral works.

circuits.title: No separate backup supply powering scheme
circuits.description: One main supply feeds VDDIO, VDDUTMII and VDDIN, decoupled to ground; the on-chip regulator output VDDOUT feeds VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC, decoupled to ground. VDDIO stays up in Backup mode, so I/O settings hold.
notes: Below 2.0 V neither USB nor the ADC, DAC and analog comparator work; from 2.0 V to 3 V USB does not; below 2.7 V MediaLB does not; above 3 V every peripheral works.

circuits.title: Battery backup
circuits.description: An external LDO regulator makes the main rail from the main supply; two diodes join the LDO output and a backup battery onto the VDDIO, VDDUTMII and VDDIN node, decoupled to ground, so the battery takes over in Backup mode. VDDOUT feeds VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC with its own decoupling. A PIO line held low in Backup mode turns the LDO off through its ON/OFF input, and an external wake signal on a WKUP pin restarts the system.

parts.note: main supply side of the switchover

notes: U1.PA0 stands for any wakeup input WKUPx (WKUP0 is on PA0); U1.PA6 stands for any free PIO line driven as an output.
After a backup reset the PIO line is an input with pull-up.

circuits.title: Low-power debouncer with push-to-make switches and pull-up resistors
circuits.description: Two tamper switches to ground on WKUP0 and WKUP1, each input pulled up by a resistor fed from RTCOUTx; RTCOUTx pulses the pull-ups only at the debouncer's sample points, so a closed switch draws current only during the pulse.
notes: U1.PB0 stands for RTCOUTx (RTCOUT0 is on PB0, RTCOUT1 on PB1); WKUP0 is on PA0 and WKUP1 on PA1.

circuits.title: Low-power debouncer with push-to-break switches and pull-down resistors
circuits.description: Two normally closed tamper switches from RTCOUTx to WKUP0 and WKUP1, each input pulled down to ground by a resistor; opening a switch lets its input fall to the pull-down level at the next RTCOUTx sample pulse.
notes: U1.PB0 stands for RTCOUTx (RTCOUT0 is on PB0, RTCOUT1 on PB1); WKUP0 is on PA0 and WKUP1 on PA1.

circuits.title: WKUP pins without the RTCOUTx pins
circuits.description: Two tamper switches to ground on WKUP0 and WKUP1 with pull-up resistors held at VDDIO; the RTC still sets the debouncer's internal sample point.
notes: WKUP0 is on PA0 and WKUP1 on PA1.

circuits.title: 8-bit NAND Flash
circuits.description: A 2 Gbit 8-bit NAND Flash (K9F2G08U0M, TSOP48) on the external bus. Its I/O0 to I/O7 take the data bus D0 to D7; CLE and ALE take the address lines used as NANDCLE (A22) and NANDALE (A21); RE takes NANDOE and WE takes NANDWE. Chip enable is driven from a spare PIO line so it can stay low through the busy period, and ready/busy goes to another PIO line with a 10K pull-up to 3V3. Write protect is pulled up to 3V3 through 10K; PRE is tied to ground. Both VCC pins are on 3V3, decoupled by two 100 nF capacitors to ground.
notes: U1 pin numbers: CLE 16, ALE 17, RE 8, WE 18, CE 9, R/B 7, WP 19, I/O0 to I/O7 29, 30, 31, 32, 41, 42, 43, 44, PRE 38, VCC 12 and 37, VSS 13 and 36; the remaining 28 pins are not connected.

circuits.title: NOR Flash
circuits.description: An 8-bit NOR Flash on chip select NCS0. Its address inputs A0 to A21 take the bus lines A0 to A21 and DQ0 to DQ7 the data lines D0 to D7. RESET follows the MCU's NRST, WE takes NWE, CE takes NCS0 and OE takes NRD. WP and VPP are tied to 3V3; VCC and VCCQ are on 3V3, decoupled to ground by two 100 nF capacitors.

circuits.title: Dual microphone
circuits.description: Two I2S microphones on one I2SC receive line. Both take the serial clock from I2SC_CK and word select from I2SC_WS, and both drive I2SC_DI. The left-channel microphone has its L/R input tied to 1, the right-channel one to 0, so each answers in its own half of the word select period. I2SC_MCK and I2SC_DO are not used.
notes: Misprint: the word select pin is labelled I2SC_CK; it should read I2SC_WS.

circuits.title: Audio codec
circuits.description: An I2S audio codec on the I2SC. I2SC_MCK supplies the codec's master clock, I2SC_CK and I2SC_WS carry its bit clock and word clock, I2SC_DO carries playback data to the codec's DAC input, and the codec's ADC output returns on I2SC_DI, in left and right time slots of each frame.

circuits.title: SSC audio, I2S receiver
circuits.description: An I2S receiver driven from the SSC transmitter: TK gives the serial clock, TF the word select and TD the data, left channel then right channel, MSB first. The receive pins RD, RF and RK are not used.

circuits.title: SSC codec
circuits.description: A codec on the SSC: TK drives the serial data clock (SCLK), TF the frame sync (FSYNC), TD the codec's serial data input, and the codec's serial data output returns on RD, in the first time slot after frame sync.

circuits.title: SSC time slots, two codecs
circuits.description: Two codecs share the SSC's SCLK (TK), FSYNC (TF), data out (TD) and data in (RD) lines; the first codec uses the first time slot after frame sync and the second codec the second time slot.

circuits.title: I2SC client transmitter, stereo DAC
circuits.description: The I2SC as client transmitter feeding a stereo audio DAC. The DAC drives the serial clock into I2SC_CK and the word select into I2SC_WS; I2SC_DO sends the data MSB first. I2SC_DI is not used.

circuits.title: USART hardware handshaking
circuits.description: A USART linked to a remote device with RTS/CTS flow control: TXD to the remote RXD, RXD from the remote TXD, CTS from the remote RTS and RTS to the remote CTS.

circuits.title: USART smart card
circuits.description: A smart card on a USART in ISO7816 mode: SCK drives the card clock (CLK) and TXD is the bidirectional I/O line.

circuits.title: USART IrDA transceiver
circuits.description: An IrDA transceiver on a USART in IrDA mode: the internal modulator drives TXD into the transceiver's TX input, and the transceiver's RX output returns on RXD to the demodulator.

circuits.title: USART RS485 bus
circuits.description: A USART in RS485 mode on a differential bus: TXD feeds the line driver, RTS enables the driver, and the line receiver's output goes to RXD. Driver outputs and receiver inputs share the two bus wires.

circuits.title: 3-pin MediaLB connection
circuits.description: A MediaLB Controller, bridged to the MOST Network through its RX and TX lines, shares one 3-pin bus with three MediaLB Devices. The Controller drives the clock through a 100 Ω series resistor into every Device clock input. Data and signal are shared bidirectional lines: the Controller and each Device reach them through their own 100 Ω series resistors, which damp edges and terminate the line. Each of the three lines has a 47 kΩ pull-down so it sits at a known level when nobody drives it. At the clock input of the farthest Device an optional 100 Ω and 27 pF in series to ground form an AC termination against reflections. The values are starting points that depend on clock speed, trace impedance and load.
notes: R13 and C1 are optional.

circuits.title: Half-bridge converter, no feedback regulation
circuits.description: A half-bridge converter driven by one PWM channel in push-pull mode. Two series capacitors split the DC input; two MOSFETs in series across the input are switched by PWMxH and PWMxL, and the transformer primary sits between their midpoint and the capacitor midpoint. A center-tapped secondary with two rectifier diodes feeds an LC output filter. Push-pull alternates the two switches on even and odd cycles so the core carries no DC.
notes: PWM settings for this circuit: PPM = 1 with CPOL = 0 and DPOLI = 0, or CPOL = 1 and DPOLI = 1; DTHI = 0, DTLI = 1, DTH = DTL = 0.

circuits.title: Half-bridge converter, feedback regulation
circuits.description: The same half-bridge converter with its output regulated. An error amplifier compares VOUT with VREF and, through an optocoupler for isolation, drives a PWM external trigger input PWMEXTRGx (x = 0 or 1), which with cycle-by-cycle duty mode cuts each on-pulse short once VOUT reaches VREF. The switches are driven by PWMxH and PWMxL of channel 1 or 2.
notes: PWM settings for this circuit: PPM = 1, CPOL = 1, DPOLI = 1, MODE (PWM_ETRGx) = 3, DTHI = 0, DTLI = 1, DTH = DTL = 0.

circuits.title: Power factor correction with external PWM reset mode
circuits.description: A boost power factor corrector. A diode bridge rectifies the AC line onto CIN; the inductor, the MOSFET switched by PWMH1 and the boost diode charge COUT to VOUT. In external reset mode an external circuit senses the inductor current and pulses TRGIN1 when it falls to IREF, which restarts the period.
notes: TRGEDGE (PWM_ETRG1) = 1.

circuits.title: Buck DC/DC converter with external PWM start mode
circuits.description: A buck converter: the MOSFET switched by PWMH1 connects VIN to the switching node, the diode freewheels the inductor current, and L with COUT filters VOUT. In external start mode TRGIN1 reports whether VOUT is below VREF; each period gives a fixed on-time, and a new period starts only after the minimum off-time and while VOUT is below VREF.
notes: TRGEDGE (PWM_ETRG1) = 0.

circuits.title: LED string control with cycle-by-cycle duty mode
circuits.description: A boost stage switched by PWMH0 raises VDC to VOUT. A string of three LEDs in series with an inductor runs from VOUT through a second MOSFET switched by PWMH1 and a shunt resistor to ground, with a freewheel diode from the string's low end back to VOUT. TRGIN1 pulses when the string current ILED reaches IREF; in cycle-by-cycle duty mode that ends the PWMH1 on-pulse, limiting the LED current each cycle.
notes: TRGEDGE (PWM_ETRG1) = 1.

circuits.title: Power supplies from one supply with the internal regulator
circuits.description: One main supply with a 4.7 µF bulk capacitor feeds VDDIO, VDDIN and VDDUTMII directly and VDDPLLUSB through a 2.2 Ω and 10 µH filter with 4.7 µF. The on-chip regulator output VDDOUT, held by 1 µF and 100 nF, feeds VDDCORE directly and VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC each through a 470 Ω ferrite bead. VDDIO and VDDCORE each carry five 100 nF capacitors; every other supply pin has one 100 nF to its own ground (GND, GNDANA, GNDUTMI, GNDPLL, GNDPLLUSB).
notes: Values are a typical example.
Below a 2.5V main supply neither USB nor the DACC works; from 2.5V to 3V USB does not; above 3.0 V every peripheral works.

circuits.title: Power supplies from a main supply and a separate VDDCORE supply
circuits.description: The main supply, with 4.7 µF, feeds VDDIO, VDDIN and VDDUTMII directly and VDDPLLUSB through a 2.2 Ω and 10 µH filter with 4.7 µF. A separate VDDCORE supply, with 4.7 µF, feeds VDDCORE directly and VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC each through a 470 Ω ferrite bead; the regulator output VDDOUT is left open. VDDIO and VDDCORE each carry five 100 nF capacitors and every other supply pin one 100 nF to its own ground.
notes: Values are a typical example.
Below a 3.0 V main supply USB does not work; below 2.0 V the AFE, DAC and analog comparator do not work; with the main supply and VDDIN above 3.0 V every peripheral works.

circuits.title: 3 to 20 MHz crystal
circuits.description: A 12 MHz crystal specified for a 15 pF load sits between XIN (PB9) and XOUT (PB8), with a 12 pF capacitor from each pin to the ground the part's GND pin uses. The load capacitors depend on the crystal's load capacitance. USB high- and full-speed host and device need a 12 MHz or 16 MHz clock.
notes: The crystal can be 3 MHz to 20 MHz; CLEXT follows from the crystal load capacitance.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal specified for a 7 pF load sits between XIN32 (PA7) and XOUT32 (PA8), with an 11 pF capacitor from each pin to the ground the part's GND pin uses.

circuits.title: Serial wire debug, 10-pin connector
circuits.description: A 10-pin debug header: pin 1 to VDDIO, pins 3 and 5 to ground, pin 2 SWDIO (PB6), pin 4 SWCLK (PB7), pin 6 TRACESWO (PB5) and pin 10 NRST. SWDIO, SWCLK and NRST each have a 33 kΩ pull-up to VDDIO. Pins 7, 8 and 9 are left open.
notes: Values are a typical example.

circuits.title: Serial wire debug, 20-pin connector
circuits.description: A 20-pin debug header: pins 1 and 2 to VDDIO, every even pin from 4 to 20 to ground, pin 7 SWDIO (PB6), pin 9 SWCLK (PB7), pin 13 TRACESWO (PB5) and pin 15 NRST. SWDIO, SWCLK and NRST each have a 33 kΩ pull-up to VDDIO. Pins 3, 5, 11, 17 and 19 are left open.
notes: Values are a typical example.

circuits.title: USB bias resistor on VBG
circuits.description: A 5.62 kΩ ±1% resistor and a 10 pF capacitor in parallel from VBG to GNDUTMI set the USB bias reference.

circuits.title: USB high-speed host connection
circuits.description: A type A receptacle: VBUS comes from +5V through a power switch controlled by a PIO line used as VBUS enable, D- goes to HSDM, D+ to HSDP and the GND pin to ground; the shell is the cable shield. VBG has its 5.62 kΩ ±1% and 10 pF to GNDUTMI.

parts.note: controlled by the VBUS enable line

parts.value: PIO of U1 used as VBUS enable

circuits.title: USB high-speed device connection
circuits.description: A type B receptacle: VBUS has a 1 µF to 10 µF capacitor to ground and feeds a PIO line used as VBUS detect through a 15 kΩ and 22 kΩ divider to ground; D- goes to HSDM, D+ to HSDP and the GND pin to ground; the shell is the cable shield. VBG has its 5.62 kΩ ±1% and 10 pF to GNDUTMI.

parts.value: PIO of U1 used as VBUS detect

notes: The 22 kΩ and 15 kΩ values suit PIOs supplied at 3.3V only.

circuits.title: 2 Gb 8-bit NAND Flash on the EBI
circuits.description: An 8-bit NAND Flash on the external bus: data I/O0 to I/O7 on D0 to D7 (PC0 to PC7), RE on NANDOE (PC9), WE on NANDWE (PC10), CE on NCS3/NANDCS (PC12, or any PIO), CLE on NANDCLE (PC17) and ALE on NANDALE (PC16). The ready/busy output goes to any PIO with a 47 kΩ pull-up to VDDIO, and write-protect is held high by another 47 kΩ. The memory runs from VDDIO with 100 nF, 100 nF and 1 µF to ground; its four right-side NC pins are joined to each other and the left-side NC pins are left open.

parts.value: any PIO of U1, ready/busy input

notes: U2 pins NCR1 to NCR4 are the memory's NC pins that are joined together; NC0 to NC4 and NCn stand for its open NC pins.

circuits.title: SD/MMC card socket on the HSMCI
circuits.description: An SD/MMC socket on the HSMCI: DAT0 to DAT3 on MCDA0 to MCDA3 (PA30, PA31, PA26, PA27), each with a 100 kΩ pull-up to VDDIO; CLK on MCCK (PA25); CMD on MCCDA (PA28) with a 10 kΩ pull-up. The card-detect switch goes to any PIO with a 10 kΩ pull-up and the write-protect switch has its own 10 kΩ pull-up; their common pin, VSS1, VSS2 and the shell go to ground. VDD comes from VDDIO with 100 nF and 10 µF.

parts.note: 7 DAT0, 8 DAT1, 9 DAT2, 1 DAT3, 5 CLK, 2 CMD, 4 VDD, 3 VSS1, 6 VSS2, 10 C/D, 12 W/P, 11 COM, 13-16 shell

parts.value: any PIO of U1, card detect input

circuits.title: QSPI serial Flash
circuits.description: A quad-SPI Flash on the QSPI: SI/IO0 on QIO0 (PA13), SO/IO1 on QIO1 (PA12), WP/IO2 on QIO2 (PA17), HOLD/IO3 on QIO3 (PD31), SCK on QSCK (PA14) and CS on QCS (PA11) with a 100 kΩ pull-up to VDDIO. The memory runs from VDDIO with 100 nF to ground; its exposed pad is not connected.
notes: Memory pin numbers: CS 1, SO/IO1 2, WP/IO2 3, VSS 4, SI/IO0 5, SCK 6, HOLD/IO3 7, VCC 8, pad 0.

equations.name: Minimum VDDCORE rise slope with an external core supply
equations.note: Applies when VDDCORE is not fed by the on-chip regulator; values in the DC characteristics.

equations.name: Supply monitor consumption in sampled mode
equations.expr: I(sampled) = I(continuous) / k, with k = 2, 16 or 128 for one sample every 32, 256 or 2048 slow clock periods

where.I(continuous): typical supply monitor current when always on

where.tdiv_slck: period of the divided slow clock used by the debouncing filter

equations.name: SMC read cycle
equations.expr: NRD_CYCLE = NRD_SETUP + NRD_PULSE + NRD_HOLD = NCS_RD_SETUP + NCS_RD_PULSE + NCS_RD_HOLD

where.NRD_SETUP: address valid before NRD falls, MCK cycles
where.NRD_HOLD: address held after NRD rises, MCK cycles
where.NCS_RD_SETUP, NCS_RD_PULSE, NCS_RD_HOLD: the same three times for NCS during a read

equations.note: The two hold times are not programmed; each is the cycle less its own setup and pulse.

equations.name: SMC write cycle
equations.expr: NWE_CYCLE = NWE_SETUP + NWE_PULSE + NWE_HOLD = NCS_WR_SETUP + NCS_WR_PULSE + NCS_WR_HOLD

where.NWE_SETUP: address and data valid before NWE falls, MCK cycles
where.NWE_HOLD: address and data held after NWE rises, MCK cycles
where.NCS_WR_SETUP, NCS_WR_PULSE, NCS_WR_HOLD: the same three times for NCS during a write

equations.note: The two hold times are not programmed; each is the cycle less its own setup and pulse.

operation.text: Arm Cortex-M7 at up to 300 MHz with 16 KB instruction cache and 16 KB data cache (both with ECC), a single- and double-precision FPU, a 16-zone MPU, DSP instructions and the Thumb-2 set, and an ETM with TPIU for instruction trace. Up to 2048 KB Flash with unique identifier and user signature, up to 384 KB multi-port SRAM, tightly coupled memory, a 16 KB ROM holding the UART0/USB boot loader and IAP routines, and a 16-bit static memory controller for SRAM, PSRAM, LCD modules and NOR or NAND Flash, with scrambling on the fly. An embedded regulator allows a single supply; POR, brown-out detector and two watchdogs guard operation. Clocks: a 3 to 20 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator oscillator with failure detection (12 MHz or 16 MHz is needed for USB), an optional 32.768 kHz crystal for the RTC or as device clock, a main RC oscillator defaulting to 12 MHz, a slow RC oscillator, a 500 MHz PLL for the system and a 480 MHz PLL for high-speed USB. Also an RTC with Gregorian calendar, waveform output in low-power modes and 32.768 kHz crystal calibration, a 32-bit low-power RTT, a temperature sensor and a dual-port 24-channel XDMAC. Low-power features: Sleep, Wait and Backup modes, down to 1.1 μA typical in Backup mode while the RTC, RTT and wakeup logic stay on, and 1 KB of backup RAM on its own regulator.

Ethernet MAC 10/100 (MII and RMII, own DMA, IEEE 1588 PTP, 802.3az, AVB with 802.1AS timestamping and 802.1Qav credit-based shaping); USB 2.0 high-speed device/mini host at 480 Mbps with 4 KB FIFO, up to 10 bidirectional endpoints and own DMA; a 12-bit ITU-R BT.601/656 image sensor interface; two CAN-FD controllers with SRAM mailboxes and time- or event-triggered sending; a MediaLB device (3-wire, up to 1024 x Fs, MOST25 and MOST50); three USARTs with LIN, ISO7816, IrDA, RS-485, SPI, Manchester and modem modes (LON on USART1); five 2-wire UARTs and three TWIHS (I2C) with SleepWalking; a QSPI for up to 512 MB of Flash with execute-in-place and scrambling; two SPIs; an SSC with I2S and TDM; two I2SC; an HSMCI for SDIO, SD card and e.MMC; four 3-channel 16-bit timer/counters with capture, waveform, compare, PWM, quadrature decoder and 2-bit Gray counter; two PWM controllers of four 16-bit channels each with complementary outputs, dead-time generation and eight fault inputs. Analog: two AFECs of up to 12 channels each with differential inputs, programmable gain, dual sample-and-hold up to 1.7 Msps and offset/gain correction; a 2-channel 12-bit DAC at 1 Msps per channel; an analog comparator with selectable hysteresis. Security: TRNG, AES (128/192/256-bit keys, FIPS PUB-197) and an integrity check monitor with SHA1, SHA224 and SHA256. Up to 114 I/O lines on five PIO controllers, each with edge or level interrupt, debouncing, glitch filter and on-die series termination. Supply: 3.0 V to 3.6 V for the AEC-Q100 Grade 2 devices, 1.7 V to 3.6 V for the industrial devices.
The SAM V70 and V71 are made to ISO-TS-16949 and qualified to AEC-Q100 Grade 2, -40 °C to +105 °C (temperature identifier B).
The 100-ball TFBGA has a 0.8 mm ball pitch and measures 9 x 9 x 1.1 mm; the 100-ball VFBGA has a 0.65 mm pitch and measures 7 x 7 x 1.0 mm. Both are Green parts.

VDDIN and VDDIO must be at the same level and never below VDDCORE. VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC must stay within 0.6 V of one another. USB needs VDDUTMII, VDDPLLUSB, VDDIN and VDDIO at 3.0 V or more. Breaking these rules gives unpredictable behaviour.

VDDIO and VDDIN rise together and ahead of VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC; the on-chip regulator meets this by itself. With an external core supply, VDDCORE may reach VDDCOREmin only after VDDIO and VDDIN are at their own minimum operating level, and VDDCORE must rise at least as fast as the slope given below. If VDDCORE rises together with VDDIO and VDDIN, the DC characteristics' minimum and maximum slopes for VDDIO and VDDIN apply. VREFP must rise together with VDDIO and VDDIN, or an overcurrent can flow.

With the core rails not fed by the on-chip regulator, VDDIO, VDDIN, VDDPLLUSB and VDDUTMII fall together and ahead of VDDCORE, VDDPLL and VDDUTMIC. VDDCORE must not fall faster than 20 V/ms. VREFP must fall together with VDDIO and VDDIN to avoid an overcurrent.

operation.topic: Voltage regulator and backup SRAM switch
operation.text: The embedded regulator is controlled by the supply controller; its decoupling is given in the DC characteristics. A power switch feeds the 1 KB backup SRAM: while VDDCORE is on, the backup SRAM runs from VDDCORE; when VDDCORE is off the switch keeps it powered so it holds its contents. The switch is on by default once VDDIO is up; clearing SRAMON in SUPC_MR turns it off to save current.

The normal running mode: the core clock comes from PLLA, the main crystal oscillator or the fast RC oscillator, and the PMC sets core, bus and peripheral clock frequencies and gates each peripheral clock.

The lowest-power mode, meant for systems that wake periodically and do not need a fast start. Only the SUPC, the zero-power POR, the RTC and RTT, the backup SRAM and backup registers, and the 32 kHz oscillator (RC or crystal, chosen in the supply controller) keep running; the regulator and core supply are off. It is the Cortex-M7 Deep-sleep mode with the regulator disabled: set SLEEPDEEP in the processor, then set VROFF in SUPC_CR. Exit is on an enabled event: a level change on WKUP0 to WKUP13 (with configurable debouncing), a supply monitor alarm, an RTC alarm or an RTT alarm. If PLLA runs from the main crystal oscillator as MAINCK source, before entering Backup mode switch MAINCK to SLCK with PMC_MCKR.CSS, stop PLLA (MUL = 0 or DIV = 0), stop the main crystal oscillator and wait some milliseconds.

Very low power with the whole device still powered and a restart in under 10 μs: the core, peripheral and memory clocks stop while their supplies stay on. Entered by setting WAITMODE in CKGR_MOR with FLPM in PMC_FSMR at 00 or 01. Wake sources are WKUP0 to WKUP13 set as fast-startup inputs, RTC or RTT alarms, USB wake-up events, and a debug request with CDBGPWRUPREQ set. Sequence, with the main RC oscillator as main clock: set FLPM in PMC_FSMR, set the Flash wait states to 0, set HCLK = MCK (MDIV = 0 in PMC_MCKR), set WAITMODE in CKGR_MOR, then wait for MCKRDY = 1 in PMC_SR. Some resynchronization cycles pass between the MOSCRCEN write and the entry into Wait mode; waiting for MOSCRCEN to clear keeps the core from running unwanted instructions.
Only the core clock stops; peripheral clocks may run, so the current depends on the application. Entered with the WFI instruction and left on an interrupt.

A wake event out of Backup mode makes the supply controller turn the core supply and the SRAM supply back on if they are off. From Wait or Sleep mode the processor restarts within a few microseconds on a low level of any of: WKUP0 to WKUP13, the supply monitor, an RTC alarm, an RTT alarm, the USBHS interrupt line (WAKEUP), a processor debug request (CDBGPWRUPREQ) or a GMAC wake-on-LAN event; a CAN wake needs one of the WKUP0 to WKUP13 pins. The fast restart logic is fully asynchronous: it signals the PMC, which restarts the main RC oscillator, puts the host clock on it and re-enables the processor clock.

PIO controllers manage the GPIO lines; every line has pull-up or pull-down, Schmitt trigger input, multi-drive (open drain), glitch filter, debouncing and input-change interrupt, set line by line. The PIO buffers are supplied from VDDIO. High-speed pads carry the HSMCI, SPI and QSPI clocks up to MCK/2. The pull-up and pull-down are 100 kΩ typical on every I/O. Each line has an on-die series resistor RSERIAL between a driver of about 10 Ω output impedance and a PCB trace of about 50 Ω (Z0 ~ ZOUT + RODT); it matches the trace, lowers switching di/dt and EMI, and reduces overshoot and ringing.

Oscillator, test, reset, debug and erase pins shared with PIO lines can be set by software as general-purpose I/Os or as system pins; after start-up each is in its system function. SWCLK and SWDIO come up in SW-DP mode for a debug probe and can be freed as general I/Os through the matrix registers (CCFG_SYSIO); pull-up, triggers, debouncing and glitch filters work in either mode. JTAG TDI, TDO, TMS and TCK serve boundary-scan manufacturing test only. The ETM exports trace through the TPIU: TRACECLK always runs so the data can be synchronized, TRACED0 to TRACED3 carry the instruction trace.

NRST is bidirectional and handled by the reset controller: it can drive a reset out to external parts, and a low applied from outside resets the microcontroller. It resets the core and peripherals but not the backup area (RTC, RTT, backup SRAM, supply controller). It has a permanent pull-up of about 100 kΩ to VDDIO and is an input by default.

A high on ERASE erases the whole Flash and then the NVM bits (GPNVM, lock and security bits). It has a pull-down of about 100 kΩ to GND, so it may be left open. It is a system I/O usable as a standard I/O, in the ERASE function at start-up, debounced by SLCK, and must be held for a minimum assertion time (in the electrical characteristics) to act. Erase is not possible in Wait mode. Used as a PIO input, the pin must be low at start-up until software has reconfigured it; driving it low as an output does not erase the Flash. To recover a device locked up by software (wrong clock switching, the pin used as I/O, Wait mode without wake events): hold ERASE at 1, hold NRST at 0, cycle the power, then release NRST and keep ERASE at 1 for no less than the minimum assertion time.

The Cortex-M7 is joined to the AHB bus matrix, to the ROM, to the Flash and to the multi-port SRAM. AHBP is a 32-bit port for data access to peripherals on the matrix, never for instruction fetch; the AHBP control register chooses AHBP or AXIM for the peripheral region 0x40000000 to 0x60000000. Peripheral accesses through AHBP need a core-to-bus frequency ratio of 1 or 1/2. AHBS is a 32-bit port giving system masters (the XDMA) access to the ITCM, D1TCM and D0TCM; DMA access through AHBS should use a ratio of 1. AXIM is a 64-bit port reaching the matrix and two SRAM ports through the AXI bridge, used for instruction fetch, data cache line fills and evictions, non-cacheable normal memory accesses, and device or strongly-ordered accesses. The bus matrix runs at up to 150 MHz.

384 KB or 256 KB of SRAM at 0x20400000, a four-port interleaved multi-port SRAM: two ports serve the Cortex-M7 and two are shared by the AHB masters. The bus matrix priority of each request (normal, bandwidth-sensitive, latency-sensitive, latency-critical) is passed to the SRAM, which serves the most urgent request first and the other no later than the next cycle. TCM runs at processor speed: ITCM is one 64-bit interface at 0x00000000, DTCM two interleaved 32-bit interfaces at 0x20000000. They are enabled in the ITCMR and DTCMR registers of the Arm SCB; DTCM is on and ITCM off after reset. GPNVM bits 8:7 choose one of four TCM sizes, taken from the SRAM. An enabled ITCM overlays the ROM or Flash at 0x0 (per GPNVM bit 1). Accesses to a disabled TCM region, or above the TCM size, go to the AHB matrix (Flash or ROM per the remap bit); SRAM accesses above the size limit do not abort, and the MPU can protect those areas.
The ROM holds SAM-BA, the IAP functions and the FFPI. It is always at 0x00800000 and may also appear at 0x00000000 depending on the GPNVM setting and ITCM use.
1 KB at 0x40074000, 32-bit word access only. Supplied by VDDCORE in normal operation; in Backup mode the power switch moves it to VDDIO when VDDCORE falls.

Internal Flash of 512, 1024 or 2048 KB at 0x00400000; the QSPI maps external SPI or QSPI Flash at 0x80000000. For programming by the Cortex-M7, the QSPI and internal Flash regions must be marked Device or Strongly Ordered in the MPU; for fetch and read, Normal memory, so the cache is used. DMA accesses need care (see the EEFC and QSPI).

The Flash is built of 128 KB sectors of 512-byte pages; sector 0 is split into two 8 KB small sectors of 16 pages and one 112 KB sector of 224 pages, the others have 256 pages. Erase is possible for the whole chip, by 8 KB block, by 128 KB sector, or by 512-byte page; page erase and the EWP and EWPL commands work only in the 8 KB sectors. One extra page serves as the user signature, reached through dedicated modes for erase, write and read; ERASE does not clear it.

operation.topic: Flash controller, wait states and lock regions
operation.text: The EEFC serves reads by the system masters and writes into the write buffer, carries a user interface on the APB, and runs the program, erase, lock and unlock sequences through a command set; one command returns a descriptor of the Flash organization. The number of wait states is set to suit the system frequency (embedded Flash characteristics). Lock bits each guard a 16 KB lock region against write and erase; asserting ERASE clears all lock bits.

GPNVM bit 0 is the security bit. When set, SW-DP, ETM and FFPI can no longer reach the Flash, SRAM, core registers or peripherals. It is set only with the EEFC command Set General-purpose NVM Bit 0 and cleared only by asserting ERASE high, which first erases the full Flash.

The unique identifier is 2 read-only pages of 512 bytes that even ERASE cannot clear: bytes 0 to 15 hold the 128-bit identifier, bytes 16 to 1023 are reserved. The 512-byte user signature can be read, written and erased by the user and survives both the ERASE pin and the software erase command; it suits trimming values and keys.

The FFPI loads the device over a multiplexed parallel port with full handshake, for gang programming on industrial programmers; its commands cover reading, programming or erasing a page, erasing everything, locking, unlocking and protecting. Fast Programming mode is entered with TST, PA3 and PA4 tied low.

SAM-BA is the default boot program for in-system programming of the Flash, over UART0 or USB, talking to the SAM-BA host application; it runs from ROM at 0x0 while GPNVM1 is 0. Nine GPNVM bits are set and cleared with the EEFC commands Set GPNVM Bit and Clear GPNVM Bit; bit 0 is the security bit, bit 1 picks ROM or Flash at boot.

The device always boots at address 0x0. Setting GPNVM1 boots from the Flash, clearing it from the ROM; asserting ERASE clears GPNVM1 and so returns to ROM boot. One external bus interface connects external memories and parallel peripherals.

Peripheral events reach other peripherals directly without the processor; the destination chooses its trigger source. Timers, PWM, I/Os and peripherals trigger the AFEC or DACC; the DMA controller takes triggers from the serial ports (UART, USART, QSPI, SPI, TWI), from the PWM, HSMCI, AES, AFEC and DACC, from TC capture and from the PIO; the PIO parallel capture logic triggers DMA for data capture; PWM fault events from the AFEC, ACC, PMC and TC are combinational; PWM comparator outputs (OCx) feed the TC; the PMC clock-failure event can switch MCK to the main RC oscillator by itself.

operation.topic: Power-on reset, brown-out detector and supply monitor
operation.text: Power-on reset cells watch VDDIO and VDDCORE, always on, at start-up and power-down; either rail below its threshold resets the whole chip. The brown-out detector watches VDDCORE, is on by default, can be turned off in SUPC_MR (advised in Wait and Sleep modes), and resets the core when VDDCORE drops below its threshold. The supply monitor watches VDDIO, is off by default, has 16 programmable thresholds from 1.6 V to 3.4 V, and a sampled mode that divides its consumption by up to 2048; the SUPC manages it.

Built on the two POR cells (VDDIO and VDDCORE) and the VDDIO supply monitor, it reports the last reset source to software: general, wakeup, software, user or watchdog reset. It drives the internal resets and the NRST pin, and can shape a reset for external devices, so a push-button on NRST gives a manual reset. Its configuration is kept in the VDDIO domain.

Two PIO controllers on the 64-pin versions (PIOA, PIOB), three on the 100-pin version (PIOA, PIOB, PIOD), five on the 144-pin version (PIOA to PIOE). A controller handles as many as 32 lines; any line may be handed to peripheral function A, B, C or D.

SW-DP for standard debugging (code download, single step) with serial wire trace; debug access to all memory and registers, including the Cortex-M register bank, while the core runs, is halted or held in reset; SW-DP is ADIv5.1 without multidrop. Also an FPB for breakpoints and code patches, a DWT for watchpoints, data tracing and profiling, an ITM for printf-style debug, a 6-pin ETM for instruction trace with a CoreSight TPIU, and IEEE 1149.1 JTAG boundary scan on all digital pins.
TST puts the device into boundary-scan production test or into fast Flash programming. A permanent pull-down of about 15 kΩ to GND lets it be left open in normal use.

JTAGSEL high selects JTAG boundary scan; low selects SW-DP. It has a permanent pull-down of about 15 kΩ to GND and may be left open. Changing between SW-DP and boundary scan needs a chip reset after JTAGSEL changes. SW-DP is active by default and TDO/TRACESWO can carry trace. TRACECLK is generated internally from PCK3.

The FPB provides hardware breakpoints. The DWT has four comparators that can emit periodic PC samples, packets on a PC or data watchpoint match, or halt the core on a watchpoint; it counts clock cycles (CYCCNT), folded instructions, load-store unit operations, sleep cycles, CPI (all instruction cycles but the first) and interrupt overhead. The ITM traces operating-system and application events as packets from software (writes to its stimulus registers), from the DWT, and as timestamps from a 21-bit counter.

In asynchronous mode the TPIU sends trace on the single TRACESWO pin, shared with TDO, so it needs Serial Wire Debug mode. Output encoding is Manchester (reset value) or NRZ UART bytes. ITM setup: write 0xC5ACCE55 to the lock access register at 0xE0000FB0, write 0x00010015 to the trace control register (ITM on, synchronization packets, SWO, ATB ID 1), write 0x1 to the trace enable register (stimulus port 0) and 0x1 to the trace privilege register, then write data to stimulus port 0. TPIU setup: set TRCENA in the debug exception and monitor register (0xE000EDFC), write 0x2 to the selected pin protocol register (serial wire output, NRZ), 0x100 to the formatter and flush control register, and a prescaler to the async clock prescaler register for the baud rate.

Boundary scan is on when TST is high, PD0 low and JTAGSEL high during power-up, and these levels are held for the whole scan. SAMPLE, EXTEST and BYPASS are implemented; each pin has a 3-bit cell (output, input, control). In Serial Wire Debug mode the processor returns a non-JTAG chip ID, which is not IEEE 1149.1 compliant. A BSDL file is available for download. The JTAG ID code reads 0x5B3D_D03F: version 0x0, part number 0x5B3D, manufacturer identity 0x01F, bit 0 set to 1.

SAM-BA serves UART0 and USB device (up to 1 MB/s) and uses the first 2048 bytes of SRAM for variables and stacks. USB needs an external crystal or clock of 12 MHz or 16 MHz; an external clock must be within 2500 ppm and a VDDIO square wave. UART0 needs nothing more: the internal 12 MHz RC meets RS-232 at room temperature. At start the program looks for a clock from the main oscillator with a crystal or on XIN in bypass; a supported frequency enables USB, otherwise the 12 MHz RC oscillator is used and USB stays off because of its drift. It then waits for USB enumeration or a '#' on UART0 and runs the monitor on the interface that answered.

Stack setup; Flash controller setup; detection of an external crystal or clock on XIN; USB allowed only with a supported frequency, otherwise the internal 12 MHz RC oscillator; host clock switched to the main oscillator; C variables initialized; PLLA set for 48 MHz; watchdog disabled; UART0 at 115200 baud, 8, N, 1; USB device port initialized when allowed; wait for USB enumeration or UART0 characters; jump to the monitor, which loops on commands.

UART0 runs at 115200 baud, 8, n, 1. Send File and Receive File use Xmodem with 128-byte blocks and a two-byte CRC-16. A block is SOH (0x01), the block number (from 01, wrapping from 0xFF to 0x00), its one's complement, 128 data bytes and the CRC. The file must be smaller than the SRAM, since Xmodem needs SRAM to run.

The device enumerates as a USB CDC class device (virtual COM port) with vendor ID 0x03EB and product ID 0x6124. Endpoint 0 handles enumeration, endpoint 1 is a 64-byte bulk OUT endpoint that carries commands, endpoint 2 a 64-byte bulk IN endpoint for responses.

A ROM function, entered through the address held in the ROM NMI vector at 0x00800008, passes a command to the EEFC, polls FRDY in the Flash status register, so code running in Flash can program the Flash. It takes the Flash bank index (0 for EEFC0, 1 for EEFC1; either value reaches EEFC0 on single-bank devices) and the command word for the EEFC command register (key 0x5A in bits 31:24, page number from bit 8, command code), and returns EEFC_FSR.

Fast Flash programming is a test mode for high-volume programming with a gang programmer, not for in-situ programming; the device looks like a standard EEPROM behind a 16-bit fully handshaked parallel port. It gives read and write access to the Flash plane, controls lock and GPNVM bits and can set the security bit; once that bit is set the FFPI is disabled. Only the FFPI pins matter; other PIOs are inputs with pull-up. The crystal oscillator runs in bypass and an external clock must drive XIN.

To enter: apply the supplies, apply a clock on XIN within the VDDCORE POR reset time-out, wait for the reset period to end, then start a read or write handshake. With RDY high, the programmer starts a handshake by pulling NCMD low; it ends when NCMD and RDY are both high again. The data latched depends on MODE (command, address bytes or data).

A new command completes the previous one, so a read after a write flushes the load buffer. Reads and writes chain with an automatically incrementing address. The one-page load buffer is written to the Flash before an access to another page or when MODE = CMDE validates the next command; an extra WP is needed for a partial page or a write from a non-zero page offset. WPL locks the region after writing (use it for the last page of a region), EWP erases first, EWPL does both. Full erase needs every lock region unlocked with CLB first, or it is aborted and nothing is erased. SLB and CLB take a bit mask (bit 0 = first lock bit); SGPB and CGPB a GPNVM bit pattern. With the security bit set (SSE) no FFPI command runs; to clear it: power off, power on with TST = 0, assert ERASE for at least the ERASE assertion time, power off. WRAM writes any memory location. GVE returns 0x29.

A multi-layer AHB-Lite matrix linking 13 hosts to 9 clients, with an APB user interface. A host reaches a client in one cycle, or zero cycles when it is that client's default host. One decoder and one remap function per host, several boot memories per host before remap, bursts of 32, 64, 128 and up to the 256-beat AHB limit, round-robin or fixed-priority arbitration per client, a programmable default host per client (none, last access, fixed), deterministic worst-case latency, zero or one cycle arbitration latency on a burst's first access, bus-lock and host-number forwarding, automatic clock-off and register write protection. All hosts share the same address decoding.

operation.topic: Bus matrix default host and arbitration
operation.text: MATRIX_MRCR remaps each host. Each client's MATRIX_SCFG sets the default host type (DEFMSTR_TYPE: none, last access, fixed) and the fixed host (FIXED_DEFMSTR). No default host costs one cycle on the first access after idle; a last access or fixed default host removes it for that host. Arbitration happens on idle cycles, single cycles, end of burst and at the slot cycle limit. Undefined-length bursts can be cut at 1, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 beats or left unlimited (ULBT in MATRIX_MCFG; default unlimited, which is also best for power; 16 beats or fewer lowers bandwidth). SLOT_CYCLE in MATRIX_SCFG breaks long accesses on slow clients; 0 disables it, which is advised in most cases. Priority pools: round-robin in the highest and lowest pools, fixed priority between pools and in the middle ones (MxPR in MATRIX_PRAS and MATRIX_PRBS); after reset every host but the Cortex-M7 is in the lowest pool. No host gets two consecutive grants while another host is waiting.

CCFG_SYSIO switches lines between system I/O mode (JTAG, ERASE, USB and so on) and general-purpose I/O; PIO_PER and PIO_PDR do not change this, but direction, pulls and other modes stay with the PIO controller. CCFG_SMCNFCS assigns each NCSx to NAND Flash, which then uses NANDOE and NANDWE. CCFG_DYNCKG enables automatic clock gating of the matrix, bridge and EFC (MATCKG, BRIDCKG, EFCCKG). Setting WPEN in MATRIX_WPMR write-protects the host and client configuration, priority and remap registers; a blocked write sets WPVS and records the register in WPVSRC.
The UTMI registers (32-bit) control product-specific behaviour of the integrated USB transceiver macrocell not covered by the USB controller.

Two read-only hard-wired registers identify the device. CHIPID_CIDR gives the silicon revision (VERSION), the processor (EPROC), the type and size of non-volatile memory (NVPTYP, NVPSIZ), the SRAM size (SRAMSIZ), the peripheral set (ARCH) and whether the extension register is used (EXT). CHIPID_EXID reads 0 when EXT = 0.

The EEFC links the Flash to the 32-bit internal bus through a 128-bit memory interface, for performance in Thumb-2 up to 150 MHz, with code loop optimization, 128 lock bits, 9 GPNVM bits, keyword-protected commands, erase of the whole Flash, by sector or by page, the unique identifier, a 512-byte user signature, erase before programming, ECC single and multiple error flags, read of the calibration bits and register write protection. It is always clocked (the PMC has no effect on it); its interrupt fires only when EEFC_FMR.FRDY is 1.

One code plane of equal-size pages; a separate 2 x 512-byte area holding the unique ID; a separate 512-byte user signature area; two 128-bit read buffers for code and one for data; a write buffer the size of a page, write-only and mapped across the whole Flash address space so each word is written at its final address; lock bits over multi-page lock regions; and GPNVM bits. Size, page size, lock regions and GPNVM bits are given by the Get Flash Descriptor command.

8-, 16- and 32-bit reads are allowed. The Flash repeats through the reserved internal memory area. Wait states are set in FWS of EEFC_FMR; FWS = 0 gives single-cycle access. Sequential code fetch uses 2 x 128-bit buffers (on by default, off when SCOD is set); with FWS from 1 to 3 the first sequential access takes FWS + 1 cycles and the next ones one cycle. Loop optimization (CLOE set, on by default) caches the first two 128-bit words at a backward branch target in 2 x 128-bit buffers so whole loops run without wait states. A 128-bit data read buffer speeds sequential data reads (on by default, off when SCOD is set).

A command is written to FCMD in EEFC_FCR with the key in the top eight bits; this clears FRDY and FVALUE in EEFC_FRR, and FRDY sets again when the command ends (except after STUI), raising the interrupt if enabled. A wrong key or an invalid command does nothing and sets FCMDE; a write or erase in a locked region does nothing and sets FLOCKE; both flags clear when EEFC_FSR is read. Get Flash Descriptor returns 7 words read one after the other from EEFC_FRR; all lock regions are the same size.

Only zeros are programmed; 1 is the erased state, so each page needs an erase before it is written (EWP and EWPL erase automatically). Data go first into the latch buffer, mapped over the Flash space, with 32-bit word writes only, in continuous ascending or descending order and at the Flash read wait states; DMA writes must be 32-bit aligned, with unused bytes of a word written as ones. The buffer refills with ones after each command. Sequence: fill the latch buffer, write the command to EEFC_FCR (FRDY clears), wait for FRDY. Errors: FCMDE (bad key), FLOCKE (locked region), FLERR (write-verify failed after the maximum number of programming pulses). One page at a time; no Flash access until FRDY rises. Full page: erase, then fill the buffer from the first address of that page in ascending order. Partial page: whole 128-bit aligned words over erased bits only; a single 128-bit word programs faster. A single byte needs its own 128-bit area.

Erase works only on unlocked regions. EA erases everything (no code fetch from Flash meanwhile). EPA erases 4, 8, 16 or 32 pages, with the first page number in FARG[15:2] a multiple of 8, 16 or 32 and the count in FARG[1:0]. ES erases the sector holding page number FARG. If any sub-sector of sector 0 is locked, ES on sector 0 is refused: clear all sector 0 lock bits first and restore them after. Code fetched from Flash during EPA or ES stalls until the command ends; running from SRAM avoids this. Errors are FCMDE, FLOCKE (nothing erased) and FLERR (erase-verify failed).

SLB with a page number in FARG locks the region holding it, CLB unlocks it; FARG must not exceed the highest lock bit index. GLB returns the lock bits in EEFC_FRR, 32 per read, extra reads return 0. Flash reads remain allowed during SLB, CLB and GLB.

SGPB and CGPB with the bit number in FARG set or clear a GPNVM bit; GGPB returns them in EEFC_FRR, 32 per read. A FARG above the highest GPNVM index leaves the Flash untouched; a command error is flagged only when FARG is greater than 8. Flash reads remain allowed during these commands.

The calibration bits are read-only and separate from the code plane; GCALB returns them in EEFC_FRR, 32 per read. The 8 MHz and 12 MHz settings of the internal RC oscillator are calibrated in production; the 4 MHz setting is fixed at 1000000.

operation.topic: Security bit, unique ID and user signature access
operation.text: With the security bit (GPNVM0) set, the ETM is off and Flash access through SWD and FFPI is forbidden; only ERASE high, with a full Flash erase, clears it. Unique ID: STUI, wait for FRDY to fall, read the 128 bits at the start of the Flash mapping, then SPUI (FRDY rises when done). User signature: STUS, wait for FRDY to fall, read the first 512 bytes of the Flash mapping, then SPUS; to write it, fill a full page at any page address and issue WUS; EUS erases it. No code can be fetched from the Flash during these read sequences.

ECC corrects a single error and detects two errors per read, with separate flags for the lower and upper 64 bits of each Flash word, held in EEFC_FSR until it is read. Because of prefetch, a reported error may belong to the next sequential Flash word. The error location is not stored, so a background check must rewrite all Flash code; a check right after programming a page (a data read, not optimized) needs only that page reprogrammed. Setting WPEN in EEFC_WPMR write-protects EEFC_FMR.

The SUPC controls the core supply through the embedded regulator, manages Backup mode (a few microamps), resets the core on a supply monitor detection on VDDIO or a brown-out on VDDCORE, derives the slow clock SLCK from either the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator or the 22-42 kHz slow RC oscillator, holds the backup SRAM, offers low-power tamper detection on two inputs that can wipe the general-purpose backup registers at once, and wakes from Backup mode on 14 debounced wakeup inputs, the RTC alarm, the RTT alarm or a supply monitor detection with programmable period and threshold.

The VDDIO domain holds the SUPC, a portion of the reset controller, the slow clock selector, the backup registers, the supply monitor, the RTT and the RTC. The core domain holds the rest of the reset controller, the brown-out detector, the processor, SRAM, Flash and peripherals. A zero-power POR lets the SUPC start as soon as VDDIO is valid; once the slow RC oscillator is stable the SUPC turns on the regulator, waits for a valid VDDCORE and releases vddcore_nreset. Software should then enable the supply monitor and/or brown-out detector, which hold the core in reset while their rail is low. Backup mode asserts vddcore_nreset and stops the regulator; leaving it follows the start-up path.

Supplied from VDDIO. When VDDIO comes up, the crystal oscillator and the RC oscillator both receive power but only the RC runs; it settles faster, the crystal is more accurate. Setting XTALSEL in SUPC_CR switches to the crystal: the XIN32/XOUT32 PIO lines go to the oscillator, the crystal oscillator starts, a count of RC periods covers its start-up time, the slow clock switches glitch-free to the crystal and the RC stops; OSCSEL in SUPC_SR shows when this is done. Returning to the RC needs VDDIO to be removed. Leave XIN32 and XOUT32 open if the crystal is not used. For an external clock on XIN32 (bypass), set OSCBYPASS in SUPC_MR before XTALSEL.

The regulator adjusts its quiescent current to the load. Writing 1 to SUPC_CR.VROFF enters Backup mode: vddcore_nreset asserts after up to two slow clock cycles of resynchronization, and processor and peripherals stop one slow clock cycle before the core supply goes off. With VDDCORE from an external supply, writing 0 to SUPC_MR.ONREG disables the regulator.

operation.topic: Backup supply schemes and supply limits
operation.text: With a backup battery or separate backup supply, only VDDIO is present in Backup mode. Without one, VDDIO stays up so all I/O settings (WKUP pins) hold in Backup mode, and VDDIORDY is set so it need not be programmed. With a separate core supply: USB needs a main supply of 3.0 V or more, MediaLB 2.7 V or more, the ADC, DAC and analog comparator 2.0 V or more; with main supply and VDDIN above 3 V everything works. With one main supply: below 2.0 V neither USB nor the ADC, DAC and comparator work; between 2.0 V and 3 V USB does not; below 2.7 V MediaLB does not; above 3 V everything works.

Since PIO states hold in Backup mode, a free PIO line driven low can switch off the external regulator (after a backup reset the PIO is an input with pull-up), and a WKUPx pin wakes the system. Two diodes form the switchover: in Backup mode the VDDIO domain runs from the battery, otherwise from the main supply.

Off by default. Its threshold is set in SMTH of SUPC_SMMR (values in the electrical characteristics). SMSMPL in SUPC_SMMR runs it continuously or for one slow clock period every 32, 256 or 2048 periods, dividing its typical consumption by 2, 16 or 128. A detection resets the core (SMRSTEN in SUPC_SMMR) or wakes the core supply (SMEN in SUPC_WUMR). SMOS in SUPC_SR is the live result; SMS latches a detection until SUPC_SR is next read and raises an interrupt when SMIEN is set.

As VDDIO rises, the slow RC oscillator powers up and the zero-power POR holds the SUPC in reset until VDDIO is valid. Then five slow clock cycles let the RC settle (seven in all with two of synchronization), the regulator turns on, and once the brown-out detector reports VDDCORE valid (bodcore_in) for at least one slow clock cycle, vddcore_nreset is released. After further slow clock cycles (3, 2 and 6.5, with the reset controller's ERSTL default of 2) periph_nreset and proc_nreset rise and the core starts fetching from the Flash.

Besides start-up and Backup mode, vddcore_nreset is asserted by a supply monitor detection when SMRSTEN in SUPC_SMMR is set (at once, for at least one slow clock cycle), and by loss of bodcore_in for more than one slow clock period while the regulator runs, when SUPC_MR.BODRSTEN is set: held at least one slow clock cycle and until bodcore_in returns. SUPC_SR.BODRSTS records a brown-out reset.

SUPC_MR.BKUPRETON sets whether the backup SRAM stays powered (1) or is switched off (0) in Backup mode; the write acts only at the next Backup entry. The SRAM is always powered while the core supply is on, and comes back on when Backup mode ends.

Each WKUPx is enabled by WKUPENx and given its active level by WKUPTx in SUPC_WUIR. The enabled inputs are wired-ORed into one debounce counter set by WKUPDBC in SUPC_WUMR; 0 means an input must be active for at least one slow clock period. An input held longer than the debounce time starts the core supply and its state is latched in SUPC_SR, which tells the wake source; a later wake condition overwrites it. With WKUPDBC above 0, no enabled WKUPx may be at its active level when Backup mode is entered: check the pins in the PIO controller first.

WKUP0 and WKUP1 have their own low-power debouncers for tamper switches. To avoid a steady current through a closed switch, the sensor bias can be pulsed by RTCOUTx (a programmable duty-cycle pulse, OUT0 = 0x7 in RTC_MR), in any mode including Backup; the falling edge of RTCOUTx is the sample point. LPDBCEN0/1 in SUPC_WUMR make a tamper detection wake the system, also usable with VDDCORE on; WKUPENx must then be cleared in SUPC_WUIR. One period applies to both debouncers: LPDBC in SUPC_WUMR sets 2 to 8 identical samples, RTC_MR.TPERIOD the time between samples, RTC_MR.THIGH the pulse width; WKUPT0 and WKUPT1 in SUPC_WUMR set each polarity, and status flags in SUPC_SR tell which input fired. With LPDBCCLR set, a detection clears the first half of the GPBR at once. RTCOUTx is optional: without it the RTC still has to make an internal sample point (TPERIOD).

operation.topic: Clock alarm and supply monitor wakeup
operation.text: RTCEN and RTTEN in SUPC_WUMR let the RTC and RTT alarms wake the core supply; their status is in the RTC and RTT, not in the SUPC. The supply monitor can also wake the core supply.

operation.topic: SYSC write protection and backup-domain registers
operation.text: Setting WPEN in SYSC_WPMR write-protects the RSTC mode register, the RTT mode and alarm registers, the RTC control, mode, time alarm and calendar alarm registers, the general-purpose backup registers, and the SUPC control, supply monitor mode, mode and wakeup mode registers. Registers held in the VDDIO backup domain: all bits of the RSTC mode, RTT mode and alarm, RTC control, mode, time alarm and calendar alarm registers, the GPBR, the SUPC supply monitor mode, wakeup mode, wakeup inputs and status registers, and some bits of the SUPC control and mode registers.

A 12-bit down counter clocked from the slow clock divided by 128, so its longest period is 16 s with a 32.768 kHz slow clock. Its clock does not depend on the processor clock. On underflow or error it can raise an interrupt or cause a general or processor-only reset, and its counting can be halted while the core is in debug state or in Idle (Sleep) mode. It runs from VDDCORE and returns to its initial values on a processor reset.

The counter loads from WDT_MR.WDV. Out of processor reset WDV is 0xFFF with WDRSTEN set (after a backup reset), so the watchdog runs at its maximum period from power-up; software either disables it with WDT_MR.WDDIS or programs the period it needs. WDT_MR can be written once only and only a processor reset clears it; writing it reloads and restarts the counter. WDV and WDD are not to be changed while WDDIS is being set or is set. After a restart through WDT_CR, WDT_MR is not to be written for three slow clock periods. Software restarts the counter by writing WDT_CR.WDRSTT with the key; a write without the key does nothing. The restart reloads from WDT_MR and resets the divide-by-128 prescaler. A restart is allowed only while the counter is between 0 and WDT_MR.WDD; a restart while it is between WDV and WDD is a watchdog error (WDT_SR.WDERR), even with the watchdog disabled, and asserts wdt_fault. Setting WDD greater than or equal to WDV removes the window, which is the reset default (WDD = WDV). An underflow sets WDT_SR.WDUNF and, with WDRSTEN set, asserts wdt_fault to the reset controller, which resets the processor and the WDT and clears both flags. WDUNF and WDERR raise an interrupt when WDFIEN is set. Reading WDT_SR or any reset clears the flags and the interrupt and releases wdt_fault. WDIDLEHLT and WDDBGHLT stop the counter in Sleep and debug states.

A second 12-bit watchdog that runs alongside the WDT and independently of it, with the same maximum period of 16 s at a 32.768 kHz slow clock and the same reset, interrupt and halt-in-debug or Idle options. Its clock is chosen automatically: the slow RC oscillator, or the main RC oscillator divided down to an equivalent slow clock. The divided main RC clock is used when the main RC oscillator is already on (CKGR_MOR.MOSCRCEN = 1) or when the WDT runs from the slow RC oscillator, so a failure of the WDT's clock (for example the 32 kHz crystal) does not leave the system unwatched. Its fault output is ORed with the WDT fault into the reset controller.

Powered from VDDCORE. It is disabled after any power-on sequence and comes out of processor reset at default values. It is not to be enabled while the WDT is disabled. The counter loads from RSWDT_MR.WDV, 0xFFF after a processor reset with WDRSTEN set after a backup reset. RSWDT_MR accepts a single write, cleared again by a processor reset alone, and writing it reloads and restarts the counter; it is not to be written for three slow clock periods after a restart through RSWDT_CR. A restart by RSWDT_CR.WDRSTT with the key reloads the counter and resets the divide-by-128 prescaler. Underflow sets RSWDT_SR.WDUNF and asserts the fault when WDRSTEN is set; WDUNF and WDERR interrupt when WDFIEN is set; reading RSWDT_SR or a reset clears them. WDIDLEHLT and WDDBGHLT halt it in Idle and debug states.

Handles every reset without external parts: the power-on reset cells, software, the NRST pin and the watchdogs. It runs from the slow clock and drives three outputs: the processor reset (which also resets the WDT), the peripheral reset, both driven the same way, and nrst_out, which pulls the NRST pin. It records which reset happened last in RSTC_SR.RSTTYP, updated when the processor reset is released. RSTC_MR sits in the VDDIO domain and keeps its contents while VDDIO is present.

NRST is sampled at the slow clock rate. A low lasting more than three slow clock cycles is reported as a user reset; the pin has to be held low at least one slow clock cycle for a user reset to happen. Clearing RSTC_MR.URSTEN stops NRST from causing a reset; setting RSTC_MR.URSTIEN makes it raise an interrupt instead. RSTC_SR.NRSTL reads the pin level at any time, and RSTC_SR.URSTS is set when NRST goes low and is cleared by reading RSTC_SR. A user reset starts 2 slow clock cycles after NRST is seen low and asserts the processor and peripheral resets. It ends when NRST rises, after two cycles of resynchronization and three of processor start-up; RSTTYP then reads 4. If NRST is held low externally beyond the external reset length, the internal resets stay asserted until it rises.

When the reset controller pulls NRST, it holds it low for 2^(ERSTL+1) slow clock cycles, set by RSTC_MR.ERSTL: about 60 µs to 2 s. ERSTL = 0 gives a two-cycle pulse. Because RSTC_MR is kept in the backup domain, ERSTL can stretch the power-up reset seen by external devices that need longer to start than the MCU. For a correct reset of the system by the WDT, ERSTL is set to 1 or more.

General reset: a VDDIO power-on reset, a brown-out or a loss of core regulation detected by the supply controller asserts vddcore_nreset; all resets are released, RSTC_MR is cleared, and NRST rises two cycles after vddcore_nreset because ERSTL defaults to 0. Backup reset: leaving Backup mode, with vddcore_nreset asserted by the supply controller. Watchdog reset: a watchdog fault with WDT_MR.WDRSTEN set; it lasts three slow clock cycles, asserts the processor and peripheral resets and pulls NRST for the ERSTL length, and that NRST low does not start a user reset. Afterwards the WDT is running again at its maximum period. With WDRSTEN clear the fault does not reach the reset controller. If NRST has an RC network on it, a watchdog reset can be reported as a user reset when NRST takes more than one slow clock cycle to rise. Software reset: RSTC_CR.PROCRST resets the processor and every peripheral, the memory system and the remap command included; RSTC_CR.EXTRST pulls NRST for the ERSTL length without causing a user reset. Either or both may be written; the reset lasts three slow clock cycles, starts as soon as the write is seen on MCK and ends in step with the slow clock. Only PROCRST is reported in RSTTYP. RSTC_SR.SRCMP is set while a software reset is in progress, and RSTC_CR writes are ignored until it clears.

A watchdog or software reset holds the processor and peripheral reset lines for 3 slow clock cycles plus 2 MCK cycles; NRST is held at least 2 slow clock cycles with ERSTL = 0 (8 with ERSTL = 2). A user reset releases the processor and peripherals 6 slow clock cycles after NRST rises. RSTTYP values: 0x2 watchdog reset, 0x3 software reset, 0x4 user reset. Priority, highest first: general, backup, watchdog, software, user. During a user reset no watchdog event or software reset can occur because the processor and WDT are held in reset. During a software reset a watchdog event takes over and NRST has no effect. During a watchdog reset neither a software reset nor a user reset can start.

A low-power, fully asynchronous calendar clock driven by the 32.768 kHz slow clock, best served by an external crystal. It keeps century, year, month, date, day, hours, minutes and seconds in BCD in RTC_TIMR and RTC_CALR, in 24-hour or 12-hour AM/PM form, with a Gregorian or Persian calendar, an alarm, a periodic interrupt, a digital calibration circuit, two waveform outputs RTCOUT0 and RTCOUT1, write protection, and checks on the values written and on the running counters. It is always clocked; the PMC has no effect on it. Its interrupt is ORed with the other system controller interrupts onto one interrupt line.

operation.topic: RTC calendar range, reading and alarm
operation.text: Years run up to 2099 in Gregorian mode (1300 to 1499 in Persian mode); every year divisible by 4 is a leap year except 1900, which is correct up to 2099. Seconds update once a second, minutes once a minute and so on. Because the RTC runs asynchronously, a time or date register is read twice and taken as valid when both reads agree: two or three reads in all. The alarm compares five fields (month, date, hour, minute, second), with an enable bit for each (SECEN, MINEN, HOUREN, DATEEN, MTHEN); all enabled gives one alarm a year at that moment, seconds alone gives one each minute. To change a field, its enable is cleared first, the value written, and the enable set again: up to three writes to RTC_TIMALR or RTC_CALALR.

Values written to the time, calendar and alarm registers are checked; an illegal value is not loaded and sets a flag in the validity register that clears only when a legal value is written. Checks: century 19 to 20 (13 to 14 in Persian mode); year a valid BCD value; date 01 to 31; month BCD 01 to 12 and consistent with the date; day 1 to 7; hour 00 to 23 with AM/PM clear in 24-hour mode, 01 to 12 in 12-hour mode; minute and second BCD 00 to 59. In 12-hour mode a 12-hour value is written and RTC_TIMR returns the 24-hour value; the AM/PM bit (bit 22 of RTC_TIMR) decides the range checked. The running counters are also checked continuously: a non-BCD or impossible value sets RTC_SR.TDERR, cleared through RTC_SCCR.TDERRCLR. TDERR sets again if its cause remains; writing correct values to RTC_CALR or RTC_TIMR removes the cause, and a counter roll-over can remove it too (every 10 s for SECONDS[3:0]), in which case TDERR stays set until cleared.

An update starts on a one-second event, seen by polling RTC_SR.SEC or by the SEC interrupt. Software then sets RTC_CR.UPDTIM for the time fields and/or RTC_CR.UPDCAL for the calendar fields, waits for RTC_SR.ACKUPD (polling or interrupt), clears ACKUPD through RTC_SCCR, writes RTC_TIMR and/or RTC_CALR, and clears UPDTIM and/or UPDCAL. Only the ACKUPD interrupt may be enabled during the update. Updating the calendar stops both time and calendar. Between two updates at least one second passes after UPDTIM/UPDCAL are cleared, done by waiting for the SEC flag before setting them again; SEC is cleared after UPDTIM/UPDCAL are cleared.

A digital correction for crystal error, programmable at any time. Typical crystal error at room temperature (20 to 25 °C) is ±20 ppm; across the operating temperature range the 32.768 kHz crystal can be off by up to -200 ppm. The correction range is 1.5 ppm to 1950 ppm, positive or negative, and does not vary with temperature, voltage or process. With a correction set from an accurate measurement, the remaining error is below 1 ppm for an initial error of 1.5 to 20 ppm or 30 to 90 ppm, below 2 ppm for 20 to 30 ppm or 90 to 130 ppm, and below 5 ppm for 130 to 200 ppm. The crystal frequency is left alone; instead the 1 Hz period is lengthened or shortened by about 4 ms (one 128 Hz edge, 3.906 ms: a corrected second lasts 1.003906 s or 0.996094 s) once every 1 + [(20 - (19 × HIGHPPM)) × CORRECTION] seconds, set by CORRECTION, NEGPPM and HIGHPPM in RTC_MR. The setting is held in the backup area and lost when backup power is removed. For measurement in production the RTC output can carry 1 Hz, 32 Hz, 64 Hz or 512 Hz derived from the 32.768 kHz clock; the correction shows on 1 Hz, 32 Hz and 64 Hz but not on 512 Hz. Temperature drift can be corrected by updating RTC_MR from a temperature sensor near the crystal and a table of the crystal's curve, or from a network time reference compared against RTC_TIMR.

RTCOUT0 and RTCOUT1 each select, through RTC_MR.OUT0 and OUT1, one of: 0 a low level, 1 1 Hz, 2 32 Hz, 3 64 Hz, 4 512 Hz, 5 toggle on alarm, 6 alarm flag, 7 pulse. The alarm flag output goes high on an alarm match and low when RTC_SCCR.ALRCLR is written; toggle on alarm changes state at each alarm match; pulse gives a high of length Thigh each period Tperiod. The outputs keep running in Backup and low-power modes.

A 32-bit counter that counts roll-overs of a 16-bit prescaler on the slow clock, or counts the RTC's calibrated 1 Hz signal when RTT_MR.RTC1HZ is set (RTPRES then has no effect and the counter steps once a second). It gives a periodic interrupt (RTTINC, set at each prescaler roll-over whatever the counter source) and an alarm. RTPRES = 0x8000, the default, gives 1 Hz from a 32.768 kHz slow clock; the counter then spans 2^32 s, more than 136 years, before rolling to 0. RTPRES = 3 gives the finest time base; 1 and 2 are forbidden.

An interrupt from the RTT comes two slow clock cycles after RTT_SR is read; to avoid repeated entries the interrupt is disabled in its handler and re-enabled once RTT_SR is cleared. RTT_VR.CRTV can be read at any time but changes asynchronously, so it is read twice until two reads agree. When the counter equals RTT_AR.ALMV, RTT_SR.ALMS is set; RTT_AR resets to 0xFFFFFFFF. ALMS always drives the RTT alarm signal, which can wake the system from low-power modes. ALMIEN is cleared before ALMV is written, and RTTINCIEN before RTPRES is written. Reading RTT_SR clears RTTINC and ALMS. RTT_MR.RTTRST reloads the prescaler and resets the counter; RTT_MR.RTTDIS stops the RTT to save power.

Eight 32-bit registers, 128 bits in all, in the system controller's backup domain. Registers 0 to 3 can be cleared at once by a low-power debouncer (tamper) event on WKUP0 or WKUP1; registers 4 to 7 keep their contents. This needs SUPC_WUMR.LPDBCCLR and LPDBCEN0 and/or LPDBCEN1 set and LPDBC non-zero. After a tamper event the registers cannot be written until SUPC_SR.LPDBCS0 or LPDBCS1 is cleared.

Its sources: a 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator, low power and able to be bypassed; a slow RC oscillator, also low power, near 32 kHz; a main crystal oscillator for 3 to 20 MHz, which can also be bypassed; a main RC oscillator at 4, 8 or 12 MHz (12 MHz by default; 8 and 12 MHz trimmed in production), a 480 MHz UTMI PLL for the USB high-speed controller, and a 160 to 500 MHz PLL (PLLA) with an 8 to 32 MHz input. Its outputs: SLCK, the slow clock and the only clock that is always running; MAINCK, from the main crystal or main RC oscillator; PLLACK, from the divider and PLLA; and UPLLCK, from the UTMI PLL. Its registers are named CKGR_ and sit in the PMC.

The slow clock generator is in the supply controller, powered from VDDIO. When VDDIO comes up both slow oscillators get power, yet the RC one alone is started, so SLCK is valid after about 100 µs. The slow RC oscillator is the default SLCK source: it starts faster and is fully internal, but its frequency varies more with supply, temperature and process. Setting SUPC_CR.XTALSEL switches SLCK to the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator: the XIN32 and XOUT32 lines are handed to the oscillator, the oscillator starts, then the slow RC oscillator stops; the switch is glitch-free. Going back to the slow RC oscillator is possible only by removing VDDIO. XIN32 and XOUT32 take a 32.768 kHz crystal or ceramic resonator; unused, they may be left open, being PIO inputs with pull-up after reset. In bypass mode an external clock drives XIN32; SUPC_MR.OSCBYPASS is set before SUPC_CR.XTALSEL.

Enabled at reset at 12 MHz and selected as MAINCK, so the system starts on it. CKGR_MOR.MOSCRCEN turns it on or off and CKGR_MOR.MOSCRCF selects 4, 8 or 12 MHz. Changing the frequency clears PMC_SR.MOSCRCS and stops MAINCK until the oscillator settles, then MOSCRCS sets again (and can interrupt). Turning it on and choosing a new frequency take two separate writes, never one. Disabling it clears MOSCRCS. Only the 8 and 12 MHz settings are trimmed in production, by Flash calibration bits that differ from device to device and that no Flash erase or ERASE pin clears; they can be read with the EEFC GCALB command. Software can override the trim through PMC_OCR: setting SEL4, SEL8 or SEL12 makes CAL4, CAL8 or CAL12 the trim for that frequency, even while running from it. PMC_OCR returns to its default at each power-up or peripheral reset. The main frequency counter can measure the result.

Disabled and not selected after reset; it gives the accurate main clock. Setting CKGR_MOR.MOSCXTEN with a start-up count in CKGR_MOR.MOSCXTST hands the XIN and XOUT lines to the oscillator, clears PMC_SR.MOSCXTS and starts a counter on SLCK divided by 8. MOSCXTST is 8 bits, so the start-up delay reaches 2048 SLCK periods, about 62 ms at 32.768 kHz. When the counter reaches 0, MOSCXTS sets and can interrupt. Clearing MOSCXTEN clears MOSCXTS. Bypass: with a stable external clock on XIN within the XIN clock characteristics, set CKGR_MOR.MOSCXTBY, then clear MOSCXTEN.

MAINCK comes from the main RC oscillator, the main crystal oscillator, or an external clock on XIN in bypass. CKGR_MOR.MOSCSEL selects; the switch is glitch-free, so MCK need not be moved off MAINCK first, and PMC_SR.MOSCSELS signals the end of the switch. The main RC oscillator is selected before entering Wait mode. Going from the crystal to the RC oscillator takes three steps: start the RC oscillator with MAINCK still on the crystal, switch MAINCK to the RC oscillator with the crystal still running, then stop the crystal.

CKGR_MCFR counts cycles of the main RC or main crystal oscillator (chosen by CKGR_MCFR.CCSS) over 16 SLCK periods. A count starts when RCMEAS is written to 1, when the selected main oscillator becomes stable (MOSCRCS or MOSCXTS sets), or when the MAINCK source changes; it stops at the 16th falling SLCK edge, sets MAINFRDY and leaves the count in MAINF. To move MAINCK from the RC to the crystal oscillator safely: enable the crystal with its start-up time in MOSCXTST, wait for MOSCXTS, set CCSS, set RCMEAS, wait for MAINFRDY, read MAINF and check the frequency, then switch MAINCK.

PLLACK is made from MAINCK by a divider DIVA (1 to 255) and PLLA with multiplier MULA, giving MAINCK × (MULA + 1) / DIVA. DIVA = 0, the reset value, holds the PLL input at 0; MULA = 0 or DIVA = 0 turns the PLL off, two SLCK cycles after the write. Enabling the PLL or changing its settings clears PMC_SR.LOCKA and loads CKGR_PLLAR.PLLACOUNT into a counter that runs down on SLCK; LOCKA sets (and can interrupt) at 0, so PLLACOUNT holds enough SLCK cycles to cover the PLL settling. PMC_PMMR.PLLA_MMAX caps the multiplier sent to the PLL. MAINCK is not to be changed (source or main RC frequency) while it feeds PLLA and MCK runs from PLLA; instead switch MCK to MAINCK (PMC_MCKR.CSS), change CKGR_MOR.MOSCRCF or MOSCSEL, wait for MOSCRCS or MOSCSELS, disable and re-enable the PLL, wait for LOCKA, and switch MCK back to PLLA.

The UTMI PLL runs from the main crystal oscillator and gives UPLLCK and UPLLCKDIV. It multiplies by 40 or 30, so 480 MHz for USB comes from a 12 MHz or 16 MHz crystal, written to UTMI_CKTRIM.FREQ before the PLL is enabled. Setting CKGR_UCKR.UPLLEN clears PMC_SR.LOCKU and loads CKGR_UCKR.PLLCOUNT into a counter clocked by SLCK divided by 8; LOCKU sets (and can interrupt) at 0.

Gates the clocks of the core and of each peripheral.
