It provides: MCK, the host clock, from a few hundred Hz to the device maximum, used by always-running blocks such as the Flash controller; HCLK, the processor clock, stopped in Sleep mode; FCLK, the free-running processor clock; the Cortex-M7 SysTick external clock; USB_48M for USB; peripheral clocks with separate on/off control; programmable clock outputs PCKx on the PCK pins; internal PCKx clocks independent of MCK and HCLK for USART, UART, TC, ETM and CAN; and generic clocks (GCLK) with their own divider and enable. It also has a main crystal failure detector, a 32.768 kHz crystal frequency monitor, the main frequency counter and on-the-fly trim of the main RC oscillator. The device starts on MCK from the main RC oscillator at 12 MHz; the supply controller picks the SLCK source and turns off the unused slow oscillator.

PMC_MCKR.CSS selects SLCK, MAINCK, PLLACK or UPLLCKDIV; PMC_MCKR.PRES divides by 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64; PMC_MCKR.MDIV then divides by 1, 2, 3 or 4 to make MCK. UPLLCKDIV is UPLLCK divided by 1 or 2 (PMC_MCKR.UPLLDIV2). Each new setting clears PMC_SR.MCKRDY until MCK is stable, then MCKRDY sets and can interrupt. MDIV and CSS are changed in separate writes with a wait for MCKRDY in between. MCK is the source of the peripheral clocks.

HCLK stops when the core executes WFI or WFE with PMC_FSMR.LPM = 0; that is Sleep mode. Any enabled interrupt or a reset restarts it. The current instruction completes before the clock stops, and other bus hosts keep transferring. HCLK is on after reset.

The SysTick external clock is HCLK divided by 2, and its calibration value is fixed at 150000, giving 1 ms at the maximum HCLK. SysTick may lose counts when it runs from the external clock and the core enters Sleep mode.

PMC_USB.USBS selects PLLA or the UPLL as the source of USB_48M, divided by PMC_USB.USBDIV (1 to 16); the chosen PLL is set to give the right frequency. Once PMC_SR.LOCKA and LOCKU are set, PMC_SCER.USBCLK enables USB_48M and PMC_SCDR.USBCLK disables it; PMC_SCSR.USBCLK shows its state. The USB port needs this clock and its peripheral clock.

operation.topic: Clocks independent of core and bus
operation.text: Internal PCKx clocks let some peripherals keep a fixed bit rate or timing while the core, bus and peripheral clocks change. PMC_PCKx.CSS picks SLCK, MAINCK, a PLL clock or MCK and PMC_PCKx.PRES divides it (1 to 256). PMC_SCER.PCKx and PMC_SCDR.PCKx enable and disable each one, PMC_SCSR.PCKx shows its state, and PMC_SR.PCKRDYx shows it is set up. Each peripheral also selects the independent clock on its side. For accesses through the AHBP the core-to-bus frequency ratio is 1 or 1/2. USB, GMAC and MLB run independently of the core and bus clocks without a PCKx.

PMC_PCR sets up each peripheral's clocks: write CMD = 1 with the peripheral's PID and the other fields to configure it, or CMD = 0 with the PID alone to read its configuration back from PMC_PCR. Peripheral clocks (periph_clk[PID]) come from MCK and go to every peripheral. Generic clocks (GCLK[PID]) go to I2SC0 and I2SC1, are independent of HCLK, MCK and the peripheral clocks, and are made from SLCK, MAINCK, UPLLCKDIV, PLLACK or MCK divided by 1 to 256. Peripheral clocks can also be switched with PMC_PCERx and PMC_PCDRx and read in PMC_PCSRx, where the bit number is the peripheral identifier, the same as its interrupt number. A clock stops at once when disabled, and all are off after reset; a peripheral is left to finish its last operation before its clock is stopped.

UARTx and TWIHSx can have their clock managed by the PMC from activity on their line, both while the system sleeps in Wait mode (SleepWalking) and while it runs. In Wait mode every clock but SLCK is stopped; when such a peripheral asks for its clock, the PMC feeds only that peripheral, which then either wakes the whole system, if its configured condition is met, or lets its clock stop again until the next request. After a wakeup, SleepWalking for that peripheral stays off until PMC_SLPWK_ER.PIDx is written again. In Active mode the peripheral's clock is stopped until it asks for it, and the PMC supplies it without the processor; once its condition is met, partial wakeup is turned off for it until re-enabled through PMC_SLPWK_ER. Set-up, with the peripheral clock enabled (PMC_PCSR.PIDx set): check PMC_SLPWK_ASR.PIDx is 0, write PMC_SLPWK_ER.PIDx, check PMC_SLPWK_ASR.PIDx is still 0; if it became 1, disable through PMC_SLPWK_DR, wait for the activity to end and start again. Before entering Wait mode PMC_SLPWK_AIPR.AIP is checked clear. While SleepWalking is enabled and the core runs, the peripheral is not accessed until it has been woken.
FCLK keeps running while the core sleeps so that interrupts are sampled and sleep events can be traced by the debug blocks.

Three clock outputs on the PCKx pins, each set by PMC_PCKx: CSS selects SLCK, MAINCK, PLLACK, UPLLCKDIV or MCK (SLCK by default) and PRES divides by 1 to 256 (the reset value passes SLCK undivided). PMC_SCER.PCKx and PMC_SCDR.PCKx enable and disable each output, PMC_SCSR.PCKx shows which are on, and PMC_SR.PCKRDYx shows the output matches its programming. Switching is not glitch-protected, so the output is disabled before CSS or PRES is changed and enabled again after, then PCKRDYx is awaited. All outputs are off after reset.

The core restarts from Wait mode within a few microseconds when the code that enters and leaves Wait mode runs from on-chip SRAM; with the first instruction after wakeup in Flash the fast start-up time is not reached. A fast start-up is triggered by a programmed level on any of the 14 wakeup inputs WKUP0 to WKUP13, polarity set in PMC_FSPR, or by the RTC alarm, RTT alarm or USB controller; each source is enabled in PMC_FSMR, which also offers the GMAC wake-on-LAN event and the processor debug power-up request. A WKUPx active level lasts longer than four MAINCK cycles. The circuit is asynchronous, and the main RC oscillator restarts as soon as it fires. The PMC holds no status of the wakeup source; the PIO controller and the RTC, RTT and USB status registers do. PMC_FSMR.FLPM sets the Flash state for the next Wait mode: 1 deep power-down (lowest consumption), 0 standby (slightly higher), 2 the same as Active mode without reads.

When fast start-up is not needed, the first instruction after leaving Wait mode may sit in Flash; the Flash controller is then set to 0 wait states before entering Wait mode. Entry and exit are otherwise as for fast start-up. With the Flash in standby (FLPM = 0) or deep power-down (FLPM = 1), running the wakeup routine from SRAM saves a little more power.

Enabled by CKGR_MOR.CFDEN; it is disabled after a VDDCORE reset and when the main crystal oscillator is off (MOSCXTEN = 0), and it does not work in bypass mode. A counter on the crystal output runs while the slow RC oscillator clock is high (the slow RC oscillator is started automatically when CFDEN = 1); fewer than eight crystal periods in that half-period reports a failure, so detection takes one slow RC period, and up to two slow RC cycles just after the detector is enabled. A failure sets PMC_SR.CFDEV (cleared by reading PMC_SR, and the only one of the two that can interrupt) and PMC_SR.FOS (cleared by PMC_FOCR.FOCLR); PMC_SR.CFDS shows the present state. On a failure MAINCK is forced to the main RC oscillator, which is re-enabled if it was off; if MCK ran from PLLACK or UPLLCKDIV (CSS = 2 or 3) with the crystal as MAINCK, MCK is first forced to MAINCK. The switch takes two slow RC cycles when MCK runs from MAINCK and three when it runs from PLLACK or UPLLCKDIV. The failure also drives a fault input of the PWM controller so it can force its outputs to a safe state.

Enabled by CKGR_MOR.XT32KFME once the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator has started and its start-up time has passed. It measures the crystal against the main RC oscillator and sets PMC_SR.XT32KERR when the frequency is outside ±10% of 32.768 kHz, after at least 4 consecutive periods out of range. The flag clears only with the monitor disabled. Accuracy is ±10% with the main RC oscillator at 8 or 12 MHz and ±40% at 4 MHz, which is not trimmed; changing PMC_OCR can upset it. Deviations beyond ±10% are always flagged; between 1% and 10% either way they may not be. Allowed crystal drift is 10000 ppm (1%), so any standard crystal fits. To change the main RC frequency the monitor is stopped first and re-enabled once PMC_SR.MOSCRCS is set. XT32KERR can interrupt (PMC_IER.XT32KERR) and is routed to the reset controller, where it may reset the device.

1. Without a main crystal, go to step 6. 2. Set CKGR_MOR.MOSCXTEN with a start-up time in MOSCXTST and wait for PMC_SR.MOSCXTS (poll or interrupt). 3. Set CKGR_MOR.MOSCSEL. 4. Poll PMC_SR until MOSCSELS is 1. 5. Read CKGR_MCFR until MAINFRDY is set, then read MAINF once more: the main clock cycles in 16 SLCK cycles; if MAINF is 0, clear MOSCSEL to return to the main RC oscillator. 6. Write CKGR_PLLAR in one access: DIVA 0 to 127 (0, the default, turns off divider and PLLA), MULA 0 to 62 (0 turns PLLA off, otherwise output = input × (MULA + 1)), PLLACOUNT the SLCK cycles before LOCKA sets; wait for PMC_SR.LOCKA before using PLLACK, and again after any change of MULA or DIVA. 7. Set PMC_MCKR, never in one access: CSS selects the MCK and HCLK source (MAINCK by default), PRES the prescaler (1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64), MDIV 0 to 3 divides HCLK by 1 to 4 to give MCK (0, the default, makes MCK equal to HCLK). Going to a PLL clock: write PRES, wait MCKRDY, write MDIV, wait MCKRDY, write CSS, wait MCKRDY. Going to MAINCK or SLCK: write CSS, wait MCKRDY, write PRES, wait MCKRDY. Any change of CSS, MDIV or PRES clears MCKRDY until MCK and HCLK are ready. If CKGR_PLLAR is rewritten while PLLA drives MCK, MCKRDY drops while PLLA is unlocked and MCK runs from SLCK meanwhile, then LOCKA and MCKRDY set again. 8. Set up each PMC_PCKx in one write, enable it through PMC_SCER and wait for PCKRDYx; to change CSS or PRES, disable it first. 9. Enable peripheral clocks through PMC_PCERx and PMC_PCDRx.
The worst-case times for MCK to move from one source to another assume the prescaler is off; with the prescaler on, 64 cycles of the new clock are added.

Setting PMC_WPMR.WPEN write-protects PMC_SCDR, PMC_PCER0, PMC_PCDR0, CKGR_MOR, CKGR_MCFR, CKGR_PLLAR, CKGR_UCKR, PMC_MCKR, PMC_USB, PMC_PCKx, PMC_FSMR, PMC_FSPR, PMC_PCER1, PMC_PCDR1, PMC_OCR, PMC_SLPWK_ER0, PMC_SLPWK_DR0, PMC_PMMR, PMC_SLPWK_ER1 and PMC_SLPWK_DR1. A write to a protected register sets PMC_WPSR.WPVS and records the register in WPVSRC; reading PMC_WPSR clears WPVS.

Each PIO controller manages a set of I/O lines, one bit per line in each of its 32-bit registers. A line is either a general-purpose I/O or given to one of up to four peripheral functions (A, B, C, D). Every line, whether a GPIO or a peripheral pin, has: an input change interrupt and additional rising-edge, falling-edge, low-level and high-level interrupt modes; a glitch filter rejecting pulses shorter than half a peripheral clock; a debouncing filter for keys and push-buttons; multi-drive (open-drain) output; pull-up and pull-down control; a pin data status register that reads the pin level at any time; configuration lock by the connected peripheral; programmable Schmitt trigger and drive. Set and clear registers program everything; a synchronous output sets and clears several lines in one write; registers can be write-protected; and an 8-bit parallel capture mode reads a CMOS image sensor, ADC or synchronous DSP port.

operation.topic: PIO clock, interrupts and external interrupt lines
operation.text: The PIO registers can be written with the PIO's peripheral clock off, so lines can be configured without it; but glitch filtering, the input change and event interrupts and reading the pin level need the clock, which is off after a hardware reset, so the PMC is set up before input levels are read. Each PIO controller has its own interrupt line in the interrupt controller, and interrupts arise only with its clock on. A line that is general-purpose only is unaffected by peripheral assignment and is always driven by the PIO. To use a WKUPx pin as an external interrupt line, the PIO's peripheral control of that line is disabled and the line set as an input.

Every line has an internal pull-up and pull-down. PIO_PUER and PIO_PUDR enable and disable the pull-up, shown in PIO_PUSR (1 = disabled, 0 = enabled); PIO_PPDER and PIO_PPDDR do the same for the pull-down in PIO_PPDSR. A pull-down cannot be enabled while the pull-up is on, nor the reverse: the write is ignored. Pull-up control works whatever the line's configuration. The state after reset depends on the line. For analog inputs (AFE_ADx, DACx) both resistors are disabled through PIO_PUDR and PIO_PPDDR.

PIO_PER gives a line to the PIO and PIO_PDR to a peripheral; PIO_PSR reads 1 for PIO control and 0 for the peripheral chosen in PIO_ABCDSR0 and PIO_ABCDSR1. For a GPIO-only line PER and PDR have no effect and PSR reads 1. Lines come out of reset under PIO control (PSR at 1), but where a line must be driven by its peripheral from reset, such as a memory chip select held inactive or an address line held low to boot from external memory, the reset value is set by the device's multiplexing. The ABCD selection affects only the output; peripheral inputs always see the pin. Giving a line to a peripheral takes an ABCDSR write and a PDR write. ABCDSR0 and ABCDSR1 are 0 after reset (peripheral A), though A does not drive the pin while the PIO has it. Selecting a function that does not exist on a pin is accepted and enables nothing. With the line given to a peripheral, that peripheral decides whether the pin is driven.

Under PIO control, PIO_OER and PIO_ODR set PIO_OSR: 0 input only, 1 driven. PIO_SODR and PIO_CODR set and clear PIO_ODSR, the level driven. OSR and ODSR can be written whether the line is under PIO or peripheral control, so the first level driven can be set before the PIO takes the line. Synchronous output: one write to PIO_ODSR changes several lines together, only bits enabled in PIO_OWSR (set through PIO_OWER, cleared through PIO_OWDR) being written; OWSR is 0 after reset. Multi-drive: PIO_MDER and PIO_MDDR make a line open drain, shown in PIO_MDSR, usable under PIO or peripheral control; an external or the internal pull-up gives the high level; off on every line after reset. A level written through SODR, CODR or ODSR reaches PIO_PDSR 2 peripheral clock cycles after the APB write.

PIO_PDSR reads every line's level whatever its configuration, if the PIO clock is on; with the clock off it holds the levels from when the clock stopped. Each line can have a glitch filter or a debouncing filter, enabled through PIO_IFER and PIO_IFDR (status PIO_IFSR) and chosen through PIO_IFSCDR and PIO_IFSCER (status PIO_IFSCSR: 0 glitch filter on the peripheral clock, 1 debouncing filter on the divided slow clock, whose period PIO_SCDR.DIV sets). A pulse shorter than half the selected clock period is rejected, one of a full period or more is passed, and one in between may go either way. The filters act only on PIO_PDSR and the input change interrupt, not on peripheral inputs, and need the peripheral clock. The glitch filter adds up to 2.5 peripheral clock cycles of delay; the debouncing filter up to 1.5 divided slow clock cycles plus up to 2 peripheral clock cycles.

operation.topic: PIO input edge and level interrupts
operation.text: PIO_IER and PIO_IDR set the mask in PIO_IMR. By default an interrupt follows any edge on the input, found by comparing two samples, so the peripheral clock is needed; it works whatever the line's configuration. PIO_AIMER and PIO_AIMDR (status PIO_AIMMR) turn on the additional modes: PIO_ESR or PIO_LSR choose edge or level (status PIO_ELSR), and PIO_FELLSR or PIO_REHLSR choose falling/low or rising/high (status PIO_FRLHSR). A detected event sets PIO_ISR; with the mask set, the PIO interrupt line is asserted, the lines of one controller being ORed into one interrupt. Reading PIO_ISR clears all of its flags, so every pending event is handled on that read; a level interrupt keeps coming back while the level remains.

operation.topic: I/O line lock, drive and Schmitt trigger
operation.text: A peripheral, the PWM in particular, can lock a line it controls; writes to PIO_PER, PDR, MDER, MDDR, PUDR, PUER, ABCDSR0 and ABCDSR1 for that line are then ignored. PIO_LOCKSR shows locked lines; only a hardware reset of the PIO unlocks them. Pad drive strength is programmable. Each input's Schmitt trigger can be switched; it is on by default and is turned off for the QTouch library.

Reads an 8-bit synchronous source such as a CMOS image sensor: clock on PIODCCLK, data on PIODC[7:0], data enables on PIODCEN1 and PIODCEN2 (an image sensor's PCLK, DATA[7:0], VSYNC and HSYNC). Setting PIO_PCMR.PCEN makes those lines inputs automatically. Data is sampled on the rising sensor clock edge and resynchronized to the peripheral clock. PIO_PCMR.DSIZE sets the word read from PIO_PCRHR; above 8 bits, successive samples are packed into the word (first sample in the low byte), then PIO_PCISR.DRDY sets. With ALWYS = 0 a sample is taken only when both enables are high; with ALWYS = 1 every clock edge is sampled. HALFS = 1 keeps only one sample in two, for example the luminance of a YUV422 stream, the even-numbered samples with FRSTS = 0 and the odd ones with FRSTS = 1. A word not read before the next one arrives is lost and sets OVRE, cleared by reading PIO_PCISR. A DMA receive channel can move the data to memory without the CPU (PDC status shows in ENDRX and RXBUFF). DRDY, OVRE, ENDRX and RXBUFF can interrupt. DSIZE, ALWYS, HALFS and FRSTS change only with PCEN = 0. The peripheral clock has to run at more than twice the frequency of the source's clock.

Without DMA: set the interrupt mask through PIO_PCIDR and PIO_PCIER; write the PIO_PCMR fields DSIZE, ALWYS, HALFS, FRSTS while PCEN stays 0; set PCEN alone; wait for DRDY (poll or interrupt); check OVRE; read PIO_PCRHR; repeat from the wait while data is expected; clear PCEN. With DMA: set the interrupt mask, set up the DMA transfer, write the PIO_PCMR fields, set PCEN, wait for the DMA to report the buffer done, check OVRE, repeat while buffers are expected, clear PCEN.

Setting PIO_WPMR.WPEN write-protects these PIO registers: PER, PDR, OER, ODR, IFER, IFDR, MDER, MDDR, PUDR, PUER, both peripheral ABCD select registers, OWER, OWDR, PPDDR, PPDER and PCMR. A write to a protected register sets PIO_WPSR.WPVS and records the register in WPVSRC; reading PIO_WPSR clears WPVS.

Connects external memories and peripherals to the internal memory controller: SRAM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and Flash through the static memory controller (SMC), and NAND Flash through built-in logic that saves external parts. Up to 24 address bits (16 Mbytes linear per chip select), a 16-bit data bus, up to four chip selects NCS0 to NCS3 (each usable for SMC or NAND Flash) and control lines shared between the controllers. The EBI supports 1.8 V or 3.3 V supplies; SAMV7x devices run it at 3.3 V only. Its pins are PIO lines, assigned to the EBI peripheral function in the PIO controller; unused ones stay available as I/O. All EBI pins are powered from VDDIO.

Multiplexing logic shares the data, address and control lines among the memory controllers according to which memory area is addressed. It keeps address and output control lines stable while no external access runs and respects the data float times set in the controllers.

operation.topic: NAND Flash support in the EBI
operation.text: NANDCS is driven by the SMC on whichever of NCS0 to NCS3 is selected in CCFG_SMCNFCS (SMC_NFCSx) in the chip configuration registers; with NCS3 selected, the NAND Flash is reached in the NCS3 space, 0x6300 0000 to 0x6FFF FFFF. NANDOE and NANDWE carry the SMC read and write strobes while that chip select is active and go inactive as soon as an address falls outside its space. A21 drives the NAND ALE and A22 its CLE, so command, address and data words are told apart by their address within the space. The NAND Flash address space is declared as Device or Strongly-ordered in the Cortex-M7 MPU so that the core keeps the access order. The NAND chip enable and ready/busy go to PIO lines, so CE can stay low while NCSx is not selected and the device does not drop into standby.

Part of the EBI; drives SRAM, PSRAM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, LCD modules, NOR Flash and NAND Flash. Four chip selects with 16 Mbytes each, a 24-bit address bus, an 8-bit or 16-bit data bus per chip select, 8-, 16- and 32-bit transfers, a strobe per byte for writes or a select line per byte, separate read and write strobes, setup, pulse and hold times programmable per chip select for reads and for writes, a data float time per chip select, an external wait input, an automatic slow clock mode, asynchronous page-mode reads with 4 to 32-byte pages, data scrambling with a user key at no extra wait state, and register write protection. Its clock is enabled in the PMC before use, and its pins are assigned in the PIO controller.

operation.topic: SMC memory mapping and bus width
operation.text: A[23:0] gives each chip select 16 Mbytes; a smaller device wraps and repeats inside that space. SMC_MODE.DBW chooses an 8-bit or 16-bit bus per chip select. A 512-Kbyte × 8 device on NCS2 takes D[7:0], A[18:2], A1 and A0, with NWE to its write enable, NRD to its output enable and NCS2 to its chip enable. A 512-Kbyte × 16 device takes D[15:0], SMC A[19:2] to its A[18:1] and SMC A1 to its A0, with NBS0 and NBS1 to its low and high byte enables.

operation.topic: Byte write and byte select access
operation.text: A chip select with a 16-bit bus uses byte write or byte select, set by SMC_MODE.BAT. Byte write joins two 8-bit devices into a 16-bit memory with one write strobe per byte (NWR0 lower, NWR1 upper) and one NRD; the SMC cannot boot in byte write mode. Byte select drives one 16-bit device with NBS0 and NBS1 selecting the lower and upper byte and one NRD and one NWE. For 16-bit devices A0 is unused; byte select leaves NWR1 unused and byte write leaves NBS0 unused. Two 8-bit devices on NCS3 in byte write share SMC A[24:2] on their A[23:1] and SMC A1 on their A0, NRD on their read enables and NCS3 on their chip enables, one on D[7:0] with NWR0, the other on D[15:8] with NWR1.

Up to four NAND Flash devices, each on its own chip select chosen by CCFG_SMCNFCS.SMC_NFCSx. NANDOE and NANDWE follow NRD and NWE while that chip select is active. With the NAND logic active, the NWE pin works only in its NWE peripheral function; when no other external memory needs it, it is left as a PIO input with pull-up (its reset state) or a PIO output at 1. A22 and A21 normally drive CLE and ALE, though any address bit may be used. A standard NAND Flash needs CE held low through the busy period before read-out, and since the SMC raises NCSx, its CE goes to a GPIO; a 'CE don't care' NAND Flash may take NCSx on CE directly. Ready/busy goes to a PIO input.

Set CCFG_SMCNFCS.SMC_NFCSx for the chosen chip select; keep A21 and A22 for ALE and CLE, which are driven by setting those address bits during the access; assign NANDOE and NANDWE to their peripheral function in the PIO controller; set a PIO line as input for ready/busy; set the SMC CS3 setup, pulse, cycle and mode for the NAND timings, bus width and bus clock. For a 'CE don't care' device NCS3 goes to CE when SMC_NFCS3 is set. For the NOR Flash example, the SMC CS0 setup, pulse, cycle and mode are set from the Flash timings and the bus clock.

Byte select lines follow the address timing; NWR0 and NWR1 follow the NWE timing; D[15:8] follows D[7:0]. A read starts by setting the address. NRD has a setup (address before NRD falls), a pulse (NRD low) and a hold (address after NRD rises); NCS has its own read setup, pulse and hold. The cycle, from address set to address free, is common to both and every value is a whole number of MCK cycles per chip select; the hold is whatever the cycle leaves after setup and pulse. With zero setup and hold, NRD and NCS stay low through back-to-back reads of the same memory. A pulse of 0 is not allowed (unpredictable); the minimum is 1.

SMC_MODE.READ_MODE says which strobe ends the read, as the SMC does not compare the NRD and NCS timings. READ_MODE = 1 (NRD controls), as for an asynchronous RAM whose data is valid tPACC after NRD falls: data is sampled on the MCK edge that raises NRD. READ_MODE = 0 (NCS controls), as for an LCD module whose data is valid tPACC after NCS falls until NCS rises: data is sampled on the MCK edge that raises NCS.

operation.topic: SMC write cycle and write mode
operation.text: NWE has a setup (address and data before NWE falls), a pulse and a hold (address and data after NWE rises); NCS has its own write setup, pulse and hold. The write cycle is common to both, in MCK cycles per chip select, and the hold is what remains after setup and pulse. With zero setup, NWE and NCS stay low through back-to-back writes of the same memory, but an SRAM, or any device latching data as NWE or NCS goes high, needs a setup or a hold. A pulse of 0 is not allowed. SMC_MODE.WRITE_MODE = 1: NWE controls, and data is driven from the end of NWE setup to the end of the cycle. WRITE_MODE = 0: NCS controls, and data is driven from the end of NCS write setup to the end of the cycle.

SMC_SETUP holds NRD_SETUP, NCS_RD_SETUP, NWE_SETUP and NCS_WR_SETUP; SMC_PULSE holds the four pulses; SMC_CYCLE holds NRD_CYCLE and NWE_CYCLE. The SMC does not check the values: setup plus pulse longer than the cycle gives unpredictable behaviour. Zero setup or hold on reads cannot be guaranteed positive at the memory because of delays in pads and external logic, so non-zero values are used where they must be met. With WRITE_MODE = 1 and NWE hold 0, address and NCS still hold after NWE rises. Setup and hold are counted from the address bus, so a device's NCS-to-NRD or NCS-to-NWE times are converted to address-referred times. Setting SMC_WPMR.WPEN write-protects SMC_SETUP, SMC_PULSE, SMC_CYCLE, SMC_MODE and SMC_OCMS; a blocked write sets SMC_WPSR.WPVS and records the register in WPVSRC, and reading SMC_WPSR clears WPVS.

Data on the external bus can be scrambled to protect code and data in off-chip memory from being read at the pins, on the fly with no added wait states. SMC_OCMS.CSxSE enables it per chip select. The scrambling uses the keys SMC_KEY1 and SMC_KEY2, which are write-once after reset and unreadable, plus a device-specific random value. The key or its seed is kept in reliable non-volatile memory; data scrambled with a lost key cannot be recovered.

Chip select wait state: one idle cycle between accesses on different chip selects, with NWR, NCS[0..3] and NRD all high. Early read wait state: one cycle between a write and a read on the same chip select when the write strobe has no hold and the read strobe no setup; or in NCS-controlled write with no NCS hold and NCS_RD_SETUP = 0; or in NWE-controlled write with NWE_HOLD = 0 when load capacitance keeps the external NWE from releasing in time, holding address, data and control one more cycle. Reload configuration wait state: inserted before the next access to the same device after an SMC_MODE write (not added on top of a chip select wait state), and at entry to and exit from slow clock mode. Timing register changes take effect only when SMC_MODE is written, even unchanged. A chip select's settings are not changed while it is being accessed, for example while code runs from it; the change runs from internal RAM or another chip select. Read to write wait state: one cycle always between a read and a following write, added to any chip select or reload wait state.

For a device slow to release the bus, SMC_MODE.TDF_CYCLES (0 to 15) sets data float cycles after a read, before a read on another device or a write to any device. They do not delay internal memory accesses. With READ_MODE = 1 the float period starts when NRD rises; with READ_MODE = 0 when NCS rises; it lasts TDF_CYCLES MCK cycles. TDF_MODE = 1 lets the next access's setup overlap the float period, so no wait is added when the period has already ended. TDF_MODE = 0 inserts the waits at the end of the read so the float period is over when the next access starts, less any overlap with the read's hold.

NWAIT, active low, stretches an access when SMC_MODE.EXNW_MODE is 10 (frozen) or 11 (ready); with 00 it is ignored. At least one hold cycle is then programmed on the controlling strobe, so NWAIT cannot be used in page mode or slow clock mode. NWAIT counts only during the pulse of the controlling strobe; outside that it is ignored. Frozen mode: the resynchronized NWAIT freezes the SMC counters and all control lines, and the access resumes where it stopped when NWAIT rises. Ready mode: in the last pulse cycle, if NWAIT is low, the access waits there and continues with its hold step once NWAIT rises; NWAIT going high while the pulse still runs, or low only once it has ended, leaves the access length unchanged. In either mode the strobe pulse is at least the device's NWAIT latency plus 2 resynchronization cycles plus 1 cycle, or the SMC may reach the hold step without seeing NWAIT.

When the PMC switches MCK to a very slow rate (typically 32 kHz), it signals the SMC, which then uses fixed slow clock waveforms on every chip select instead of the programmed ones, so no reprogramming is needed. When MCK returns to a fast rate, the transfer under way finishes at the fast rate with the slow clock parameters, which an external device may not support; the safe way is to let the SMC go idle across the change, after which a reload configuration wait state applies the normal settings.

With SMC_MODE.PMEN = 1, reads burst within memory pages of 4, 8, 16 or 32 bytes (SMC_MODE.PS), each aligned to its own size. The first access to a new page takes tpa, programmed in NCS_RD_PULSE; later accesses within it take tsa, programmed in NRD_PULSE. NRD and NCS stay low throughout, whatever setup and hold are programmed, and READ_MODE, NCS_RD_SETUP, NRD_SETUP and NRD_CYCLE have no effect. The SMC does not check that tpa is longer than tsa. Page mode and NWAIT together give unpredictable behaviour. An access with the same chip select and the same page address bits as the previous one needs no new page, sequential or not; a different page, a different chip select, or any other access in between (which deasserts the chip select) starts a new page.

A central DMA controller that moves data between peripherals and memory, either way, or from memory to memory, over one or two bus ports, each channel programmable. It handles 8-, 16- and 32-bit data, hardware-paced or software-started transfers, linked lists, fixed or incrementing addresses, separate data and microblock strides for source and destination, priority groups and arbitration, programmable burst length, a multiport FIFO, several descriptor views, automatic flush of trailing bytes, coarse and fine clock gating and a memset pattern accelerator. It is configured through the APB and moves data through a dual AHB host interface.

A channel links a source and a destination, each a memory-mapped client. A transfer paced by a peripheral request is hardware-synchronized; otherwise it runs by itself (memory to memory). A host transfer is a linked list of blocks; channel registers may change between blocks, by descriptor, and interrupts can occur per block or at the end of the list. A block is a programmable number of microblocks, between which configuration stays fixed and addresses may step by a programmable signed amount. A microblock is a programmable number of data, at a fixed address (a FIFO or peripheral register) or an address stepping by a signed amount. Memory transfers go in bursts up to a per-channel maximum, the trailing bytes in a shorter burst; peripheral transfers go in chunks of programmable size, larger being faster, the last one possibly short.

When a peripheral is ready for a chunk it raises its request line and the XDMAC moves the data. Software can stand in for the request: each bit of XDMAC_GSWR.SWREQ triggers one request, and XDMAC_GSWS shows it pending while set.

One block of one microblock: find a free channel in XDMAC_GS; read XDMAC_CISx to clear pending flags; write XDMAC_CSAx and XDMAC_CDAx; write the data count to XDMAC_CUBCx.UBLEN; set XDMAC_CCx (TYPE clear for memory to memory, set otherwise; MBSIZE burst size; SAM and DAM addressing; DSYNC direction; CSIZE chunk size; DWIDTH data width; SIF and DIF bus interfaces for reading and writing; PERID request line; SWREQ for a software request); clear XDMAC_CNDCx, XDMAC_CBCx, XDMAC_CDS_MSPx, XDMAC_CSUSx and XDMAC_CDUSx (no linked list, one block, no striding); set XDMAC_CIEx.BIE and XDMAC_GIE.IEx; set XDMAC_GE.ENx, which sets XDMAC_GS.STx. At the end XDMAC_CISx.BIS sets with an interrupt and STx clears. One block of several microblocks is the same with XDMAC_CBCx.BLEN set to the microblock count and XDMAC_CBCx left alone.

Pick a free channel and clear its flags; build a word-aligned linked list of descriptors in memory, each with its own view, the last one with MBR_UBC.NDE = 0; write the first descriptor's address to XDMAC_CNDAx.NDA and its bus interface to NDAIF; in XDMAC_CNDCx set NDE to fetch descriptors, NDSUP and NDDUP to load source and destination addresses at fetch, and NDVIEW for the first descriptor's view; set XDMAC_CIEx.LIE for the end-of-list interrupt; set XDMAC_GE.ENx. The hardware clears XDMAC_GS.STx when the transfer completes; writing XDMAC_GD.DIx stops a channel early, then XDMAC_GS is polled.

View 0 holds the next descriptor address (MBR_NDA, 0 for none; it replaces XDMAC_CNDAx at fetch), the microblock control (MBR_UBC) and one transfer address (MBR_TA): the destination when the target is memory (from memory or from a peripheral), loaded into XDMAC_CDAx when the previous descriptor's NDEN is set, or the source for memory-to-peripheral, loaded into XDMAC_CSAx when its NSEN is set. View 1 has separate source and destination addresses (MBR_SA, MBR_DA). View 2 adds MBR_CFG, copied into XDMAC_CCx. View 3 adds MBR_BC, MBR_DS, MBR_SUS and MBR_DUS, copied into XDMAC_CBCx, XDMAC_CDS_MSPx, XDMAC_CSUSx and XDMAC_CDUSx. For the first descriptor, XDMAC_CNDCx.NDSUP and NDDUP decide whether its addresses are loaded.

Disable (XDMAC_GD): on a source-peripheral-synchronized channel (TYPE set, DSYNC clear) the bytes in the FIFO are written to memory first; otherwise the current read or write ends; then XDMAC_CISx.DIS sets, STx clears and the channel is free. Suspend: XDMAC_GRS stops reads, XDMAC_GWS writes and XDMAC_GRWS both, at once; a transaction in progress finishes, the channel stays enabled, the FIFO keeps its contents and is not written out, and clearing the bit resumes; with writes suspended, reads go on until the FIFO is full. Flush (XDMAC_SWF): writes the FIFO to memory without disabling the channel and sets XDMAC_CISx.FIS after the last byte; reads may continue meanwhile; it matters for peripheral-to-memory transfers. Priorities: a disable on a suspended channel clears its write suspend, drains a source-synchronized FIFO and sets DIS; a disable after a flush whose last transaction is not yet scheduled cancels the flush (no FIS), otherwise both FIS and DIS set; a flush on a suspended channel writes out any pending bytes and sets FIS; a flush or a write suspend after a disable is ignored.

Channel registers are not written while the channel is active; reprogramming waits until it is disabled. XDMAC_CSAx and XDMAC_CDAx are aligned to the data width in DWIDTH. With XDMAC_CC.INITD = 0, XDMAC_CUBC.UBLEN and XDMAC_CNDA.NDA may be mid-update; to read the current descriptor and the remaining count, read NDA, INITD twice, UBLEN, INITD and NDA again, and accept UBLEN and NDA only if both NDA reads match and both later INITD reads are 1; otherwise retry.

Takes the image data stream of a CMOS sensor and writes it to memory by DMA, converting it on the way when needed. Colour sensors and grayscale sensors are both accepted; grayscale gets a reduced set of functions and its data is stored unprocessed, so it does not suit the LCD controller. A preview path delivers RGB that the LCD controller can show, with a downscaler to fit the display; a codec path delivers YCbCr. Pre-processed RGB or YCbCr input is accepted. Synchronisation is either by the ISI_VSYNC and ISI_HSYNC lines, with programmable polarity, or by the ITU-R BT.656-4 SAV and EAV codes embedded in the data, which frees the two sync pins.

ITU-R BT.601/656 8-bit sensor interface; grayscale sensors up to 12 bits; BT.656-4 SAV/EAV synchronisation; resolution to 2048 × 2048 in each direction; RGB preview at 640 × 480 at most; codec capture at 2048 × 2048 at most; a FIFO on each path; packed YCbCr 4:2:2 storage; a preview scaler; a programmable frame capture rate; VGA, QVGA, CIF and QCIF preview formats, and custom preview sizes whose width and height are multiples of 16.

The ISI pins are PIO lines assigned to the ISI peripheral function in the PIO controller. The ISI clock is enabled in the PMC before use. The ISI has one interrupt line to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the ISI.

The ISI connects directly to ITU-R BT.601/656 8-bit sensors and grayscale sensors up to 12 bits, taking up to 12 data bits, the two syncs and the ISI_PCK clock. It can interrupt when a frame begins and when a DMA frame transfer completes, and on each SAV/EAV delimiter when those are used. An 8-bit colour sensor may send YCbCr 4:2:2, RGB 8:8:8 or RGB 5:6:5. With the preview DMA channel set up and enabled, the preview path runs and writes RGB frames; its frame rate is set by ISI_CFG1.FRATE. With the codec DMA channel set up and enabled, a YCbCr 4:2:2 frame is captured once ISI_CR.ISI_CDC is set. With ISI_CFG1.FULL set both channels run together; with FULL cleared a hardware scheduler looks at FRATE: at zero a preview frame is dropped in favour of the codec frame, otherwise the codec frame waits for the next free frame slot. The codec path is best enabled only when a capture is wanted, to save bandwidth. In grayscale mode the 12-bit samples go to memory unprocessed, one or two samples per word as set by ISI_CFG2.GS_MODE, and the codec path is unavailable. A frame rate counter captures every frame or one frame in 2 to 8.

With VSYNC/HSYNC synchronisation, sampling starts on the active ISI_PCK edge once ISI_CR's SFD count of blanking lines and SLD count of ISI_PCK periods have passed. With BT.656-4 synchronisation each video block is framed by SAV (0xFF000080) at its start and EAV (0xFF00009D) at its end; only data between them is captured and blanking is ignored. Frame and line sync can only be recovered when the vertical blanking lasts one line or more.

RGB is needed for display preview and YCbCr for encoding. Sensors differ in the order they send components, so the ISI can be set to the sensor's order, which saves software reordering. RGB 5:6:5 input is shown as RGB 5:6:5, matching the 16-bit mode of the LCD controller.

The sensor's host clock ISI_MCK comes either from a PMC programmable clock output (PID 59) or from an oscillator at the sensor; using the PMC lets the system control the sensor's power. The ISI has two unsynchronised clock domains, the host clock and the sensor's ISI_PCK; ISI_MCK has to run faster than ISI_PCK.

The preview path only scales down, by one ratio for both directions, followed by fractional decimation. The decimation factor is the programmed value divided by 16; values 0 to 15 are not allowed. For a 1280 × 1024 input and a 640 × 480 output, the horizontal ratio is 2 and the vertical 2.1333, so the factor is 2, a value of 32.

operation.topic: ISI preview colour conversion and storage
operation.text: A programmable matrix converts YCbCr (or YUV) to RGB, with clipping to keep each result in range. The preview formatter packs 8:8:8 samples into RGB 5:6:5 for the 16-bit LCD format by dropping low-order bits: three from red and blue and two from green. In 12-bit grayscale mode ISI_DATA[11:0] is sampled and stored two samples per word (GS_MODE = 0) or one (GS_MODE = 1); ISI_CFG1.GRAYLE swaps the sample order within a word.

ISI_DATA[7:0] is sampled and stored, four samples per word, through the codec path. Set up ISI_CFG2 with GRAYSCALE, RGB_SWAP and COL_SPACE cleared, YCC_SWAP = 0, IM_VSIZE = vertical resolution minus 1 and IM_HSIZE = horizontal resolution divided by 2; the horizontal resolution must be even. Then set ISI_DMA_C_CTRL.C_FETCH, write the descriptor address to ISI_DMA_C_DSCR.C_DSCR and write 1 to ISI_DMA_CHER.C_CH_EN.

Each path has an asynchronous FIFO carrying formatted data from the ISI_PCK clock domain into the AHB domain. A video arbiter watches the FIFO thresholds and requests bursts from the AHB host interface. The DMA works through linked lists of frame buffer descriptors (FBD), each three words: the frame buffer address (DMA_X_ADDR), control (DMA_X_CTRL) and the next descriptor address (DMA_X_DSCR). One FBD covers a whole frame and may chain to another, so two or more frame buffers can be used in turn, on both paths. Example with two ping-pong buffers: the first FBD at 0x00030000 is written to DMA_P_DSCR and 0x00000001 to DMA_P_CTRL to start descriptor fetch; LLI_0 holds buffer address 0x02A000, control 0x00000003 and next 0x00030010; LLI_1 at 0x00030010 holds buffer 0x0003A000, control 0x00000003 and next 0x00030000, wrapping. With three preview buffers, frames n, n+1 and n+2 go to buffers 0, 1 and 2 and then wrap, while a codec request stores one full-size 4:2:2 frame in its own space.

Its colour conversion can be bypassed so YCbCr input goes straight to the formatter; with RGB input it converts RGB to YCbCr by a programmable matrix. YCbCr components are stored packed, a 32-bit word at a time, in scan-line order; planar storage is not supported. Its DMA uses linked lists like the preview path.

A 10/100 Mbit/s Ethernet MAC to IEEE 802.3, half or full duplex at both speeds; named GMAC although gigabit operation is not supported. MII or RMII to the PHY with an MDIO management interface; DMA to memory with priority queues, 8 Kbytes of transmit RAM and 4 Kbytes of receive RAM; programmable DMA burst length and endianness; RMON/MIB statistics counters; automatic pad and CRC on transmit and automatic discard of errored receive frames; IP, TCP and UDP checksum offload on receive and transmit for IPv4 and IPv6; address filtering on four 48-bit specific addresses and four type IDs, copy-all (promiscuous) mode, unicast and multicast hash matching and Wake-on-LAN; jumbo frames to 10240 bytes; full-duplex pause-frame flow control and half-duplex flow control by forced collisions; 802.1Q VLAN tags; 802.1Qbb priority flow control; programmable inter-packet gap stretch; IEEE 1588 PTP frame recognition and a time stamp unit; 802.1AS; 802.1Qav credit-based shaping on the two highest-priority queues; 802.3az Energy Efficient Ethernet.

Interfaces: MII or RMII to an external PHY, MDIO for PHY management, an APB slave for the registers, an AHB master for memory, and the GTSUCOMP output for the TSU timer comparison. GTXCK is an input only and is fed from a 25 MHz external oscillator for MII or 50 MHz for RMII. The GMAC pins are PIO lines assigned in the PIO controller; unused ones stay general I/O. The GMAC clock is enabled in the PMC before use. Its interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, with separate interrupt numbers for the priority queues.

The transmit side takes data from the FIFO and adds preamble, padding and the frame check sequence. In half duplex it follows CSMA/CD: it defers while CRS is active, and on COL sends a jam and retries after a random back-off; CRS and COL have no effect in full duplex. The receive side checks preamble, FCS, alignment and length and passes frames to address checking and the FIFO; it can take jumbo frames up to 10240 bytes and can strip the CRC. The address checker holds four 48-bit specific addresses, four type ID values and a 64-bit hash register, recognises broadcast (0xFFFFFFFFFFFF), can copy all frames, can reject untagged frames and detects Wake-on-LAN events. Receive checksum checking for IP, TCP and UDP can discard frames with bad checksums.

A 94-bit timer: bits [93:46] count seconds (GMAC_TSH and GMAC_TSL), bits [45:16] nanoseconds (GMAC_TN) and bits [15:0] sub-nanoseconds. The lower 46 bits roll over at 1 s, and an interrupt can be raised when the seconds increment. Each MCK period adds a programmable increment with about 15.2 fs resolution, and the timer can be read, written and stepped up or down in 1 ns steps over APB. GMAC_TI[7:0] is the normal increment in ns, GMAC_TISUBN adds 16 bits of sub-nanosecond increment (about 15 fs), GMAC_TI[15:8] is an alternative increment in ns and GMAC_TI[23:16] how many normal increments pass before one alternative increment (0 disables it). Example: a 10.2 MHz clock adds 98 ns for 50 cycles then 100 ns (98 ns × 50 + 100 ns = 5000 ns), GMAC_TI = 0x00326462; a 49.8 MHz clock adds 20 ns for 248 cycles then 40 ns, GMAC_TI = 0x00F82814. The 8-bit count field supports clocks up to 50 MHz in 200 kHz steps; without the alternative increment only 8, 10, 20, 25, 40, 50, 100, 125, 200 and 250 MHz would be exact. Capture registers record when PTP event frames are sent and received, each update raising an interrupt. The timer is also compared with GMAC_NSC, GMAC_SCL and GMAC_SCH (48 bits of seconds and the upper 22 bits of nanoseconds); on equality GTSUCOMP is asserted and interrupt status bit 29 can be set. GTSUCOMP can be routed to the timer to toggle TIOA11/PD21, usable as the reference for an external PLL regenerating an Ethernet AVB audio clock.

The DMA gives scatter-gather packet storage through separate receive and transmit lists of buffer descriptors, and buffers several frames in dual-port SRAM packet buffers. Full store and forward holds a whole packet: collided transmit frames are replayed from the buffer without refetching over AHB, errored receive frames are dropped before reaching AHB, and transmit checksum offload works. Partial store and forward (full duplex only, GMAC_TPSF and GMAC_RPSF) starts forwarding once a programmable watermark of data is buffered, for lower latency; the transmit watermark must be at least 20, the receive one has no limit. Manual receive packet flush is supported (GMAC_NCR.FNP, acted on only while the receive DMA is idle), and optionally automatic discard when no AHB buffer is free (GMAC_DCFGR.DDRP, off by default; with it off, frames wait in the packet buffer, which can overflow). Three words per packet at the end of the packet data hold status and statistics. A transmit frame too large for the packet buffer in full store and forward is flushed and the DMA halts with an error, so the buffer must hold the largest frame sent. After 16 failed half-duplex attempts a frame is flushed. In partial store and forward a transmit underflow ends the frame early, flushes the buffer and needs GMAC_NCR.TSTART to restart.

Received frames, optionally with FCS, go to AHB buffers of 64 bytes to 16 Kbytes (GMAC_DCFGR, default 128 bytes) listed in a descriptor queue whose base is GMAC_RBQB. Each descriptor is two words, address and status. A frame longer than one buffer fills several; the last descriptor carries the whole frame status. The first buffer of a frame may start up to three bytes late (GMAC_NCFGR bits 14 and 15), shortening it. GMAC_RBQB is written before reception is enabled and writes are ignored afterwards. The internal queue pointer steps two words per buffer and returns to the base at a descriptor with the wrap bit. A used buffer found already owned by software sets 'buffer not available', raises an interrupt and counts a resource error. A receive error recovers only the buffer being written, so a fragment can be left in earlier buffers; software sees it as a start-of-frame after a buffer without end-of-frame. With 128-byte buffers collision fragments (under 128 bytes) rarely leave such fragments. A receive overrun raises an interrupt and recovers the current buffer.

Transmit frames of 1 to 16384 bytes are built from up to 128 buffers, zero-length buffers allowed, listed in a two-word descriptor queue (byte address, then control and status) whose base is GMAC_TBQB. With automatic CRC, frames are padded to 64 bytes; without it the frame must already be at least 64 bytes. GMAC_TBQB can only be written while transmit is disabled or halted; disabling transmit (GMAC_NCR.TXEN = 0) resets the pointer to it, halting keeps it. GMAC_NCR.TSTART starts transmission and may be rewritten while active (GMAC_TSR.TXGO); transmission halts on a used descriptor, a transmit error or GMAC_NCR.THALT (after the current frame), and pauses on a received pause frame when enabled. A used bit read mid-frame is a transmit error: GTXER is asserted and the FCS is bad. After an error the frame restarts from its first descriptor when TSTART is written again.

Buffer management uses SINGLE or INCR accesses. Data transfers use SINGLE or fixed INCR4, INCR8 or INCR16 bursts chosen by GMAC_DCFGR.FBLDO, falling back to SINGLE at buffer ends and at 1-Kbyte boundaries. A fixed burst is not ended early except on an AHB error or when receive or transmit is disabled.

Six queues, each with its own descriptor lists and its own region of the transmit packet buffer. Transmit serves queues in strict priority, highest first; if every queue's next descriptor is owned by software a resource error interrupt is raised and transmission halts until TSTART is written. Queue 0 (lowest) has its transmit queue base at 0x1C, receive queue base at 0x18 and interrupt status at 0x24; the other queues' registers start at 0x440, 0x480 and 0x400. Received frames pass address filtering first and then screeners that pick a queue: type 1 screeners match the IPv4 DS field, IPv6 TC field and/or UDP destination port; type 2 screeners (GMAC_ST2RPQ) combine any of a VLAN priority match, an EtherType match against GMAC_ST2ER, and compares A, B and C, each a 16-bit masked compare (COMPVAL, MASKVAL) at an offset of 0 to 127 bytes from the frame start, after the EtherType, after the IP header or after the TCP/UDP header, drawn from a shared pool of GMAC_ST2CW0/1 registers; together they can match 48 bits such as a MAC address. All enabled compares are ANDed; when two screeners match, the one at the lower register address wins. IP fragmentation is not supported by the header decoding. With queues enabled each queue has its own interrupt line and status register for DMA events; other events go to the lowest-priority queue's interrupt.

Takes data in 32-bit words and works in bytes afterwards. Adds preamble and SFD, pads to 60 bytes and appends an inverted 32-bit CRC to reach at least 64 bytes, unless the last descriptor carries the no-CRC flag. In full duplex frames go immediately, at least 96 bit times apart. In half duplex it waits for carrier sense to drop plus 96 bit times; on collision it sends a 32-bit jam and backs off by truncated binary exponential back-off (IEEE 802.3 clause 4.2.3.2.5) using 1 to 10 bits of a pseudo-random number XORed with data, giving up after 16 attempts. At 10/100 late collisions are treated like collisions and retried up to 16 times, reported in descriptor bit 26, transmit status bit 7 and interrupt status bit 5. A DMA underrun appends a bad CRC and asserts GTXER; with packet buffers it cannot happen. With GMAC_NCFGR bit 28 set the gap can be stretched in full duplex: GMAC_IPGS[7:0] multiplies the previous frame length and GMAC_IPGS[15:8] + 1 divides it, never below 96 bits. Back pressure (GMAC_NCR) or GMAC_UR.HDFC in half duplex sends 64 bits on each incoming frame to force a collision, for half-duplex flow control.

Works on a 16-bit path; checks preamble, FCS, alignment and length and keeps the destination address for the address checker. A frame found too long is marked bad and its data stops going to memory; bad frames have their buffer recovered. GMAC_NCFGR bit 17 strips the FCS, shortening the reported length by four. Bit 26 ignores FCS errors (the error counter still counts), and without jumbo mode descriptor bit 13 then gives each frame's FCS status. Bit 16 discards frames of 64 to 1518 bytes whose measured length is shorter than their length field, counted in a 10-bit counter; length fields of 0x0600 and above are not checked.

Receive offload (GMAC_NCFGR bit 24, RXCOEN) checks the IPv4 header checksum (RFC 791) for frames with at most a 4-octet VLAN header without CFI, RFC 894 or RFC 1042 SNAP encapsulation and a valid header length, and the TCP (RFC 793) or UDP (RFC 768) checksum for unfragmented IPv4 or IPv6 packets with a good IP header. Results and SNAP status replace the type ID match bits in the descriptor; frames with a bad checksum are discarded and counted. Transmit offload (GMAC_DCFGR bit 11) needs full store and forward; the frame must be supplied without FCS (descriptor bit 16 clear). If a checksum cannot be generated, descriptor bits [22:20] give the reason and the frame is sent without substitution.

Whether a frame is stored depends on GMAC_NCFGR, on the contents of the specific address, type ID and hash registers, and on the destination address and type field the frame carries. Unless GMAC_NCFGR bit 25 is set, frames arriving while transmitting in half duplex are not copied. Each specific address is two registers: bottom (first four bytes) and top (last two); writing bottom disables it and writing top enables it. Four type ID registers each match when bit 31 is set; they reset to zero (disabled). Example for MAC address 21:43:65:87:A9:CB: GMAC_SAB1 = 0x87654321, GMAC_SAT1 = 0x0000CBA9, and type ID 0x4321 matched with GMAC_TIDM1 = 0x80004321. Broadcast frames are stored only while the no-broadcast bit is 0. Copy-all-frames stores every frame except too long, too short, FCS errored (unless bit 26) or GRXER frames. GMAC_NCFGR bit 23 stops pause frames being copied in every case.

A 64-bit hash register (bottom and top) indexed by six bits, each the XOR of every sixth bit of the 48-bit destination address: hash_index[n] = da[n] ^ da[n+6] ^ da[n+12] ^ ... ^ da[n+42] for n = 0 to 5, where da[0] is the first received bit (the multicast bit) and da[47] the last. A multicast frame (da[0] = 1) matches when multicast hash is enabled and its indexed bit is set, a unicast frame likewise with unicast hash. All ones in the hash register with multicast hash enabled receives every multicast frame.

An 802.1Q tag adds four bytes at the 13th byte; GMAC_NCFGR bit 8 accepts frames up to 1536 bytes for it. A VID of 0x000 marks a priority-tagged frame. Receive descriptor bit 21 marks a VLAN tag (type 0x8100), bit 20 a priority tag (bit 21 also set), bits 19 to 17 the priority and bit 16 the CFI. Non-VLAN frames can be discarded.

Four events, enabled by Wake on LAN register bits 16 to 19: a magic packet (destination matches specific address 1, error-free, at least six 0xFF bytes followed by 16 repeats of specific address 1); an ARP request (broadcasts allowed by GMAC_NCFGR bit 5, broadcast destination, type 0x0806, operation 0x0001, and the low 16 bits of the target protocol address equal to Wake on LAN register bits [15:0], 0x0000 never matching; VLAN tags are allowed for); a specific address 1 match; and a multicast hash match (GMAC_NCFGR bit 6 set, not broadcast). Receive must be enabled but no receive buffer is needed. ARP, address and multicast events fire even on errored frames.

The GMAC flags the message time-stamp point (SFD to end of frame) for all frames and PTP event frames. It recognises sync frames at both the IEEE 1588 addresses and the 802.1AS multicast address 0180C200000E, so both work together. A time stamp is taken when the SFD passes the MII; sync and delay_req times go to GMAC_EFTx and GMAC_EFRx, Pdelay_Req and Pdelay_Resp times to GMAC_PEFTx and GMAC_PEFRx, each optionally interrupting; filtering must still be set up for the frame to reach memory. Four encapsulations are recognised: 1588 v1 over UDP/IPv4, and 1588 v2 over UDP/IPv4, UDP/IPv6 and Ethernet multicast. Version 1 sync and delay request frames are TCP/IP type, UDP, destination IP 224.0.1.129 to 132, UDP port 319, control field 0x00 (sync) or 0x01 (delay request). Version 2 frames are told by the message type in the first PTP byte: sync 0x0, delay_req 0x1, Pdelay_Req 0x2, Pdelay_Resp 0x3. At multicast address 011B19000000 sync and delay request are recognised; at 0180C200000E sync, Pdelay_Req and Pdelay_Resp.

Reception: with GMAC_NCFGR bit 13 set, a valid pause frame (destination specific address 1 or 0x0180C2000001, type 0x8808, opcode 0x0001, no FCS error) loads the pause time register, and after the current frame no new frame is sent until it counts down, every 512 bit times (every GTXCK cycle with the retry-test bit 12). This only happens in full duplex; the interrupt fires in either. Interrupt status bit 12 marks a non-zero quantum, bit 13 a zero quantum or the count reaching zero. 802.3 pause frames are ignored once PFC has been negotiated. Transmission: GMAC_NCR bit 11 sends a pause frame with the quantum from the transmit pause quantum register (reset 0xFFFF), bit 12 one with zero quantum; full duplex and transmit enable are needed. The frame goes to 01-80-C2-00-00-01 from specific address 1 with type 88-08, opcode 00-01, the quantum, zero fill and a valid FCS, and sets interrupt status bit 14.

With GMAC_NCR bit 16 set, the GMAC receives classic and PFC pause frames; after the first PFC frame it acts only on PFC frames. A valid PFC frame (opcode 0x0101) loads up to eight pause time registers, one per priority, in full duplex only; they count down every 512 bit times from reception. GMAC_NCR bit 17 sends a PFC frame built from the transmit PFC pause register: bits [7:0] are the priority enable vector, and for each priority a 0 in bits [15:8] takes the transmit pause quantum and a 1 sends zero.

The transmit path can enter low-power idle (LPI) when it has nothing to send and the link partner's state can drive the receive path low-power, each direction independently, without dropping the link or frames. Both sides must advertise EEE in auto-negotiation. LPI is requested on the MII transmit lines as the code 0x01 on txd while tx_er is high and tx_en is low, and not before 1 s of continuous link; the PHY then sends sleep, goes quiet and refreshes periodically, and LPI ends after normal idle for the wake time. Firmware control is recommended: advertise EEE with next-page auto-negotiation; set GMAC_NCR.TXLPIEN after 1 s of link with nothing to send and clear it to wake; for receive enable the RXLPIS interrupt, which signals LPI start and, on clearing, the return of normal idle.

Applies to queues 5 and 4, the top two priorities, and is switched on in the CBS control register. A queue may transmit only with non-negative credit; while waiting it gains credit at its IdleSlope (GMAC_CBSISQx), which must be below the port transmit rate; while sending it loses credit at sendSlope = portTransmitRate − IdleSlope and can go negative until its frame ends. The maximum IdleSlope is portTransmitRate divided by the bits per MII clock: 0x17D7840 at 100 Mbit/s. The highest-priority queue always goes first regardless of credit.

MII uses txd[3:0] and rxd[3:0], RMII txd[1:0] and rxd[1:0], both for 10/100 operation; the speed bit in GMAC_NCFGR picks 10 or 100 Mbit/s. Jumbo frames up to 10240 bytes are enabled in GMAC_NCFGR (outside IEEE 802.3, normally off); larger frames are then discarded.

Configuration such as loopback is changed with transmit and receive disabled, in three separate writes to the network control register: disable, change, re-enable. Receive list: allocate N buffers of the DMA buffer length and an 8N-byte descriptor list, mark every entry owned by the GMAC (word 0 bit 0 = 0), set the wrap bit (word 0 bit 1) on the last, write the list address to the receive queue pointer, then enable reception via the address registers and network control. Transmit list: N buffers of 1 to 2047 bytes, up to 128 per frame, an 8N-byte list with word 1 bit 31 = 0, wrap bit 30 on the last, then the transmit queue pointer and network control. The queue pointers of every queue, used or not, must point to used descriptors. Address pairs are written bottom first; matching for a pair stops on the bottom write and resumes on the top write, at any time.

Writing the PHY maintenance register shifts a management frame (IEEE 802.3 clause 22.2.4.5) out on MDIO, MSB first, while the LSB fills from MDIO, one bit per MDC cycle; completion sets network status bit 2 and an interrupt, about 2000 MCK cycles later with GMAC_NCFGR bits 18:16 at 010. MDC, divided from MCK by a three-bit field in GMAC_NCFGR, must not exceed 2.5 MHz (400 ns minimum period).

18 interrupt conditions are ORed onto the interrupt lines. The interrupt status register clears on read by default and can be made write-one-to-clear. All interrupts are disabled at reset; enable and disable registers set them, and a 1 in the mask register means disabled.

To send: enable transmit, place the data in memory (not necessarily contiguous, any byte length), fill the descriptors (address in word 0, control and length in word 1), write the first descriptor's address to the transmit queue pointer, enable interrupts and set TSTART. A received frame is stored when it matches a specific address, a type ID, the hash, an allowed broadcast, or copy-all; the descriptor is then updated with the match reason and handed to software, and receive complete is flagged. Software copies the data out and returns the buffer by clearing the ownership bit. Overrun and buffer-not-available set their own interrupts; a failed frame is counted and silently dropped.

Counters from 0x100 to 0x1B0: octets, frames, broadcast, multicast and pause frames sent and received; frames sent and received by size (64, 65–127, 128–255, 256–511, 512–1023, 1024–1518, above 1518 bytes); transmit underruns, single, multiple, excessive and late collisions, deferred frames, carrier sense errors; undersize, oversize and jabber frames, FCS, length field, symbol and alignment errors, receive resource errors and overruns; IP header, TCP and UDP checksum errors. Each clears on read and sticks at all ones; receive counters count only while RXEN is set. Read bits 31:0 of the octet counters before bits 47:32.

A USB 2.0 device and host controller at high speed (480 Mbit/s), full speed (12 Mbit/s) and low speed (1.5 Mbit/s), with an on-chip UTMI transceiver and its pull-ups and pull-downs, 4096 bytes of dual-port RAM (DPRAM) for pipe and endpoint data, and pipe/endpoint management with dedicated DMA channels. Each pipe/endpoint takes one transfer type and one, two or three DPRAM banks (up to 3, not for the control endpoint); with two or three banks the CPU or DMA works on one bank while the core uses another, which isochronous pipes/endpoints require. High-bandwidth isochronous transfers work in device mode only, and mixed-speed devices behind a hub may not be supported.

Normal mode (SPDCONF = 0) offers high, full and low speed and needs the 480 MHz UTMI PLL (USB_480M). Low-power mode (SPDCONF = 1) offers full and low speed only and needs just the 48 MHz USB_48M clock. The bus interface clock comes from the PMC; the USBHS is best disabled before its clock is stopped, so it is not frozen in an undefined state, and is enabled (USBHS_CTRL.USBE = 1, FRZCLK = 0) before the USB clock is enabled in the PMC. Start-up in normal mode: turn on the peripheral clock (PMC_PCER); set UIMOD, USBE = 1 and FRZCLK = 0; start the 480 MHz UPLL; wait for the PMC to report it locked. Start-up in low-power mode: set USB_48M to 48 MHz from PLLA or the already running UPLL through PMC_USB (source and divider); turn on the peripheral clock (PMC_PCER); set SPDCONF = 1; set UIMOD, USBE = 1 and FRZCLK = 0; set USBCK in PMC_SCER.

operation.topic: USBHS pins, interrupt and FIFO access
operation.text: HSDM/DM and HSDP/DP are the differential data lines. VBUS is controlled from an ordinary PIO line set up in the I/O controller; the USBHS does not generate VBUS, which must come from the board. One interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller. Each pipe/endpoint FIFO is reached through its own 32-Kbyte address window; the hardware steps the DPRAM address, so a 64-Kbyte buffer can be accessed linearly or at a fixed address, by byte, half-word or word, in big-endian order. Disabling the USBHS does not clear the DPRAM.

After a hardware reset the USBHS is disabled (USBE = 0), its clock is stopped (FRZCLK = 1), the UTMI is suspended, device and host states and registers are reset, and the DPRAM keeps its contents and stays accessible. Writing USBE = 1 enters device mode (UIMOD = 1) or host mode (UIMOD = 0) in the idle state. Writing USBE = 0 at any time acts as a hardware reset, except that FRZCLK, UIMOD and USBHS_DEVCTRL.LS keep their values. One interrupt vector serves the whole interface; its sources are processing events and exception (error) events.

In device mode USBHS_DEVISR.SUSP flags a suspended bus and the transceiver suspends itself. With the bus suspended, writing FRZCLK = 1 freezes the USBHS clock to save power; only FRZCLK, USBE and USBHS_DEVCTRL.LS remain accessible, and only the asynchronous wake-up interrupts (USBHS_DEVISR.WAKEUP, USBHS_HSTISR.HWUPI) can raise the USB interrupt.

In device mode the USBHS picks full or high speed while the host drives the bus reset, following what the host supports, then enables or disables the high-speed terminations and pull-up; USBHS_DEVCTRL.SPDCONF can also be set. In host mode internal pull-downs sit on D+ and D− and the speed of the attached device is reported in USBHS_SR.SPEED.

Pipes/endpoints are allocated in ascending order from 0 and should be configured in that order. Setting ALLOC for pipe/endpoint x inserts its DPRAM area between x−1 and x+1: the area of x+1 slides up and its data is lost, while x+2 and beyond do not move. Clearing ALLOC frees the area and x+1 slides down, again losing its data. Disabling a pipe (USBHS_HSTPIP.PENx = 0) or endpoint (USBHS_DEVEPT.EPENx = 0) keeps ALLOC and the configuration (pipe banks, size, token, type, endpoint number and interrupt frequency; endpoint banks, size, direction and type). Example: with 0 to 5 allocated, disabling 3 keeps its memory; freeing it slides 4 down but not 5; reallocating 3 larger slides 4 up into 5, so the two overlap and their data may be lost. Pipe/endpoint 0 data is never lost unless 0 itself is freed. Disabling and re-enabling a pipe/endpoint with the same configuration moves nothing in the DPRAM. CFGOK is set after ALLOC only when the size and bank count are within that pipe/endpoint's limits and the DPRAM size; it does not detect overlaps.

The pad is idle while the USBHS is disabled or USBHS_DEVCTRL.DETACH = 1, or after a bus suspend is detected: its differential receiver is off and strong 15 kΩ pull-downs on HSDP/DP and HSDM/DM keep the lines from floating. It is active when USBE = 1 and DETACH = 0. Detecting suspend sets SUSP and clears WAKEUP and idles the pad; any non-idle bus event sets WAKEUP, clears SUSP and wakes the pad.

High, full and low speed, the default control endpoint plus further endpoints configurable as isochronous, bulk or interrupt. Device mode starts idle with minimum pad current. After a hardware reset its clock is stopped, its registers reset, endpoint banks freed and neither D+ nor D− pulled up (DETACH = 1); clearing DETACH connects the pull-up for the chosen speed. Enabling with UIMOD = 1 enters the idle state without needing the USB clock. Disabling the USBHS or choosing host mode resets device mode.

operation.topic: USBHS device USB reset and endpoint reset
operation.text: A host-driven bus reset disables every endpoint but the default control endpoint, resets that endpoint and its data toggle, and sets USBHS_DEVISR.EORST at the end; a high-speed host gives a high-speed reset, and USBHS_SR.SPEED gives the result. Writing USBHS_DEVEPT.EPRSTx resets an endpoint's state machine, bank counters and registers, keeping its configuration and data toggle; it is advised after a hardware or bus reset. USBHS_DEVEPTISRx interrupt flags are not cleared by a bus reset. RSTDTS also clears the data toggle, for CLEAR_FEATURE. Clearing EPRSTx ends the reset.

A disabled endpoint is held inactive and reset, DTSEQ included. To activate: set USBHS_DEVEPT.EPENx; configure type, direction, size and banks in USBHS_DEVEPTCFGx and set ALLOC; then check CFGOK. Until CFGOK is set the controller does not acknowledge host packets to the endpoint.

After any reset the address is 0. On a SET_ADDRESS request, write the address to USBHS_DEVCTRL.UADD with ADDEN = 0, answer with a zero-length IN on endpoint 0, then set ADDEN; UADD and ADDEN are not written together. The controller then accepts only packets for UADD. UADD and ADDEN clear on a hardware reset, on USBE = 0 and on a USB reset, returning the address to 0.

operation.topic: USBHS device suspend, wake-up, detach and remote wake-up
operation.text: After 3 ms of idle bus SUSP is set and FRZCLK may be written to 1; on WAKEUP (any non-idle event) FRZCLK is written back to 0. SUSP and WAKEUP each clear the other. DETACH resets to 1; writing 1 then 0 forces re-enumeration. Remote wake-up, when the host has allowed it, is sent only after SUSP: writing USBHS_DEVCTRL.RMWKUP sends an upstream resume (the controller does it after 5 ms of bus inactivity), which sets UPRSM and clears SUSP; RMWKUP clears at the end, and EORSM is set when the host's end of resume is seen.

STALLRQS sets STALLRQ, so every following request is discarded and answered with STALL, each setting STALLEDI and the endpoint interrupt, until STALLRQ is cleared by STALLRQC or, on a control endpoint, by a new SETUP. A SETUP to a stalled control endpoint sets RXSTPI, clears STALLRQ and STALLEDI and is acknowledged, so firmware can stall an unsupported request and wait for the next SETUP. A retry takes priority over a STALL.

A SETUP is always acknowledged and sets RXSTPI (not RXOUTI). FIFOCON and RWALL do not apply to control endpoints and read 0. RXSTPI and RXOUTI are cleared by firmware to accept the packet and free the bank; TXINI is cleared to send an IN packet. In a control write, firmware may send the zero-length status packet early if it knows the byte count, or wait for NAKINI. In a control read, the first status-stage token is always NAKed; once the status stage is detected, anything the CPU has put in the bank is discarded and a TXINI clear has no effect. The OUT retry is always acknowledged and sets both RXOUTI and TXINI, handled by setting TXINI, waiting for RXOUTI or TXINI, and returning on RXOUTI. A SETUP has priority over everything, so on a SETUP all other flags are cleared and the FIFO reset. A zero-length OUT packet resets the byte counter.

TXINI and FIFOCON are set together when the current bank is free, interrupting if TXINE = 1. Firmware clears TXINI (TXINIC), writes through USBFIFOnDATA until the whole frame is in or the bank fills (RWALL clears, BYCT reaches the endpoint size), then clears FIFOCON (FIFOCONC) to send it and move to the next bank; TXINI is always cleared before FIFOCON. With several banks one is filled while the host reads another, so TXINI may be set again at once. A zero-length OUT during the IN stage of a control or isochronous transfer is an abort: disable the TXINI interrupt, and if banks are busy kill the last written bank with KILLBKS and wait for KILLBK to clear, repeating until NBUSYBK = 0, then reset the endpoint with EPRSTx.

RXOUTI and FIFOCON are set together when the current bank is full, interrupting if RXOUTE = 1. Firmware clears RXOUTI (RXOUTIC), reads BYCT for the byte count, reads the data through USBFIFOnDATA until the bank is empty (RWALL clears, BYCT = 0), then clears FIFOCON to free it and move on; RXOUTI is always cleared before FIFOCON. With several banks one is read while the host fills another. At high speed the USBHS handles PING and NYET: with one bank it answers bulk OUT with NYET (accepted, no room for the next); with two banks it answers ACK while the second bank is free.

Underflow (isochronous only, UNDERFI): the host reads an empty IN bank, and a zero-length packet is sent automatically; or the host sends OUT data into a full bank, and the packet is lost. Overflow (all types, OVERFI): an OUT packet larger than the bank is acknowledged, RXOUTI is set and the bank keeps the first bytes that fit. High-bandwidth isochronous IN error (HBISOINERRI): at the end of a microframe with at least one packet sent, fewer banks were validated than NBTRANS asks (for example 2 of 3), also giving UNDERFI with a zero-length packet unless an IN token was missing. High-bandwidth isochronous IN flush: if an IN token is missing in a microframe, that microframe's remaining banks are discarded to keep host and device aligned. CRC error (isochronous OUT only, CRCERRI): a corrupted packet is still stored and RXOUTI set.

Global processing: suspend, start of frame and micro start of frame without frame-number CRC error (USBHS_DEVFNUM.FNCERR = 0), end of reset, wake-up, end of resume, upstream resume, endpoint x, DMA channel x. Global exception: SOF or micro SOF with a frame-number CRC error. Endpoint processing: transmitted IN, received OUT, received SETUP, short packet, number of busy banks, isochronous MDATA and DATAX received. Endpoint exception: underflow, NAKed OUT, high-bandwidth isochronous IN error, NAKed IN, high-bandwidth isochronous IN flush, overflow, STALLed, CRC error, transaction error. DMA processing: end of USB transfer, end of channel buffer, descriptor loaded; no DMA exception.

Setting USBHS_DEVCTRL.TSTPCKT makes the transceiver send the packet in the current bank over and over, for measuring rise and fall times, eye pattern and jitter: set TSTPCKT, put the data in an endpoint bank, clear FIFOCON. Clearing TSTPCKT ends the mode, and the endpoint is then reset by software.

In host mode each pipe corresponds to an endpoint of the attached device, set up from the device's configuration descriptors. Enabling with UIMOD = 0 enters idle, waiting for a connection at minimum power with the pad idle; a connection enters the ready state, which needs no USB clock. Clearing USBHS_HSTCTRL.SOFE stops SOFs and suspends the bus; generating SOFs again leaves suspend. A device is detected when D+ or D− is pulled up, provided USBHS_SFR.VBUSRQS = 1; disconnection when both are pulled down.

operation.topic: USBHS host USB reset and pipe reset
operation.text: USBHS_HSTCTRL.RESET sends a bus reset and RSTI is set when done; all pipes are then disabled and freed. If the bus was suspended (SOFE = 0) the USBHS goes to resume, sets HWUPI and sets SOFE so SOFs follow the reset. The device speed is then read from USBHS_SR.SPEED. USBHS_HSTPIP.PRSTx resets a pipe's state machine, bank counters and registers, keeping its configuration and data toggle; RSTDTS also clears the toggle; clearing PRSTx ends it. A reset is advised before using a pipe after a hardware or bus reset.

operation.topic: USBHS pipe activation and host address
operation.text: A disabled pipe is held inactive and reset, DTSEQ included. To activate: set USBHS_HSTPIP.PENx; set INTFRQ, PEPNUM, PTYPE, PTOKEN, PSIZE and PBK in USBHS_HSTPIPCFGx and set ALLOC; check CFGOK, without which no packet is sent. Once configured only PTOKEN and INTFRQ may be written; INTFRQ matters for interrupt pipes only. At enumeration the device descriptor's bMaxPacketSize0 is used to resize the default control pipe. After a USB reset and SET_ADDRESS, the new address goes to HSTADDR.HSTADDRPx for each pipe; a USB reset returns it to 0.

operation.topic: USBHS host suspend and remote wake-up
operation.text: Clearing SOFE stops SOFs and the device suspends 3 ms later. A non-idle bus sets HWUPI, and an upstream resume (K state) also sets RXRSMI; firmware must then send a downstream resume within 1 ms lasting at least 20 ms by setting USBHS_HSTCTRL.RESUME, after first setting SOFE, or RESUME has no effect.

operation.topic: USBHS host control, IN and OUT pipes
operation.text: A control transfer has SETUP, data and status stages, and firmware changes the pipe token for each; the initial data toggles are DATA0 for SETUP and DATA1 for IN and OUT. IN pipes: INMODE = 0 sends INRQ + 1 IN requests and then freezes the pipe, INMODE = 1 keeps requesting while the pipe is unfrozen; requests start when PFREEZE is cleared. RXINI and FIFOCON are set when a bank is full; firmware clears RXINI, reads the data and clears FIFOCON. OUT pipes, configured and unfrozen: TXOUTI and FIFOCON are set when a bank is free; firmware clears TXOUTI, writes the data and clears FIFOCON to send. Suspending (SOFE = 0) with a bank ready leaves suspend and sends it. At high speed the host runs PING automatically, tunable with PINGEN and BINTERVAL in USBHS_HSTPIPCFGx. A CRC error on an isochronous IN pipe sets CRCERRI and still stores the packet.

Global processing: device connection, device disconnection, USB reset sent, downstream resume sent, upstream resume received, host SOF, host wake-up, pipe x, DMA channel x; no global exception. Pipe processing: received IN, transmitted OUT, transmitted SETUP, short packet, number of busy banks. Pipe exception: underflow, pipe error, NAKed, overflow, received STALL, CRC error. DMA processing: end of USB transfer, end of channel buffer, descriptor loaded; no DMA exception.

Transfers use sequential addresses with word incrementing bursts of unspecified length, up to 256 beats, for data and descriptor loading; a burst may span a whole USB packet unless broken by arbitration or a 1-Kbyte boundary. Bursts may be locked per DMA buffer so they are not broken by other masters, giving up to 128-word unbroken bursts for bulk and 256 words for isochronous, limited by the smaller of the pipe/endpoint size and BUFF_LENGTH. Average throughput approaches 480 Mbit/s. Word access needs a quarter of the AHB bandwidth of byte access; with zero-wait-state word bursts from the other slaves, each DMA AHB bus needs under 60 % of its bandwidth at 33 MHz and under 30 % at 66 MHz for full USB rate. Channels follow chained lists of transfer descriptors in memory: offset 0 the next descriptor address (USBHS_xxxDMANXTDSCx), offset 4 the AHB address (USBHS_xxxDMAADDRESSx), offset 8 the control word (USBHS_xxxDMACONTROLx), each aligned to its offset. Write the first descriptor's address to USBHS_xxxDMANXTDSCx and set LDNXT_DSC; the descriptor loads on the next packet request of the pipe/endpoint.

A card host for MultiMedia Card V4.3, SD Memory Card V2.0, SDIO V2.0 and CE-ATA V1.1. Command, response and data registers, timeout counters and error detection send commands and collect responses and data with little CPU work. The card clock runs up to the host clock divided by 2. One slot, used either for a high-speed MMC bus of up to 30 cards or for one SD card, chosen in the SD card register. SD uses 9 pins (clock, command, four data, three power), MMC 7 (clock, command, one data, three power, one reserved). The SD interface also runs MMC; the two differ in initialisation and bus topology. Also: boot operation mode, high-speed mode, clock slow-down when idle, stream, block and multi-block transfers, a 16- to 256-byte FIFO with a large aperture for incrementing access, the CE-ATA completion signal disable command, and write protection of the configuration registers. Dedicated hardware issues the CE-ATA command completion signal and captures the host's completion signal disable.

The card pins are PIO lines assigned to the HSMCI in the PIO controllers. The HSMCI clock is enabled in the PMC first.
