One interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the HSMCI. With SD cards, HSMCI_SDCR.SDCBUS selects a 1-bit (0) or 4-bit (1) data bus; MMC uses only data line 0, and the other data lines are free as PIOs. The MMC bus is a 13-pin serial bus with three signal lines and four supply lines; the MMC cards on a slot share MCDA0, MCCDA and MCCK.

After power-on the cards are initialised by a message protocol of three tokens: commands, sent on CMD to one card or all; responses, sent on CMD by the addressed card or by all cards together; and data, on the data lines. Cards get a session address during initialisation and are told apart by their unique CID. Addressed operations always have a command and a response, and some a data token. All bits move synchronously with the HSMCI clock. Sequential (stream) commands run until a stop command; block commands send blocks with CRC, single or multiple, ended by a stop command or by a preset block count.

The HSMCI is enabled by HSMCI_CR.MCIEN. With PWSEN set, the clock is divided by 2^PWSDIV + 1 while the bus is idle. RDPROOF and WRPROOF in HSMCI_MR stop the clock when the FIFO is full during reads or writes, protecting data at the cost of bandwidth. HSMCI_CMDR selects open-drain or push-pull bus mode per command. To send a command, write the argument to HSMCI_ARGR and then HSMCI_CMDR; the command goes out at once. No command may be sent while the card signals busy (for example after CMD12); HSMCI_SR.NOTBUSY shows its release. Responses of 48 to 136 bits are read from HSMCI_RSPR. Flow: write ARGR and CMDR, wait for CMDRDY, check the error flags, read the response if any, and for a command with busy wait for NOTBUSY; interrupts via HSMCI_IER can replace polling. The CRC error flag is always set for SEND_OP_COND because of its R3 response.

HSMCI_CMDR.TRTYP selects single block, multiple block, stream and the rest. BLKLEN in HSMCI_MR or HSMCI_BLKR sets the block size. Multiple-block transfers are either open-ended, running until a stop command, or (MMC 3.1 and later) with a preset count in HSMCI_BLKR.BCNT of 1 to 65535 blocks, needing no stop command unless an error ends them; BCNT = 0 means unlimited. Single-block read without DMA: select the card, set the block length (SET_BLOCKLEN and HSMCI_BLKR), clear HSMCI_DMA.DMAEN, send READ_SINGLE_BLOCK, then read HSMCI_RDR each time RXRDY is set, BlockLength/4 words in all; with DMA, set DMAEN, set the DMA source, length BlockLength/4 and enable the channel, send the command and wait for XFRDONE. Writes go the same way through HSMCI_TDR and TXRDY. HSMCI_MR.PADV sets the padding byte for a partial block: 0x00 when 0, 0xFF when 1.

operation.topic: HSMCI transfers with the DMA controller
operation.text: Write: wait for CMDRDY and NOTBUSY; set the block length in the card and in the HSMCI; set HSMCI_MR.FBYTE when the length is not a multiple of 4; send WRITE_SINGLE_BLOCK (HSMCI_ARGR then HSMCI_CMDR); choose a free DMA channel, clear its old interrupts by reading DMAC_CISx, set the source to the data and the destination to the HSMCI FIFO address, DWIDTH = WORD for lengths that are a multiple of 4 and BYTE otherwise, CSIZE to match HSMCI_DMA.CHKSIZE, UBLEN = block_length/4 (or block_length when not a multiple of 4); enable the channel; wait for XFRDONE. Read: the same, with HSMCI_MR.RDPROOF set to avoid overflow, the source at the HSMCI FIFO address and a word-aligned destination.

SD and SDIO cards follow the MMC format with a slightly thicker body, faster transfers, a write-lock switch and security features; SDIO cards bring functions such as GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, modems and cameras. They use 9 pins and differ from MMC mainly in initialisation. HSMCI_SDCR selects the slot and bus width; after power-up a card uses DAT0 only and the host may widen the bus after initialisation. SDIO transfers are byte mode (1 to 512 bytes) or optional block mode (1 to 511 blocks), chosen by TRTYP, with the count in HSMCI_BLKR.BCNT and, in block mode, the block size in BLKLEN; SD memory cards use blocks only. Suspend and resume for multi-function and combo cards are sent through HSMCI_CMDR.IOSPCMD. SDIO card interrupts arrive on DAT[1], are enabled in HSMCI_IER and are sampled whichever slot is selected.

CE-ATA carries the ATA command set over MMC, with the ATA task file in MMC register space, using CMD0 (GO_IDLE_STATE, hard reset), CMD12 (STOP_TRANSMISSION, aborts the running ATA command), CMD39 (FAST_IO, one 8-bit task file register), CMD60 (RW_MULTIPLE_REGISTERS, issues an ATA command or reaches control/status) and CMD61 (RW_MULTIPLE_BLOCK, data), and the MMC initialisation sequence. Polled command: CMD60 with READ_DMA_EXT for 8 KB, poll the ATA status until DRQ, CMD61 for the data, poll until DRQ and BSY are 0. Interrupt command: CMD60 with nIEN = 0 to enable the completion signal, CMD61, wait for the completion signal interrupt. To abort before completion, send the completion signal disable command (HSMCI_CMDR.SPCMD = 3) to avoid a collision on CMD. Failures include no response, a bad command or response CRC, a bad data CRC16, ATA ERR set, and a completion timeout. After a timeout: send completion signal disable if nIEN was 0 and the CMD61 response came, then CMD12 with its R1 response, then a software reset through CMD39; if that fails, CMD0 resets the device completely and it must be initialised again. ATA ERR with correct MMC exchanges needs no recovery and the command may be retried.

The MMC device sends boot data when CMD is held low after power-on before CMD1, from the boot or user area. Processor mode: set the bus width in HSMCI_SDCR.SDCBUS to match the device's BOOT_BUS_WIDTH; set BLKLEN = 512 and BCNT to the block count; write HSMCI_CMDR with SPCMD = BOOTREQ, TRDIR = read, TRCMD = start transfer, and BOOT_ACK = 1 if the device's BOOT_ACK is 1; copy data on each RXRDY; end with SPCMD = BOOTEND. DMA mode: the same, with DMA enabled in HSMCI_DMA and a DMA channel set up for the total length before BOOTREQ.

operation.topic: HSMCI transfer done and write protection
operation.text: HSMCI_SR.XFRDONE marks exactly when a read or write sequence ends; CMDRDY is released 8 bit times after the end of the card response, and on writes the card holds D0 until it is done. HSMCI_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the mode, data timeout, SD card/SDIO, completion signal timeout, DMA configuration and configuration registers; a write to one sets HSMCI_WPSR.WPVS, WPVSRC names the register, and reading HSMCI_WPSR clears WPVS.

A synchronous serial port working as host or client, for external devices or another processor. The host drives the clock and the data flow; several CPUs may take turns as host. A host can shift data into many clients at once but only one client may drive data back at a time. Each client is selected by its own chip select (NPCS) driving the client's NSS. Lines: MOSI (host out, client in), MISO (host in, client out, one client at a time), SPCK (clock from the host, one pulse per bit, at a range of baud rates) and NSS (client select).

Host or client; 8- to 16-bit data length, clock phase and polarity, delay between consecutive transfers and delay before SPCK, all set per chip select; a programmable delay between chip selects; optional mode fault detection. In host mode SPCK reaches the peripheral clock rate at most, and the bit rate need not follow the core or peripheral clock. Client mode runs on SPCK, asynchronous to the core and bus clocks. Four chip selects, decodable externally for up to 15 peripherals. Suits serial memories (DataFlash, 3-wire EEPROMs), serial peripherals (ADCs, DACs, LCD controllers, CAN controllers, sensors) and coprocessors. One DMA channel each for receive and transmit. Register write protection.

The SPI pins are PIO lines assigned to the SPI in the PIO controllers. The SPI clock is enabled in the PMC first. One interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the SPI. The DMA controller can serve the SPI to cut processor load.

SPI_MR.MSTR = 1 selects host mode: NPCS0 to NPCS3 are outputs, SPCK is driven, MISO feeds the receiver and MOSI is driven by the transmitter. MSTR = 0 selects client mode: MISO is driven by the transmitter, MOSI feeds the receiver, SPCK clocks the receiver, NPCS0 becomes the NSS input and NPCS1 to NPCS3 are not driven and free for other uses. Transfers are programmed the same way in both modes; the baud rate generator runs only in host mode.
CPOL and NCPHA in SPI_CSRx give four combinations that are mutually incompatible, so host and client must match; a host talking to clients with different settings reconfigures itself for each.

The host runs from its baud rate generator and drives the chip select and SPCK. SPI_TDR and SPI_RDR are holding registers around one shift register. With the SPI enabled, writing SPI_TDR starts a transfer: the data moves to the shift register, goes out on MOSI while MISO is shifted in. Data cannot be received without sending; send dummy data (SPI_TDR all ones) if needed. With SPI_MR.WDRBT set, a transfer waits until SPI_RDR has been read. When only sending (to an LCD, say) the receive flags can be ignored. SPI_MR.PCS selects the client before SPI_TDR is written. Data written during a transfer waits in SPI_TDR until the current one ends. TDRE clears when SPI_TDR is written and sets when its data moves to the shift register; it triggers the transmit DMA channel. TXEMPTY marks the end of the transfer, after DLYBCT if that is non-zero, when the peripheral clock may be stopped. Both flags are set when the SPI is enabled. RDRF sets when received data reaches SPI_RDR and clears when it is read; data arriving before SPI_RDR is read sets OVRES (cleared by reading SPI_SR) while SPI_RDR keeps being loaded.

SPCK is the peripheral clock divided by SPI_CSRx.SCBR, 1 to 255; SCBR = 1 gives the peripheral clock (the maximum SPCK frequency is set in the electrical characteristics). SCBR resets to 0 and must be set before the first transfer, since a transfer with SCBR = 0 is unpredictable. Each chip select has its own divider, so the baud rate follows the selected peripheral.

SPI_MR.DLYBCS, common to all chip selects, is the delay between deasserting one chip select and asserting another, covering the client's deactivation time; it need not be set with a single client and is set for the slowest client otherwise. SPI_CSRx.DLYBS, per chip select, is the delay from chip select to the first SPCK edge, covering the client's activation time. SPI_CSRx.DLYBCT, per chip select, is the delay between consecutive transfers, giving the client time to process data.

NPCS0 to NPCS3 are high before and after each transfer by default. Fixed peripheral select (SPI_MR.PS = 0): SPI_MR.PCS chooses the one peripheral and SPI_TDR.PCS is ignored. Variable peripheral select (PS = 1): each SPI_TDR write carries its own PCS, written in one access as 7 unused bits, LASTXFER (optional, per CSAAT), 4 unused bits, the 4-bit PCS and 8 to 16 bits of data. If LASTXFER is used it is issued after the last character; alternatively, after the DMA transfer wait for TXEMPTY and write SPIDIS to SPI_CR, which releases NPCS after the last character without changing the configuration. With the DMA, fixed mode moves 8- or 16-bit data to one peripheral (SPI_MR must be rewritten to change it); variable mode needs 32-bit buffers with data in the low bits and PCS and LASTXFER in the high bits, using more memory but reaching several peripherals with no CPU work.

SPI_MR.PCSDEC lets an external 1-of-n decoder on NPCS0 to NPCS3 address up to 15 clients; the PCS value is output directly, and 0xF (all high) is the idle state, which is why 15 and not 16. Without decoding only one NPCS line is ever low; if PCS has two bits low only the lowest-numbered line is driven. Each of SPI_CSR0 to SPI_CSR3 then sets the format for four decoded peripherals (SPI_CSR0 for PCS 0x0 to 0x3, and so on), so compatible peripherals must share each group 0–3, 4–7, 8–11 and 12–14. When CSAAT is used, with or without DMA, mode fault detection on NPCS0 must be disabled.

Without DMA, the chip select stays low between transfers to the same peripheral only if software reloads SPI_TDR before the current transfer ends, which interrupts or other tasks may prevent, especially with DLYBCT = 0. SPI_CSRx.CSAAT = 1 keeps the chip select low until a transfer to another chip select, and setting SPI_CR.LASTXFER after the last data releases it. With DMA, reloads are faster but still not guaranteed in time, so CSAAT and LASTXFER are the only safe way for clients that need the select held. Conversely, for clients that need a deselect after every transfer, SPI_CSRx.CSNAAT = 1 (used only when CSAAT = 0) raises the chip select for DLYBCS between transfers.

For multi-host buses the SPI watches NPCS0/NSS: in host mode a low level driven on it by another host is a mode fault, which sets SPI_SR.MODF (until SPI_SR is read) and disables the SPI until SPI_CR.SPIEN is written again. NPCS0, MOSI, MISO and SPCK are then set open-drain in the PIO controller. Detection is on by default and SPI_MR.MODFDIS turns it off.

The SPI clocks on SPCK once NSS is low, shifting out on MISO and sampling MOSI, with the length, polarity and phase of SPI_CSR0 (the other chip select registers have no effect). Received data goes to SPI_RDR and sets RDRF; data arriving before SPI_RDR is read sets OVRES, cleared by reading SPI_SR. A transfer sends the shift register's content: the most recent SPI_TDR value, or failing that the most recently received character, or zeros after reset. The first SPI_TDR write goes straight to the shift register and sets TDRE; later writes wait in SPI_TDR, the latest being loaded at the next transfer, so a variable can be updated often. If nothing new was written, SPI_TDR is sent again and UNDES is set. If NSS rises with a character length different from SPI_CSR0.BITS, SFERR is set.

SPI_WPMR.WPEN protects the mode and chip select registers, WPCREN the control register and WPITEN the interrupt enable and disable registers. A write to a protected register sets SPI_WPSR.WPVS, WPVSRC names the register, and reading SPI_WPSR clears WPVS.

A synchronous serial host port. In SPI mode it talks to peripherals like converters (ADC, DAC), LCD and CAN controllers or sensors; in serial memory mode it drives serial Flash and lets the system execute code straight from it (XIP) without copying to RAM, the Flash appearing in the memory map like any other memory. Quad SPI lets small, cheap serial Flash stand in for larger parallel Flash. Stacked devices whose address space rolls over at each die boundary are not supported.

SPI mode: host only, programmable clock phase and polarity, programmable delays (transfer to transfer, chip select to clock, and chip select high time), 8- or 16-bit data. Serial memory mode: single-bit, dual and quad SPI Flash at single data rate; XIP; a flexible instruction register for any serial Flash; 32-bit addressing (24-bit by default) for Flash above 128 Mbit; continuous read mode; on-the-fly scrambling. One DMA channel each for receive and transmit. Register write protection.

operation.topic: QSPI pins, clock, interrupt and DMA
operation.text: MOSI and MISO carry single-bit SPI, QIO0 and QIO1 dual SPI, QIO0 to QIO3 quad SPI. The pins are PIO lines assigned to the QSPI in the PIO controllers. The QSPI clock is enabled in the PMC first. One interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the QSPI. The XDMAC can serve the QSPI; DMA writes must be 32-bit aligned, and a single byte written within a word needs the rest of the word filled with ones.

QSCK is the peripheral clock divided by 1 to 256. CPOL and CPHA in QSPI_SCR give four mutually incompatible modes, which the client must match. The one undefined MISO bit time is normally the MSB of the previous character received (CPHA = 0) or the LSB of the previous character sent (CPHA = 1). Delays: QSPI_MR.DLYCS sets the minimum time QCS stays high between activations; DLYBS delays the first QSCK edge after QCS falls; QSPI_MR.DLYBCT inserts a delay between consecutive transfers, but in serial memory mode it is not used and must be 0. The chip select delay, generally under 60 ns, includes internal execution, arbitration and latency, so DLYCS is set a little above the client's requirement, and software waits at least as long before writing the next command.

QSPI_MR.SMM = 0 makes the QSPI a standard SPI host driving QCS and QSCK from its baud rate generator, with transmit and receive holding registers (QSPI_TDR, QSPI_RDR) around one shift register. Writing QSPI_TDR starts a transfer, MOSI shifting out as MISO shifts in; reception needs transmission, and when only sending the receive flags can be ignored. Data written mid-transfer waits in QSPI_TDR. TDRE (which drives the transmit DMA request) shows QSPI_TDR has moved to the shift register and clears on a new write; TXEMPTY marks the end, after DLYBCT, when the peripheral clock may be stopped; RDRF shows new data in QSPI_RDR and clears when read; unread data overwritten sets OVRES, cleared by reading QSPI_SR.

Without DMA, QCS stays low between transfers only if software reloads QSPI_TDR in time, which DLYBCT = 0 makes harder. QSPI_MR.CSMODE = 1 holds QCS low until QSPI_CR.LASTXFER is written, at or after the last data write. With DMA, QCS normally stays low since the DMA reloads QSPI_TDR as soon as TDRE sets, but higher priority DMA traffic or buffers in slow memory such as Flash can delay the reload and let QCS toggle, so CSMODE = 1 may be needed. With CSMODE = 0 QCS may stay low between transfers to the same peripheral; for clients that need a deselect after each transfer, CSMODE = 2.

QSPI_MR.SMM = 1 makes the QSPI a serial Flash controller for single-bit, dual and quad SPI: it reads data for XIP and sends commands such as program, erase and lock. Data is exchanged only through accesses to the QSPI memory window at 0x80000000. Because Flash instruction sets differ by vendor, a full instruction frame register (QSPI_IFR) builds each frame from: an 8-bit instruction code (optional in continuous read mode); an address of 24 or 32 bits (32 for Flash above 128 Mbit, 16 Mbytes), needed by READ, PROGRAM, ERASE and LOCK; an optional option code of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits, used by some Flash to enter XIP or continuous read; optional dummy cycles, needed by some reads; and optional data bytes. Instruction, address/option and data can each use single-bit, dual or quad lanes.

For a frame with an address but no data, write the address to QSPI_IAR.ADDR; with data, the address is that of the data access in the QSPI memory space. Write the instruction and/or option code to QSPI_ICR (INST, OPT). Then write QSPI_IFR, which sends a frame without data at once; a frame with data is sent on the first access to the QSPI memory space. QSPI_IFR fields: WIDTH (lanes for instruction, address, option and data: single-bit MISO/MOSI, dual QIO0–QIO1 or quad QIO0–QIO3), INSTEN, ADDREN, OPTEN, DATAEN, OPTL (option length, consistent with WIDTH: a 1-bit option cannot go with quad, WIDTH = 6, whose minimum is 4 bits), ADDRL (address length), TFRTYP (transfer type) and NBDUM (dummy cycles between address/option and data). TFRTYP = 0 reads non-array data (a JEDEC ID, a status register), 1 reads memory data, 2 writes non-array data (configuration, status), 3 programs memory data. For TFRTYP other than 1 only the first access's address is sent and every bus access gives an SPI transfer of the same size (a half-word gives 16 bits, a byte 8). For TFRTYP = 1 the first read's address is sent, and whenever reads become non-sequential a new frame goes out with the new address, so the transfer size may differ from the bus access size. Without data, QSPI_SR.INSTRE marks the end of the frame and QSPI_SR.CSR the rise of QCS, possibly later with a high divider or DLYBCT. With data, software writes QSPI_CR.LASTXFR when the transfer is done and waits for INSTRE. Sequence with data: dummy-read QSPI_IFR to synchronise APB and AHB, transfer the data, dummy-read QSPI_SR to clear INSTRE and CSR, write LASTXFR, wait for INSTRE and, depending on CSMODE, CSR.

operation.topic: QSPI read memory transfer and continuous read
operation.text: With DATAEN = 1 and TFRTYP = 1 the QSPI reads Flash at random addresses, bus addresses matching Flash addresses, which allows XIP. With fetch enabled, several frames may go out before LASTXFR, a new one at each non-sequential address. Continuous read mode, supported by some Flash, drops the instruction code from frames after a specific option code has stored it in the Flash, shortening the many frames that random reads cause. It must be enabled in both the Flash (by the option code) and the QSPI (QSPI_IFR.CRM = 1, with TFRTYP = 1); setting CRM when the Flash does not support or has not enabled it makes read data unpredictable.

Memory data can be scrambled on the pins, on the fly without throughput loss, to stop off-chip code being read at the pins; it does not apply to devices other than memories. Data is scrambled on write and unscrambled on read. QSPI_SMR.SCREN enables it; the user key QSPI_SKR.USRK is write-only and locked until the next reset once QSPI_SMR.SCRKL is written to 1. With QSPI_SMR.RVDIS = 0 the algorithm adds a device-dependent random value, so data scrambled by one microcontroller cannot be unscrambled by another; with RVDIS = 1 only the user key is used. The key or seed must be kept in reliable non-volatile memory; data cannot be recovered without it.

QSPI_WPMR.WPEN protects the mode, serial clock, scrambling mode and scrambling key registers. A write to a protected register sets QSPI_WPSR.WPVS, WPVSRC names the register, and reading QSPI_WPSR clears WPVS.

A byte-oriented two-wire bus port, one clock line and one data line, for serial EEPROMs and I2C-compatible parts such as real-time clocks, LCD controllers and temperature sensors. It runs as host or client, with single-byte or sequential access, and supports more than one host on the bus. Its baud rate generator suits many core clock rates. Fast mode tops out at 400 kbit/s; High-speed mode, client only, at 3.4 Mbit/s.

Three TWIHS instances. One, two or three bytes of client internal address; sequential read and write; host and multihost operation in Standard and Fast modes only; client operation in Standard, Fast and High-speed modes; general call in client mode; SleepWalking (asynchronous partial wakeup); SMBus support; DMA channels; register write protection.

TWD and TWCK are both bidirectional and are pulled up to the positive supply by a resistor or current source, so both sit high when the bus is free; every device on the bus drives them open-drain or open-collector, forming a wired-AND. The lines are PIO pins handed to the TWIHS in the PIO controller; the open-drain output is made by the hardware and must not be set in the PIO. High-speed client mode needs the analog pad filter on. The TWIHS clock is enabled in the PMC first, and its one interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the TWIHS.

Data on TWD is 8 bits long, sent MSB first, each byte followed by an acknowledge; a transfer may hold any number of bytes. A transfer opens with START (TWD falling while TWCK is high) and closes with STOP (TWD rising while TWCK is high). The modes are host transmitter and receiver, multihost transmitter and receiver (all Standard and Fast only), and client transmitter and receiver (Standard, Fast and High-speed).

The host starts a transfer, makes the clock and stops it; host mode is unavailable when High-speed mode is selected. Before entering it, set TWIHS_MMR.DADR (with IADRSZ and IADR for a 10-bit device), the clock waveform in TWIHS_CWGR (CKDIV, CHDIV, CLDIV), then TWIHS_CR.SVDIS to disable the client and TWIHS_CR.MSEN to enable the host. DADR may be changed while already in host mode.

Writing TWIHS_THR makes a START and sends the 7-bit address from DADR with the direction bit 0 (MREAD = 0). During the ninth clock the host releases TWD for the client's acknowledge. Without one, TWIHS_SR.NACK is set and a STOP is sent; Reading TWIHS_SR clears NACK, and that read has to come before THR is written again. With one, the data byte is shifted out and TXRDY is set until THR is written again; TXRDY also drives the transmit DMA channel. While THR stays empty the clock is held low; writing THR releases it. TWIHS_CR.STOP makes a STOP. After a host write the clock is stretched until new data or a STOP. TXRDY is cleared by setting TWIHS_CR.MSDIS then TWIHS_CR.MSEN.

Setting START sends the START and the address with direction bit 1 (MREAD = 1); a missing acknowledge sets TWIHS_SR.NACK. The host acknowledges each received byte except the last. RXRDY marks a byte in TWIHS_RHR and clears when it is read; it also drives the receive DMA channel. For a single-byte read, START and STOP are set together; for a multi-byte read, STOP (or START for a repeated start) is set after the next-to-last byte is received. With RHR still full the clock is held low before the last bit until RHR is read. If the next-to-last byte is left unread, the last access stalls on its next-to-last bit; once RHR is read only half a bit period remains to set STOP or START before a spurious extra read can begin, so STOP (or START) can be set before reading RHR on the next-to-last byte, inside the interrupt handler.

Transfers work with 7-bit and 10-bit client addresses. With 7-bit clients, up to three internal address bytes (set in TWIHS_MMR, IADRSZ) give random access inside the client, such as a memory location; a read with an internal address first writes the address and then switches to receive through a repeated start. IADRSZ = 0 for a client with no internal address. For a 10-bit address b1..b10: IADRSZ = 1, DADR = 1 1 1 1 0 b1 b2, and TWIHS_IADR = b3..b10; IADR[15:8] and IADR[23:16] then serve as internal address bytes just as for 7-bit clients.

operation.topic: TWIHS repeated start, bus clear and quick command
operation.text: A repeated start can be made by writing START instead of STOP at the end of a transfer, with the next transfer's direction and address set beforehand. A repeated start after a single-byte read is not supported; for a write followed by a read, START is set before the last byte of the write. A bus clear command is sent by setting up host mode and then TWIHS_CR.CLEAR. The SMBus quick command (host only) sends the one-bit command held in TWIHS_MMR.MREAD when TWIHS_CR.QUICK is set.

Transmit: the DMA moves the buffer size minus 1; after the DMA completes and is disabled, wait for TXRDY, set TWIHS_CR.STOP and write the last byte to THR by hand, then wait for TXCOMP if the peripheral clock is to be stopped. Receive: the DMA moves the buffer size minus 2; after it completes and is disabled, wait for RXRDY, set STOP, read the next-to-last byte, wait for RXRDY again and read the last byte, then wait for TXCOMP if the clock is to be stopped. Handling the last bytes by hand keeps the byte count exact whatever the bus latency.

Host-mode sequences cover writes and reads of one or several bytes, with or without internal address, with SMBus PEC, with the alternative command mode, and write-then-read or read-then-write transfers joined by a repeated start. Status bits may be polled or used as interrupts, the latter needing TWIHS_IER set first.

Several hosts may share the bus by arbitration: it begins when two hosts drive the bus together and is lost by the one sending a one while another sends a zero. The loser stops, listens for a STOP and then tries again. As a host only (MSEN always 1), software watches ARBLST and restarts a lost transfer; a transfer started while the bus is busy waits for a STOP automatically. Bus busy or free is not shown to software.

There is no automatic change from host to client when arbitration is lost, so software runs a pseudo multihost scheme: sit in client mode (SADR, MSDIS, SVEN); to become host, wait for TXCOMP, switch to host (DADR, SVDIS, MSEN) and begin, for instance with START and a THR write; the TWIHS waits for a free bus, then from start to STOP software watches ARBLST; on lost arbitration it returns to client mode in case the winner addresses it, waiting for TXCOMP first. An address aimed at the TWIHS right after it loses arbitration gets no acknowledge even once in client mode, so the host must resend the address.

In client mode the device takes the clock and address from a host and never makes START, repeated START or STOP. Set TWIHS_SMR.SADR (optionally TWIHS_SMR.MASK to ignore some address bits and match several addresses), then TWIHS_CR.MSDIS and TWIHS_CR.SVEN. TWIHS_CWGR is ignored. On a matching address SVACC is set and SVREAD gives the direction; SVACC stays set until a STOP or repeated START, which sets EOSACC. A general call sets GACC, and software decodes what follows (a reset or a write command, then a programming sequence that may load a new SADR).

Host read (SVREAD high): the TWIHS sends the bytes written to TWIHS_THR until a STOP or a repeated START with another address; then TXCOMP is set and SVACC cleared. TXRDY clears when THR is written and sets once the shifter is empty and the byte has been acknowledged or not; a non-acknowledge sets NACK and is always followed by STOP or repeated START. TXRDY is cleared by setting SVDIS then SVEN. Host write (SVREAD low): RXRDY sets when a byte arrives in TWIHS_RHR and clears on reading it, until a STOP or a repeated START with another address, after which TXCOMP is set and SVACC cleared.

When THR is not written or RHR not read in time, the TWIHS holds TWCK low, shown by SCLWS. In read mode the clock is held after the acknowledge while the shifter is empty (TWD undefined meanwhile); in write mode it is held while the shifter and RHR are both full. TWIHS_SMR.SCLWSDIS turns stretching off, and then UNRE and OVRE flag a THR underrun and an RHR overrun. After a repeated start that reverses direction, TXCOMP is set only at the end, since SADR is matched again; on a write-to-read reversal an unwritten THR stretches the clock before the acknowledge.

Set up the DMA, set client mode, enable the DMA, wait for its completion flag and disable it; wait for TXCOMP only when the peripheral clock is to be stopped. The receive sequence assumes the byte count is known.

TWIHS_CR.SMBEN turns on SMBus mode, which works like I2C except: only 7-bit addresses; SMBus timeouts are set in TWIHS_SMBTR, and on a timeout the client leaves the bus and TWIHS_SR.TOUT is set; a transfer may end with a CRC byte, the PEC; and matching on the reserved alert response and host header addresses can be enabled in TWIHS_CR. TWIHS_CR.PECEN sends or checks the PEC in the current transfer; the PEC generator follows every bit so linked transfers stay correct. As a client receiver the TWIHS acknowledges a matching PEC and does not acknowledge a wrong one, setting PECERR. As a client transmitter it sends its PEC and the host checks it.

TWIHS_CR.HSEN turns on High-speed mode, with the analog pad filter on (TWIHS_FILTR.PADFEN = 1) and FILT cleared. A high-speed frame starts at normal speed with START, a host code 0000 1XXX and a non-acknowledge; host code matching and high-speed timings are then active, and transfers reach 3.4 Mbit/s. Clock stretching is only allowed after ACK, NACK, START or repeated START, and client stretching must be disabled (SCLWSDIS = 1), so overrun may occur. The peripheral clock must be at least 11 MHz, assuming no system latency. With stretching disabled, RHR must be read before the next byte arrives and THR must hold the first byte before a host read frame begins; polling RXRDY/TXRDY or using the DMA is advised, or an interrupt of suitable priority and low latency. Usage otherwise matches standard mode.

An asynchronous START detector can wake the device on an address match, optionally also a match on the first data byte, even from sleep modes that stop the TWIHS peripheral clock. After a START the TWIHS stretches TWCK until its clock is running (the delay depends on the sleep mode), then takes the address byte with only a small part of the device clocked. On a match the whole device wakes and the transfer proceeds; otherwise the clock stops and the device goes back to sleep. TWIHS_SMR.SADR1EN to SADR3EN add three more addresses, set in TWIHS_SWMR.SADR1 to SADR3; TWIHS_SMR.DATAMEN adds matching of the first byte against TWIHS_SWMR.DATAM. Entering this mode with the system active, SVACC must be the only TWIHS interrupt source and data matching off. After leaving Wait mode, SVACC tells whether the TWIHS caused the wakeup.

Client-mode sequences cover plain reads and writes, reads and writes with SMBus PEC, and with PEC and the alternative command mode; status bits may be polled or used as interrupts, the latter needing TWIHS_IER set first.

With SleepWalking disabled, address matching can still cover up to three extra client addresses through SADR1EN to SADR3EN in TWIHS_SMR and SADR1 to SADR3 in TWIHS_SWMR; DATAMEN has no effect. SVACC is set on a match.

TWIHS_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the clock waveform generator register (TWIHS_CWGR). A write to it while protected sets WPVS in TWIHS_WPSR, with WPVSRC naming the register; reading TWIHS_WPSR clears WPVS.

A synchronous serial link for the protocols of audio and telecom work: I2S, short and long frame sync and others. It has an independent receiver and transmitter sharing one clock divider; each side has a data line (TD, RD), a clock (TK, RK) and a frame sync (TF, RF). Transfers start automatically or on chosen events on the frame sync line. With DMA it serves codecs as host or client, DACs over a serial link such as I2S, and magnetic card readers with little processor load.

Example connections: an I2S receiver driven from TK (clock), TF (word select) and TD (data), left channel then right channel MSB first; a codec on TK (SCLK), TF (FSYNC), TD (serial data out) and RD (serial data in), using a time slot; and two codecs sharing SCLK, FSYNC and the data lines, each in its own time slot of the frame.

The SSC pins are PIO lines; the receiver's lines and the transmitter's lines are each handed to the SSC in the PIO controller before that side is used. The SSC is not clocked continuously: its clock is enabled in the PMC first. One interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the SSC; each pending unmasked source in SSC_IMR asserts it and SSC_SR tells which.

Receiver and transmitter run separately but can be tied together: the receiver can use the transmit clock or start when transmission starts, and the reverse. Either side can run from the clock on TK or RK, which suits many client transfers. The fastest clock allowed on TK and RK is the peripheral clock divided by 2.

The transmit clock comes from the TK pin, the receive clock or the internal divider; the receive clock from the RK pin, the transmit clock or the divider. The transmitter can drive a clock out on TK and the receiver on RK. The clock is chosen by CKS in SSC_TCMR or SSC_RCMR and can be inverted by CKI there; CKI does not affect the clock outputs. The output on TK or RK can run continuously or only during data transfers (CKO). Selecting the pin as clock source (CKS) together with a continuous clock output (CKO) gives unpredictable results.

A 12-bit DIV field in SSC_CMR (maximum 4095) divides the peripheral clock by up to 8190; the divided clock feeds both receiver and transmitter. DIV = 0 turns the divider off. For DIV of 1 or more, the divided clock is the peripheral clock over 2 × DIV, each level lasting DIV peripheral clocks, so the duty cycle is 50 % for odd and even DIV alike (DIV = 1 gives f/2, DIV = 3 gives f/6).

When TK or RK supplies the clock, first-order limits are: on RK, the peripheral clock divided by 2 with RF as input and by 3 with RF as output; on TK, divided by 6 with TF as input and by 2 with TF as output.

A transmit frame begins on a start event (SSC_TCMR) and may send synchronization data before the data (SSC_TFMR). Data written to SSC_THR is moved into the transmit shifter, which runs on the transmit clock. TXRDY in SSC_SR sets when THR has moved into the shift register, and TXEMPTY when both are empty. When RCMR.START is an edge start, RFMR.FSOS is none (input) and TCMR.START is receive start, TD output is delayed by two or three system clock cycles.

A receive frame begins on a start event (SSC_RCMR), with frame sync set in SSC_RFMR. When the receive shift register is full its contents move to SSC_RHR and RXRDY sets; if another word arrives before RHR is read, OVRUN sets in SSC_SR and RHR is overwritten.

Each side's START field picks its start event: continuous (transmit starts when SSC_THR is written, receive when enabled), in step with the other side, a falling or rising edge on TF/RF, a low or high level on TF/RF, or a level change or any edge on TF/RF. The receiver can also start on a pattern found in the data by the compare functions. FSOS in SSC_TFMR/SSC_RFMR sets whether TF/RF is input or output. After the start event, STTDLY bit periods pass before the first data bit.

FSOS in SSC_RFMR and SSC_TFMR selects the waveform driven on RF and TF: a programmed low or high level during the data, a high pulse before the data, or toggling. A pulse lasts FSLEN bit times, 1 to 256, and repeats at the PERIOD set in SSC_RCMR and SSC_TCMR. During the frame sync the receiver can capture RD into SSC_RSHR while the transmitter shifts out the transmit sync holding register (with SSC_TFMR.FSDEN set), up to 256 bits; where the sync length reaches the start delay, normal data takes priority. FSEDGE selects the edge that sets RXSYN or TXSYN in SSC_SR.

Compare 0 and Compare 1 patterns, FSLEN bits long up to 256, are matched against the latest received bits. Compare 0 (SSC_RC0R) can be the receiver's start event; SSC_RCMR.STOP then chooses whether each new transfer waits for a new Compare 0 or reception runs on until Compare 1.

SSC_TFMR and SSC_RFMR set, for each side: the start event, the start delay (STTDLY), the word length (DATLEN), the words per start event (DATNB), the sync length (FSLEN) and bit order (MSBF). The transmitter can also send sync data (FSDEN) and choose the level on TD between transfers (DATDEF). In continuous mode sync data cannot be sent and FSDEN has no effect.

SSC_RFMR.LOOP connects RD to TD, RF to TF and RK to TK so the receiver takes the transmitter's output. Most SSC_SR bits can raise the interrupt: transmitter TXRDY, TXEMPTY and TXSYN; receiver RXRDY, OVRUN and RXSYN; SSC_IER and SSC_IDR set and clear their bits in SSC_IMR.

SSC_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the clock mode, receive clock mode, receive frame mode, transmit clock mode, transmit frame mode, and receive compare 0 and 1 registers. A write to one while protected sets WPVS in SSC_WPSR, with WPVSRC naming the register; reading SSC_WPSR clears WPVS.

A five-wire, bidirectional, synchronous digital audio link (I2SC_DI, I2SC_DO, I2SC_WS, I2SC_CK, I2SC_MCK) compliant with the I2S bus specification. A receiver, a transmitter and a shared clock generator can be enabled separately to make host, client or controller modes with either or both directions active. Separate DMA channels for receive and transmit keep the data moving without the processor, to audio codecs, stereo DACs and ADCs; one DMA channel can carry both audio channels, or one channel each. The 8- and 16-bit compact stereo formats pack left and right samples into one word to halve the DMA traffic. As host it can output a 32 fs to 1024 fs oversampling clock for an external codec or DSP.

Host mode (data and clocks), client mode (data only) and controller mode (clocks only). Receiver, transmitter and clocks enabled and disabled individually. Common clock generator for sample rates including 32, 44.1, 48, 88.2, 96 and 192 kHz, and a 32 fs to 1024 fs host clock for oversampling converters. Mono or stereo at 32, 24, 20, 18, 16 and 8 bits; 16- and 8-bit compact stereo. DMA with one channel for both audio channels or one per channel. Holding-register management that keeps channels from swapping after an overrun or underrun.

operation.topic: I2SC pins, clocks, DMA and interrupt
operation.text: The I2SC pins are PIO lines assigned to the I2SC in the PIO controller; unused ones stay available as PIO, and the I2SC inputs and outputs in use must be enabled. The bus interface clock comes from the PMC; the I2SC must be disabled before its clock is turned off, or it may freeze in an undefined state. A sleep mode that stops its clocks halts the I2SC until wakeup. The DMA controller and the interrupt controller are set up before the I2SC uses them. The I2SC input clock is the peripheral clock or GCLK[PID] (PID of I2SCx in the peripheral identifiers), chosen in CCFG_PCCR.

Receiver and transmitter share one serial clock and word select. Write the configuration to I2SC_MR and CCFG_PCCR (bus matrix) before enabling; with I2SC_MR.IMCKMODE set, IMCKFS is set too. Then I2SC_CR.CKEN, RXEN and TXEN enable the clock generator, receiver and transmitter. The clock generator alone (controller mode) outputs I2SC_MCK, I2SC_CK and I2SC_WS; it must also be on whenever the receiver or transmitter is. The matching disable bits in I2SC_CR stop each part independently, once the pending frame has finished.

Read I2SC_RHR when I2SC_SR.RXRDY is set and write I2SC_THR when TXRDY is set; successive words are left and right samples of successive frames. The flags can be polled, or RXRDY and TXRDY interrupts enabled in I2SC_IER.

operation.topic: I2SC host, controller and client modes
operation.text: Host and controller modes generate all three clocks (MCK, CK, WS), driving I2SC_MCK, I2SC_CK and I2SC_WS as outputs; in controller mode receiver and transmitter are off and only the clocks run, for external devices. In client mode I2SC_CK and I2SC_WS are inputs from an external host. I2SC_MR.MODE chooses the mode; since it changes the direction of the clock and word select pins, I2SC_MR is written only while the I2SC is stopped.

As the I2S protocol sets, data is left-justified in the word select slot, MSB first, starting one clock after the word select changes. Bits change on falling serial clock edges and are read on rising ones. Word select low is the left channel, high the right. I2SC_MR.DATALENGTH sets 8, 16, 18, 20, 24 or 32-bit words; a slot longer than the word gets zeros appended on transmit and extra bits dropped on receive. The first word sent right after an I2SC reset is to be ignored.

As a client the I2SC takes SCK and WS from an outside host. In host mode they are set in I2SC_MR and derived from MCK, with I2SC_MCK, I2SC_CK and I2SC_WS as outputs. In host mode with a peripheral clock above 96 MHz, GCLK[PID] must be the I2SC input clock (CCFG_PCCR.I2SCxCC = 1). Codecs may need a host clock that is a multiple of fs such as 256 fs: with IMCKMODE = 1, MCK goes out on I2SC_MCK and is divided to make the bit clock on I2SC_CK, the division set by IMCKFS and DATALENGTH. IMCKMODE must be 1 whenever the host clock is strictly faster than the serial clock. With IMCKMODE = 0 and no host clock output, MCK is used as I2SC_CK; when MCK is a multiple of the wanted I2SC_CK, the IMCKFS divider can be used instead.
At 44.1 kHz with a 256 fs host clock, the core clock must be an integer multiple of 11.2896 MHz; taking a multiple of 4, IMCKDIV = 4 and IMCKFS = 31.

I2SC_MR.TXMONO copies the left channel to the right output; RXMONO copies the received left channel to the right. RXRDY sets when a word reaches I2SC_RHR and clears when it is read; a new word before the read is an overrun, setting RXOR and bit i of RXORCH for channel i. TXRDY sets when I2SC_THR is empty and clears when written; a word needed before THR is written is an underrun, setting TXUR and bit i of the transmit channel field in I2SC_SR, and then a zero word is sent (TXSAME = 0) or the channel's previous word (TXSAME = 1). Samples sit at the low end (right-justified) of both holding registers. Compact stereo packs left in bits 15:0 and right in bits 31:16 (16-bit), or left in 7:0 and right in 15:8 (8-bit).

I2SC_MR.RXDMA and TXDMA choose one DMA channel for all audio channels (channel 0) or one per audio channel; the DMA reads RHR and writes THR for both channels in turn, as words, halfwords or bytes according to DATALENGTH. I2SC_MR.LOOP connects I2SC_DO to I2SC_DI inside for debug; receiver and transmitter are disabled before I2SC_MR is changed. An interrupt is raised by RXRDY, RXOR, TXRDY or TXUR when enabled in I2SC_IMR (set through I2SC_IER, cleared through I2SC_IDR); it stays active until the status bit is cleared through I2SC_SCR. I2SC_SSR sets status bits to simulate interrupts.

Examples: the I2SC as client transmitter feeding a stereo audio DAC over serial clock, word select and serial data out; two I2S microphones sharing serial clock, word select and the data-in line, one wired for the left channel and one for the right; and an I2S audio codec taking host clock, bit clock, word clock and DAC data from the I2SC and returning ADC data.

One full-duplex synchronous or asynchronous serial link with a widely programmable frame (data length, parity, stop bits). The receiver detects parity, framing and overrun errors; a receiver timeout handles variable-length frames and a transmitter timeguard helps with slow remote devices. Multidrop addressing is handled in both directions. Special modes serve RS485, LIN, LON and SPI buses, ISO7816 T = 0 and T = 1 smart cards, infrared transceivers and modem ports; RTS/CTS give hardware flow control. It also offers automatic echo plus local and remote loopback for testing. DMA serves transmit and receive with chained buffers.

Programmable baud rate generator; 5- to 9-bit characters, full duplex, synchronous or asynchronous; 1, 1.5 or 2 stop bits asynchronous, 1 or 2 synchronous; parity generation and checking; framing and overrun detection; digital filter on the receive line; MSB or LSB first; break generation and detection; 8x or 16x oversampling; RTS/CTS handshaking; DTR, DSR, DCD and RI modem signals; receiver timeout and transmitter timeguard; multidrop addressing on transmit and receive. RS485 driver-enable output. ISO7816 T = 0 and T = 1 with NACK handling, error counter and repetition and iteration limits. IrDA modulation and demodulation up to 115.2 kbit/s. SPI host or client with programmable clock phase and polarity, SCK up to the peripheral clock divided by 6.

LIN: LIN 1.3 and 2.0, host or client, frames up to 256 data bytes, response length set or taken from the identifier, client self-synchronization, automatic handling of synch break and synch field (break found even when partly overlapping a data byte), automatic identifier parity and checksum (each can be turned off), classic and enhanced checksums, full error checking, frame slot mode, wakeup signal. LON: CEA-709, full layer 2, differential Manchester coding, preamble with bit- and byte-sync fields, beta1, beta2, IDT and other timings, CRC, random number generation, backlog calculation, collision detection, comm_type 1 and 2, clock drift tolerance up to 16 %, no digital line filter (suited to node-to-node links). Two DMA channels; register write protection.

USART pins are PIO lines assigned to the USART in the PIO controller; unused ones stay available as PIO. Not every USART has all the modem pins; on one without a pin, its control and status bits do nothing. The USART clock is enabled in the PMC before use; turning it off while idle and back on later is allowed, and operation picks up from the same point. Its interrupt line goes to the interrupt controller, set up first.

The baud rate generator clocks receiver and transmitter. US_MR.USCLKS selects its source: the peripheral clock, the peripheral clock divided by a product-dependent DIV (generally 8), a programmable PMC clock (PCK), or an external clock on SCK. A 16-bit divider, US_BRGR.CD, follows: CD = 0 stops the clock and CD = 1 bypasses the divider. An external SCK clock needs high and low levels each longer than a peripheral clock period and a frequency at least 3 times below the peripheral clock (USART modes) or 6 times below (SPI modes, USART_MODE 0xE or 0xF). With PCK the baud rate does not change when the processor or peripheral clock does; PCKx must be at least three times slower than the peripheral clock, and with PCK selected (USCLKS = 2) and SCK driven (CLKO = 1), CD must be above 1. For baud rate detection on receive, the frame must be sent with its parity bit 0.

In asynchronous mode the selected clock divided by CD is the receiver's sampling clock, then divided by 16 (OVER = 0) or 8 (OVER = 1) for the bit rate. The highest rate is the peripheral clock divided by 8, with OVER = 1 and the peripheral clock as source. The integer divider only changes the rate in whole steps; a fractional part, US_BRGR.FP, adds steps of one-eighth of the divider when non-zero. With FP above 0 the oversampling clock on SCK has an uneven duty cycle, its high time lengthened by one selected-clock period now and then, depending on CD.

operation.topic: USART synchronous and SPI baud rate
operation.text: In synchronous mode the baud rate is the selected clock divided by CD. With the external clock (USCLKS = 3) the SCK signal is used directly, US_BRGR has no effect, and the clock must be at least 3 times below the system clock. As synchronous host (USCLKS = 0 or 1, CLKO = 1) the receive side limits SCK to the selected clock divided by 3 in USART mode or by 6 in SPI mode. With the external SCK or the divided peripheral clock as source, CD must be even for a 50:50 SCK; with the peripheral clock as source the duty cycle is 50:50 even for odd CD.

The ISO7816 bit rate is B = Di × f / Fi, with Di and Fi coded in 4-bit DI and FI fields. The selected clock divided by CD can be output on SCK (CLKO = 1) to clock the card, and is then divided by US_FIDI.FI_DI_RATIO (the sampling divider, up to 2047 in ISO7816 mode) to give the bit rate. Non-integer Fi/Di ratios are not supported; the nearest integer is programmed. FI_DI_RATIO resets to 0x174 (372), the most common ratio (Fi = 372, Di = 1). One elementary time unit (ETU), one bit time, is FI_DI_RATIO clock cycles on SCK.

Receiver and transmitter are disabled after reset and enabled by US_CR.RXEN and TXEN, together or apart; their registers can be set beforehand. US_CR.RSTRX and RSTTX reset each side at once, clearing status and state machines but keeping the configuration, and stopping any transfer immediately. RXDIS stops the receiver after the character in progress; TXDIS stops the transmitter after the current character and the one waiting in US_THR, with any timeguard handled normally.

Synchronous or asynchronous, each character leaves on TXD, one bit per falling serial clock edge, as a start bit, at most 9 data bits, parity if chosen, and one or two stop bits. US_MR.CHRL sets the data length, and MODE9 = 1 selects 9 bits whatever CHRL holds. US_MR.PAR selects even, odd, space, mark or no parity; MSBF sets bit order; NBSTOP the stop bits, 1.5 being asynchronous only. Software writes characters into US_THR. US_CSR.TXRDY shows THR empty and TXEMPTY that every written character has gone. Both are low while the transmitter is disabled, and a write to THR while TXRDY is low is lost.

US_MR.MAN = 1 encodes characters as biphase Manchester II, a transition at the middle of every bit, twice the bandwidth of NRZ but with better error checking. With default polarity, 0xB1 (10110001) becomes 10 01 10 10 01 01 01 10. A preamble of 1 to 15 bit times (US_MAN.TX_PL; 0 for none) can precede each character, with its pattern (all ones, all zeros, or alternating starting with either level) chosen in US_MAN.TX_PP. US_MAN.TX_MPOL sets the polarity: at 0 (default) a zero is a zero-to-one transition and a one a one-to-zero transition.

US_MR.ONEBIT sets the start frame delimiter: at 1, a single Manchester-coded zero; at 0, a three-bit sync pattern, itself not valid Manchester since its transition falls in the middle of the second bit. The command sync is high for one and a half bits then low for one and a half; the data sync is the reverse. US_MR.MODSYNC = 1 marks the next character a command, 0 data. With US_MR.VAR_SYNC = 1, MODSYNC is bypassed and each character carries its sync type in US_THR.TXSYNH, so DMA can set it per character.

Available with 16x oversampling only, turned on by US_MAN.DRIFT. An RXD edge within one 16x clock of where it is expected is treated as jitter. An edge 4 to 2 clocks early shortens the current bit period by one clock; an edge 2 to 3 clocks late lengthens it by one.

With SYNC = 0 the receiver oversamples RXD 16 or 8 times per bit (OVER). A start bit is a low lasting half a bit: the eighth low sample at 16x, the fourth at 8x; data, parity and stop bits then last 16 or 8 sampling clocks each. Data length, bit order and parity use the transmitter's fields. The receiver checks only one stop bit whatever NBSTOP says, and begins hunting for a new start bit right after sampling the stop bit, so it stays in step with a transmitter using one stop bit.

US_MR.MAN = 1 also enables the decoder, which finds the preamble and start frame delimiter. The receive preamble length (US_MAN.RX_PL, 0 to disable) is independent of the transmitter's; US_MAN.RX_MPOL sets input polarity. The start frame delimiter setting (ONEBIT) is shared with the encoder. A start bit is RXD low for a quarter bit; data is sampled at one quarter and three quarters of each bit, and three quarters of a bit is the shortest time used to decide a bit value. A stream that does not match resynchronizes on the next valid edge. US_MAN.RXIDLEV gives the idle line level, 1 by default, and must be set for reliable sync. A missing mid-bit transition sets US_CSR.MANERR, cleared by US_CR.RSTSTA. With sync delimiters, US_RHR.RXSYNH reports whether each character was a command (1) or data (0). In unipolar use the first bit of a frame must be a zero-to-one transition.

Low-rate RF links with ASK or FSK transmitter and receiver ICs can use the USART as Manchester encoder and decoder, full duplex on two carrier frequencies. On transmit, the coded characters, with any preamble and delimiter, drive the RF modulator: ASK switches the power amplifier on for a one and off for a zero; FSK sends F0 for a one and F1 for a zero. On receive, the RF IC checks for a valid pattern and passes the demodulated stream to the decoder; since the RF IC consumes some preamble bits, the USART preamble length is set to match the RF IC.

With US_MR.SYNC = 1 the receiver reads RXD once per baud clock period, at its rising edge; a low is a start bit, then data, parity and stop bits are sampled. Settings are as in asynchronous mode; this mode allows high-speed transfers.

A completed character goes to US_RHR and sets US_CSR.RXRDY. A character completed while RXRDY is still set sets OVRE and overwrites RHR. US_CR.RSTSTA clears OVRE, PARE, FRAME and the other error flags.

Five parity modes in US_MR.PAR, which also selects multidrop. Even parity makes the total number of ones even, odd parity odd; mark parity is always 1 and space parity always 0, and the receiver flags a received bit that differs; with no parity none is sent or checked. A parity error sets US_CSR.PARE.

US_MR.PAR = 0x6 or 0x7 selects multidrop: data characters carry parity 0 and address characters parity 1. The receiver sets PARE on a parity bit of 1. Writing US_CR.SENDA makes the next byte written to US_THR go out as an address; others go out with parity 0.

US_TTGR.TG inserts TG bit periods of idle (high) on TXD after each character, in addition to the stop bits, for slow remote devices; TG = 0 turns it off. With a timeguard, TXRDY rises only when the next character's start bit is sent, and TXEMPTY stays low until the timeguard ends, as it counts as part of the character.

The receiver timeout spots an idle RXD line to mark the end of variable-length frames. US_RTOR.TO loads a 16-bit counter that counts down each bit period and reloads on each received character; at 0, US_CSR.TIMEOUT rises and can interrupt. TO = 0 disables it. US_CR.STTTO then holds the counter until a new character arrives, so the idle time before the next frame raises no timeout; US_CR.RETTO restarts the count at once from TO, giving a periodic interrupt even with no characters.

A stop bit received low is a framing error, flagged in US_CSR.FRAME from the middle of the stop bit until US_CR.RSTSTA. US_CR.STTBRK holds TXD low for at least one whole character (like 0x00 with parity and stop at 0), after any character in progress, until US_CR.STPBRK; a stop requested early still lets the minimum break finish. The break is handled like a character: STTBRK and STPBRK act only with TXRDY = 1, and the break clears TXRDY and TXEMPTY. Further STTBRK writes are ignored until the break ends, STPBRK without STTBRK is ignored, both at once give unpredictable results, and THR writes made while a break waits to begin are dropped. Once a break ends, TXD stays high at least 12 bit times, or the timeguard if longer than 12. The receiver flags a break, all data, parity and stop bits low (FRAME stays low), in US_CSR.RXBRK; the end of break, a high for at least 2/16 of a bit (asynchronous) or one high sample (synchronous), sets RXBRK too.

US_MR.USART_MODE = 0x2 enables RTS/CTS flow control, wired TXD to RXD, RXD to TXD, CTS to RTS and RTS to CTS with the remote device. The receiver drives RTS (also controllable by US_CR.RTSEN and RTSDIS) and CTS gates the transmitter: CTS high stops it after the current character, and the next character goes as soon as CTS falls. CTS and RTS are not linked to the DMA, so flow control is not available with DMA.

Smart cards and security access modules over ISO7816, T = 0 (USART_MODE = 0x4) or T = 1 (0x6). The link is half duplex on one line: TXD becomes bidirectional, driven only while the transmitter is active and otherwise feeding the receiver, and SCK supplies the card clock, making the USART the host. The character is fixed at 8 data bits and 1 or 2 stop bits whatever CHRL, MODE9 and CHMODE hold; MSBF sets bit order and INVDATA normal or inverse format (bits sent as their complement). Receiver and transmitter must not be enabled together; software enables the one needed.

A character is a start bit, 8 data bits, parity and a two-bit guard time during which the transmitter leaves the line. Without a parity error the line stays high through the guard time. A receiver that finds a parity error pulls the line low for one bit in the guard time (NACK), lengthening the character by one bit; the USART as receiver then keeps the character out of US_RHR and sets PARE. US_NER.NB_ERRORS counts errors up to 255 and clears when read. US_MR.INACK suppresses the NACK and stores the character as good, setting RXRDY. With US_MR.MAX_ITERATION above 0 a NACKed character is resent, up to eight sends in all; when the last repeat is also NACKed US_CSR.ITER is set (cleared by US_CR.RSTIT), and an acknowledged repeat ends the repeats and clears the counter. US_MR.DSNACK limits successive NACKs sent to MAX_ITERATION, after which no NACK is driven and ITER is set.
Like asynchronous format with one stop bit; parity is generated on transmit and checked on receive, an error setting US_CSR.PARE.

Half-duplex infrared links with a built-in modulator and demodulator for a direct connection to IrDA transceivers (TXD to the transceiver's TX, RXD from its RX), IrDA 1.1, 2.4 kbit/s to 115.2 kbit/s. USART_MODE = 0x8 enables it; US_IF sets the demodulator filter, and the USART otherwise runs normal asynchronous mode. Receiver and transmitter are enabled according to the direction. To receive: disable TX, enable RX, set TXD as a PIO output at 0 so the LED stays off, with its pull-up disabled to save power. Up to 115.2 kbit/s RZI modulation is used: each zero is an infrared pulse lasting 3/16 bit.

The receive filter is an 8-bit down counter loaded from US_IF. A falling edge on RXD starts it counting at the peripheral clock; a rising edge stops and reloads it. If it reaches 0 with no rising edge, the receiver input is driven low for one bit time, so pulses shorter than the filter are rejected. US_IF must satisfy t_periph × (IRDA_FILTER + 3) < 1.41 µs. IrDA shares logic with ISO7816, so US_FIDI.FI_DI_RATIO must be above 0 for IrDA to work.

USART_MODE = 0x1 adds line-driver control to asynchronous or synchronous operation, all settings available: RTS is driven high while the transmitter is working, at the inverse of TXEMPTY, and stays high through a programmed timeguard so the line remains driven after the last character. In the typical connection TXD feeds the bus driver, RTS enables it, and RXD takes the bus receiver's output, on a differential bus.

USART_MODE = 0x3 makes the USART a DTE with asynchronous operation and all settings: it drives DTR and RTS and watches DSR, DCD, CTS and RI. US_CR.DTRDIS forces DTR inactive (high) and DTREN active (low). A change on RI, DSR, DCD or CTS sets RIIC, DSRIC, DCDIC or CTSIC in US_CSR, which can interrupt and clear when US_CSR is read. CTS going inactive disables the transmitter, after any character in progress.

A synchronous link as SPI host or client: MOSI, MISO, SCK and the client select NSS. As host the USART makes only one NSS, so it addresses one client. Host mode (USART_MODE = 0xE): TXD drives MOSI, RXD takes MISO, SCK is output and RTS drives NSS. Client mode (0xF): RXD takes MOSI, TXD drives MISO, SCK is input and CTS takes NSS. Any change of SPI mode after the first configuration is followed by a software reset of transmitter and receiver.

The generator works as in synchronous mode, with limits. Host: the external clock is not allowed (USCLKS ≠ 0x3) and CLKO must be 1 to drive SCK; CD must be 6 or more; with the divided peripheral clock CD must be even for a 50:50 SCK, but may be odd with the peripheral clock. Client: the external SCK is always used, whatever USCLKS and US_BRGR hold, and it must be at least 6 times slower than the system clock.

Up to nine data bits leave on TXD at each rising or falling clock edge (CPOL and CPHA decide), with no start, parity or stop bits; CHRL and MODE9 set the length and MSB always goes first. US_MR.CPOL and CPHA give four mutually incompatible modes; host and client must match, and a host serving clients set differently reconfigures for each.

Characters are written to US_THR; TXRDY and TXEMPTY behave as in other modes and a write while TXRDY is low is lost. In host mode US_MR.WRDBT = 1 holds each character until US_RHR has been read, avoiding receive overrun. NSS goes low one bit time before the MSB and high one bit time after the LSB, so it is released between characters with at least three bit times between them. For clients that need chip select held (CSAAT), US_CR.RCS forces NSS low until US_CR.FCS releases it. A client asked to send with THR empty sets UNRE (cleared by RSTSTA) and holds TXD high. A client needs NSS low, not a falling edge, at least one bit time before the first clock of the MSB.

A completed character goes to US_RHR and sets RXRDY; one arriving while RXRDY is set sets OVRE and overwrites it (RSTSTA clears OVRE). In client mode the host must leave at least one bit time between characters, and NSS must be low at least one bit time before the first clock. The receiver timeout cannot work in SPI mode since the baud clock runs only during transfers.

LIN host and client nodes for distributed automotive control: one host and several clients, client self-synchronization without a crystal or resonator, deterministic single-wire signalling, up to 20 kbit/s. Host node is USART_MODE = 0xA, client node 0xB; any change after the first configuration is followed by a software reset of transmitter and receiver. The host's baud rate is set in US_BRGR. A client's initial rate is set in US_BRGR, copied to US_LINBRR, and updated there by synchronization.

Each frame starts with a header from the host: break field, synch field and identifier. Writing US_LINIR sends it and drops TXRDY. The break is 13 dominant bits and one recessive bit, the synch field is 0x55, and the identifier is the byte written, with parity bits computed if enabled. TXRDY rises once the identifier is in the shift register. LINBK sets after the break and LINID after the identifier; RSTSTA clears them.

A client's break detection threshold is 11 nominal bit times at the current rate, and it ignores the bus until a break field is found; LINBK is set and the next character must be 0x55, used to resynchronize; anything else is an inconsistent synch field error. When the identifier arrives LINID is set and US_LINIR.IDCHR updated, its parity checked if enabled. A header not complete within t_Header_Maximum sets LINHTE. RSTSTA clears LINID, LINBK and LINHTE.

Running on the sampling clock, a 19-bit counter times the eight bit periods of the synch field, from its start bit; the top 16 bits (count divided by 8) become the new divider LINCD and the low three bits the fraction LINFP, loaded into US_LINBRR once the field ends unless US_LINMR.SYNCDIS is set. If the new rate differs from the initial rate by more than ±15 % (F_Tol_Unsynch), the values are kept and LINSTE is set; if the synch character is not 0x55 they are kept and LINISFE is set; RSTSTA clears both. Accuracy depends on the nominal clock, the baud rate and the oversampling. LIN allows the client clock to be up to ±15 % from nominal and two nodes' bit rates to differ by at most ±2 %, so the deviation after synchronization must stay within ±1 %. Minimum nominal clock examples: 20 kbit/s gives 2.64 MHz at 16x and 1.47 MHz at 8x; 1 kbit/s gives 132 kHz at 16x and 74 kHz at 8x.

A protected identifier holds the identifier in bits 0 to 5 and parity in bits 6 and 7. With US_LINMR.PARDIS = 0, transmit computes and sends parity with the six low bits of IDCHR (bits 6 and 7 ignored), and receive checks it, a mismatch being an identifier parity error, updating only the six low bits (bits 6 and 7 read 0). With PARDIS = 1 all eight bits are sent and received as they are.

After the identifier, US_LINMR.NACT sets what the node does with the response: PUBLISH sends it, SUBSCRIBE receives it, IGNORE neither. For example, host to both clients: host PUBLISH, both clients SUBSCRIBE; client 1 to client 2: host IGNORE, client 1 PUBLISH, client 2 SUBSCRIBE.

operation.topic: LIN response data length and checksum
operation.text: The response length counts data bytes without the checksum. With US_LINMR.DLM = 0 it is DLC + 1, DLC 0 to 255, so 1 to 256 bytes. With DLM = 1 it follows identifier bits 5 and 4 (LIN 1.1 compatible), giving 2, 4 or 8 bytes, and DLC is ignored. The checksum, the last field, is the inverted 8-bit sum with carry over the data bytes (classic, for LIN 1.3 clients) or over the data and protected identifier (enhanced, for LIN 2.0). CHKDIS = 0 with CHKTYP = 0 sends and checks enhanced, CHKTYP = 1 classic; CHKDIS = 1 neither, though software can still send it as an extra data byte by adding one to the length.

For host nodes. With FSDIS = 0, after a frame TXRDY returns only t_Frame_Maximum after the frame started, so no new header can go out earlier; with FSDIS = 1 TXRDY returns at once. t_Frame_Maximum is (77 + 14 × DLC) × t_bit with the checksum sent and (63 + 14 × DLC) × t_bit without.

Bit error (LINBE, host or client): a transmitted bit read back different on Rx; transmission stops at the next byte boundary, and the transmitter is then reset with RSTTX and re-enabled. Inconsistent synch field (LINISFE, client): synch character not 0x55. Identifier parity error (LINIPE, client, with PARDIS = 0). Checksum error (LINCE, host or client, with CHKDIS = 0). Client not responding (LINSNRE): no valid response within t_Frame_Maximum while NACT = SUBSCRIBE. Synch tolerance error (LINSTE, client): computed rate more than ±15 % from the initial rate. Header timeout (LINHTE, client): header not complete within t_Header_Maximum.

Host: enable TXEN and RXEN, select LIN host in US_MR, set CD and FP in US_BRGR, set NACT, PARDIS, CHKDIS, CHKTYP, DLM, FSDIS and DLC in US_LINMR, check TXRDY and write IDCHR to US_LINIR. Then for PUBLISH write each byte to US_THR as TXRDY rises, for SUBSCRIBE read each from US_RHR as RXRDY rises, and in every case wait for LINTC and check the errors. Client: enable, select LIN client, set the baud rate, wait for LINID, check LINISFE and LINIPE, read IDCHR, then write US_LINMR; for a PUBLISH frame NACT = PUBLISH is rewritten into US_LINMR even when it already holds that value, to raise TXRDY and the DMA request. Data then moves as for the host, ending at LINTC.

The DMA writes US_THR and reads US_RHR one byte at a time on TXRDY and RXRDY. For a host, US_LINMR.PDCM = 1 puts the LIN configuration in the write buffer, written through US_THR in two bytes (NACT, PARDIS, CHKDIS, CHKTYP, DLM and FSDIS first, then DLC); PDCM = 0 leaves US_LINMR to software. The write buffer also holds the identifier and, for PUBLISH, the data; the read buffer holds the data for SUBSCRIBE. For a client the DMA moves only data; software reads the identifier from US_LINIR and writes US_LINMR.

Any node of a sleeping cluster may request wakeup. LIN 2.0 wants the bus dominant for 250 µs to 5 ms, met at any rate from 1 kbit/s (five bits, 5 ms) to 20 kbit/s (250 µs) by sending 0xF0; LIN 1.3 uses 0x80, eight dominant bits. US_LINMR.WKUPTYP selects LIN 2.0 (0) or 1.3 (1); US_CR.LINWKUP sends it, LINTC sets at the end and RSTSTA clears it. Clients go to sleep after bus inactivity: 4 s in LIN 2.0, 25 000 bit times in LIN 1.3. A client spots the idle bus with the receiver timeout, whose US_RTOR.TO value in LIN mode fills a 17-bit counter, decremented each bit and reloaded on each character, and STTTO and RETTO work as in the normal receiver timeout.

Connectivity to a local operating network (LON), which spans all seven OSI layers on wired, power line, RF and IP media. The USART implements layer 2 in full: standard timings, PPDU framing, backlog estimation, with differential Manchester (CDP) coding. There is no digital line filter, so it is best for node-to-node links. USART_MODE = 0x9 selects it; a change of LON configuration after the first is preceded by a software reset of transmitter and receiver and followed by enabling them.

Each frame carries a preamble, then up to 256 data bytes, then a two-byte CRC; preamble and CRC are generated automatically, and transmission starts when US_LONL2HDR is written. On receive, only data and CRC bytes reach US_RHR, each setting RXRDY (OVRE on overrun). Differential Manchester codes a one as a bit that begins without an edge and a zero as one that begins with an edge; a missing mid-bit transition is a code violation. The coding is polarity insensitive; US_MAN.RXIDLEV gives the idle line level (1 by default) for reliable preamble sync.

operation.topic: LON preamble, header, CRC and end of frame
operation.text: The preamble holds bit-sync then byte-sync, its length set in US_LONPR.LONPL (0 not allowed), pattern ALL_ONE or ALL_ZERO only. Received preambles must be at least 4 bits long; their length is not otherwise checked. The L2HDR header (priority bit, alternate path bit, backlog increment) is the first data sent and the first received. Data goes MSB or LSB first per US_MR.MSBF. The last two bytes are the CRC, generated on transmit and checked on receive (LCRCE on mismatch); received CRC bytes appear as two more data bytes. A frame ends with a code violation three bit times long, no transitions after the last CRC bit.

US_LONMR.COMMT sets the CEA-709 comm_type. comm_type 1: an indeterminate time during Beta1 in which channel transitions are ignored; collisions in the first 25 % of the preamble are ignored, and optionally (US_LONMR.CDTAIL) those between CRC and end of transmission; a collision during the preamble ends the packet if US_LONMR.TCOL says so, while later collisions do not. comm_type 2: no indeterminate time, and a collision always ends the packet.

operation.topic: LON collision detection and random numbers
operation.text: Optional collision detection uses an active-low collision detect input from the transceiver, external or internal as US_LONMR.LCDS selects, turned on by US_LONMR.COLDET; CD low for at least half a bit is a collision. The p-persistent CSMA access uses an internally generated random number; US_ICDIFF seeds it so two identical chips with identical software differ after reset, the chip ID being the suggested value.

The node keeps a backlog estimate, starting at 1, never above 63; going past 63 holds it at 63 and sets LBLOVFE. It grows by the increment in each frame sent or received successfully, or by 1 after a transmit collision (the encoded increment then ignored). It falls when Wbase randomizing slots pass without channel activity while waiting to transmit, when a packet with backlog increment 0 is received or sent, and when a packet cycle expires idle.

A node about to transmit waits a random whole number of Beta2 randomizing slots; Beta2 length in bit times is set in US_FIDI (0 not allowed). Beta1 follows each packet cycle; no transmission during it means the channel is idle. Beta1 after a received and after a sent packet are set in US_LONB1RX and US_LONB1TX (0 not allowed). The packet cycle timer reloads whenever the backlog changes, counts down while the MAC is idle (not receiving, transmitting, waiting to transmit, timing Beta1, or waiting for priority slots or the first Wbase window) and halts on going to transmit or receive; its value is set in US_TTGR (0 not allowed). Wbase is 16 Beta2 slots. Optional priority slots, 0 to 127 per channel, follow the Beta1 after a transmission: US_LONPRIO.PSNB sets how many and NPS this node's slot. The indeterminate time after received and sent frames is set in US_LONIDTRX and US_LONIDTTX. A received frame ends after t_eof without transitions, set by US_LONMR.EOFS.

Flags in US_CSR, each able to interrupt through US_IER and cleared by US_CR.RSTSTA: UNRE, a character due with US_THR empty; LCOL, a valid collision reported; LFET, a frame ended early by a collision; LCRCE, a received CRC error; LSFE, a received frame shorter than the 8-byte minimum; LBLOVFE, backlog above 63.

With 16x oversampling and US_MAN.DRIFT set, an RXD edge one to three 16x clocks from where it is expected shortens or lengthens the bit period to re-centre it, recovering up to 16 % clock drift provided the system clock is fast enough for the baud rate.

Send: enable TXEN and RXEN, select LON in US_MR, set CD and FP; choose the operating mode bits (COMMT, COLDET, TCOL, CDTAIL, RDMNBM, DMAM) of US_LONMR; load the network timings (Beta2 into US_FIDI, the packet cycle into US_TTGR, the two Beta1 values, the priority slot count and slot, and the two IDT values into their LON registers); choose the preamble pattern (US_MAN.TX_PL); write the preamble length and data length registers; check TXRDY, write US_LONL2HDR, write each byte to US_THR as TXRDY rises, wait for LTXD and check errors. Receive: the same set-up, then RXIDLEV and RX_PL in US_MAN; read each byte, CRC included, from US_RHR as RXRDY rises, wait for LRXD and check errors.

The DMA writes US_THR and reads US_RHR a byte at a time on TXRDY and RXRDY. With US_LONMR.DMAM = 1 the frame data length is the first entry of the write buffer, written through US_THR instead of US_LONDL; with DMAM = 0 software writes US_LONDL. Either way L2HDR is stored in the write buffer as the first data. When a collision ends a transmission early, the USART sends the end of frame, holds TXRDY low to stop the DMA, sets LTXD, LCOL and LFET, and waits for the DMA to be set up again and for LCOL and LFET to be cleared by RSTSTA, which releases TXRDY.

Normal: RXD feeds the receiver and the transmitter drives TXD. Automatic echo: each bit received on RXD is sent on TXD; the transmitter has no effect on TXD and the receiver stays active. Local loopback: the transmitter feeds the receiver inside; RXD is ignored and TXD is held high as when idle. Remote loopback: RXD is connected straight to TXD, bit by bit, with transmitter and receiver disabled.

US_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the mode, baud rate generator, receiver timeout, transmitter timeguard, Manchester configuration, LON mode, LON Beta1 Tx, LON Beta1 Rx, LON priority, LON IDT Tx, LON IDT Rx and IC DIFF registers. A write to one while protected sets WPVS in US_WPSR, with WPVSRC naming the register; reading US_WPSR clears WPVS.

A two-wire asynchronous serial port (URXD, UTXD) with no clock pin, meant for debug traces, communication and in-system programming. Receiver and transmitter run independently from one shared baud rate generator, which can be clocked from a source independent of the processor clock. It handles 8-bit characters only, with even, odd, mark, space or no parity, and flags parity, framing and overrun errors. It also has a receive-line digital filter, automatic echo and local and remote loopback, two DMA channels (receive and transmit), a compare function on received characters, asynchronous partial wake-up (SleepWalking) on receive activity, an interrupt and register write protection. Receiver timeout and transmitter timeguard are absent; what is present behaves as in a standard USART.

URXD and UTXD are PIO lines that the PIO controller must hand to the UART first. The UART clock is enabled in the PMC; its peripheral identifier is normally 1. For SleepWalking the UART must also be enabled in PMC_SLPWK_ER; the PMC then gives or withholds the system clock according to the UART's requests. The UART interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the UART.

The bit clock is the selected source divided by 16 × CD, with CD the 16-bit value in UART_BRGR. CD = 0 stops the baud clock and the UART does nothing. UART_MR.BRSRCCK selects the source: the peripheral clock or a PMC programmable clock (PCK). The fastest rate is the source / 16 and the slowest the source / (16 × 65536). With PCK as source the baud rate does not depend on the processor/bus clock, so that clock may be changed while the UART runs, but only through PMC_MCKR.PRES; any other way (PLL multiplier and so on) is not allowed while the UART is enabled. The peripheral clock must be at least three times PCK.

Disabled after reset. UART_CR.RXEN enables it and it starts hunting for a start bit. RXDIS stops it at once if it is idle, or after the stop bit of a character in progress. RSTRX resets and disables it immediately and any character in progress is lost. URXD is sampled at 16 times the baud rate; a low level lasting more than 7 sampling cycles (over 7/16 of a bit) is a start bit, shorter lows are ignored. Each bit is then sampled at its middle: the first data bit 24 cycles (1.5 bit) after the start edge and each later bit 16 cycles after the previous one.

A complete character is moved to UART_RHR and sets RXRDY in UART_SR; reading UART_RHR clears it. A new character arriving while RXRDY is still set sets OVRE. Parity is computed per UART_MR.PAR and a mismatch sets PARE together with RXRDY. A stop bit sampled at 0 sets FRAME together with RXRDY. OVRE, PARE and FRAME stay set until UART_CR.RSTSTA is written to 1.
UART_MR.FILTER = 1 (off by default) passes the receive line through a 2-of-3 majority filter sampled on the 16x bit clock.

Disabled after reset. UART_CR.TXEN enables it; it then waits for a character in UART_THR. TXDIS stops it at once if idle, otherwise after the characters in the shift register and UART_THR have gone out. RSTTX stops it immediately. Each frame is a start bit (0), eight data bits LSB first, an optional parity bit (odd, even, space or mark per UART_MR) and one stop bit (1). TXRDY in UART_SR is set while UART_THR can take a character; the character moves to the shift register and TXRDY rises again.
