TXEMPTY rises after the last stop bit once shift register and UART_THR are both empty.
The receiver and the transmitter each connect to a DMA controller channel, programmed through the DMAC.

Each received character is compared per UART_CMPR and the result shows as the CMP flag of UART_SR at the moment the character enters UART_RHR; RSTSTA clears it. VAL1 = VAL2 matches that one value; VAL1 < VAL2 matches any value from VAL1 to VAL2; VAL1 > VAL2 matches either VAL1 or VAL2. CMPPAR adds the parity bit to the condition. With CMPMODE = 1, UART_RHR loading starts only once a character meets the condition; writing UART_CR.REQCLR rearms this.

Asynchronous partial wake-up lets the UART judge an incoming character before the system is woken. It is meant for Wait mode but also works with the system running. When it is enabled in the PMC, a falling edge on RXD requests a clock; in Wait mode the PMC turns the fast RC oscillator back on and supplies only the UART. The character is compared with VAL1 and VAL2 of UART_CMPR (same rules as the compare function, plus VAL1 = 0 and VAL2 = 255, which matches any character); a match, with correct parity if CMPPAR is set, wakes the whole system from Wait mode, otherwise the UART lets the PMC stop its clock. With the system running, a mismatch turns off only the UART's clock until the next activity. Limits: 19200 baud maximum in Wait mode; 115200 or more when running or in Sleep mode, bounded by the peripheral clock / 16. UART_RHR must be read before enabling, and the UART must not be accessed between enabling and the wake-up. CMPMODE is ignored in this mode. With the system running, CMP must be the only UART interrupt source; after a wake-up from Wait mode, RXRDY shows the UART was the cause. While SleepWalking is enabled, a peripheral clock of bus clock / 8 is not allowed; other dividers are.
UART_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the mode, baud rate generator and comparison registers.

Chosen by UART_MR.CHMODE. Automatic echo: each bit received on URXD is repeated on UTXD; the transmitter runs but does not reach UTXD. Local loopback: the transmitter feeds the receiver inside; URXD is ignored and UTXD is held high (idle). Remote loopback: URXD is connected straight to UTXD and the transmitter and receiver are disabled.

MediaLB is one standard, low-pin-count interface that carries every MOST Network data type between a MediaLB Controller and one or more MediaLB Devices. The 3-pin bus has a one-way clock line (MLBC), a two-way signal line (MLBS) and a two-way data line (MLBD). One Controller, the bridge to the MOST Network, generates MLBC locked to the network and keeps generating it when lock is lost. MLBS carries the Controller's ChannelAddresses and the Devices' Command and RxStatus bytes; MLBD carries the synchronous, asynchronous, control or isochronous data, driven by the transmitting Device and heard by all the others. Synchronous stream data can go to several receivers at once.

Once per MOST frame the Controller puts a FRAMESYNC pattern on MLBS; its end marks the byte and channel boundaries for everyone. Each four-byte block (quadlet) of a 3-pin frame is a physical channel; one or more physical channels, not necessarily adjacent, form a logical channel. The Controller arbitrates, allocates bandwidth and owns the ChannelAddresses. It sends a ChannelAddress on MLBS; one physical channel later the Device it names as transmitter puts a Command byte on MLBS and four data bytes on MLBD together, and the receiver answers with an RxStatus byte on MLBS (ready or busy). Receivers of synchronous broadcast data never answer busy and must not drive RxStatus. ChannelAddresses may be fixed or assigned at run time; for run-time assignment each Device has a preassigned unique DeviceAddress, which the Controller can scan for in the System Channel at the request of a Device such as the External Host Controller (EHC).

All MOST transport methods (synchronous stream, asynchronous packet, control message, isochronous); several clock rates; data rate scalable for every method; FRAMESYNC for synchronising Devices to the MOST Network; a system broadcast channel for administration; Controller-to-Device and Device-to-Device transfers; broadcast of synchronous stream data to many receivers.

The MLB pins are PIO lines assigned to the MLB in the PIO controllers. The MLB clock is enabled in the PMC. The MLB has two interrupt lines to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the MLB.

A single Controller drives MLBCLK into the clock input of every Device. All Devices, the Controller included, share MLBSIG and MLBDAT. In each quadlet on MLBSIG the Controller sends the ChannelAddress, the transmitter the Command and the receiver the RxStatus, so every Device holds MLBSIG at high impedance when it is not driving; the transmitter drives MLBDAT only in the physical channels it owns and holds it at high impedance otherwise. Each line needs a pull-down to keep it in a known state when nobody drives it. Series resistors near the Controller and Device outputs are recommended for termination and edge-rate control, and MLBCLK may have an AC parallel termination near the Device farthest from the Controller. The recommended values are 100 Ω series, 47 kΩ pull-down and an optional 100 Ω with 27 pF clock termination; the right values depend on the MediaLB clock speed, the trace impedance and the load capacitance on the line.

ChannelAddress: a 16-bit token the Controller sends on MLBS at the end of a physical channel; it defines a logical channel and grants the next physical channel to one transmitter and one or more receivers. Command: a byte the transmitter sends on MLBS at the start of the physical channel, giving the data type and control information, while it sends the data on MLBD. RxStatus: a byte the receiver sends on MLBS after the Command, a hardware handshake that also reports errors. Data: the four bytes on MLBD, left-justified, MSB first and most significant byte first; after a busy answer the same data is resent in the next physical channel of the logical channel. A DeviceAddress is a 16-bit address used only with MLBScan in the System Channel.

A logical channel is every physical channel carrying one ChannelAddress; it runs one way, so two-way traffic needs two logical channels. Bits 15:9 and bit 0 of a ChannelAddress are always 0; only CA[8:1] vary. The granted physical channel follows its ChannelAddress by one physical channel. 0x01FE is FRAMESYNC: its end sets the byte and physical channel boundaries, and the frame (PC0) starts one physical channel later. 0x0000 is BusIdle (unassigned and unused). Odd addresses are reserved. On 3-pin MediaLB the required weak pull-down holds MLBS in a known state when undriven.

16 bits, preassigned and unique per Device; bits 15:9 and bit 0 are 0 and only DA[8:1] vary. The Controller scans for them at the EHC's request to learn which Devices are present; they are used only with MLBScan in the System Channel, never on physical channels. Once a Device is found its ChannelAddresses can be assigned. Devices are urged to support this dynamic configuration, which avoids ChannelAddress collisions; programmable Devices should set their DeviceAddress in firmware, and fixed-function Devices should fix only the upper bits and take the lower bits from pins, so that several of the same Device can share a bus.

Command is eight bits with all odd values reserved. The transmitter (Controller included) puts it on MLBS to say what kind of data is on MLBD. Normal commands are sent by the transmitter in non-System channels, System commands by the Controller in the System Channel. RxStatus is also eight bits with odd values reserved; the receiver puts it on MLBS after the Command. Current-state responses describe the receiver in this physical channel; feedback responses answer the Command of the previous physical channel of the logical channel. Among Normal responses only ReceiverProtocolError is feedback; all System responses are feedback. A receiver of synchronous data drives nothing, and on 3-pin MediaLB the MLBS pull-down gives ReceiverReady by itself. For control or asynchronous packets the receiver answers ReceiverReady if it takes the quadlet, ReceiverBusy if it cannot, or ReceiverBreak to stop the packet, which the transmitter must then abandon. A detected error is reported as ReceiverProtocolError in the next physical channel of the logical channel.

System commands go in the physical channel that belongs to the FRAMESYNC ChannelAddress (PC0); NoData there means no command this frame. Every System command and every System response, dynamic configuration included, is optional. MOSTLock and MOSTUnlock report whether the Controller is locked to the MOST Network; when unlocked, all data to and from the network must stop, though Controller buffering may delay the stop past the appearance of MOSTUnlock. MLBReset puts the MediaLB interface of one or every Device in a known state: first two MLBD bytes zero resets all, a match with the local DeviceAddress resets only that Device. MLBSubCmd carries configuration or status to Devices in byte 0 of the MLBD quadlet (the first sent); the only sub-command defined is scSetCA (01h).

Devices and ChannelAddresses are configured statically or dynamically. Dynamically, the EHC, over logical channels opened at start-up, asks the Controller to scan for a DeviceAddress; the Controller sends MLBScan with the address in the first two MLBD bytes of the System Channel. A Device with that address answers in the next System Channel with DevicePresent if its ChannelAddresses are already set or fixed, or DeviceServiceRequest if not. The Controller tells the EHC; for a Device asking for service the EHC says which ChannelAddresses to give, and the Controller broadcasts them with MLBSubCmd. The scSetCA quadlet holds, from bit 31 down, the sub-command (01h) in bits 31:24, DA[8:1] in bits 23:16, CA[8:1] in bits 15:8 and an Index in bits 7:0. A Device whose DeviceAddress matches DA[8:1] uses CA[8:1] for the logical channel numbered Index; Indices 0 and 1 are reserved for control channels, so a Device without control channels starts at Index 2. A Device that is reset or drops off the bus returns to its power-up state and forgets its ChannelAddresses. Device documentation lists each Index with its logical channel, type and maximum bandwidth, and how many frames the Device needs to apply a scSetCA; the EHC waits that long between Indices.

A transfer is ChannelAddress (Controller), then Command (transmitter), then RxStatus (receiver), with four data bytes. The Controller sends the ChannelAddress and releases MLBS. A fixed 4 bytes (one quadlet) later the addressed transmitter shifts out the Command on MLBS while starting the four data bytes on MLBD; the receiver follows in the same physical channel with RxStatus. For asynchronous, control and non-broadcast isochronous data the quadlet is accepted on ReceiverReady and refused on ReceiverBusy, in which case the transmitter repeats both Command and data when that ChannelAddress next comes round. For synchronous and broadcast isochronous data receivers drive nothing and the bus defaults to ReceiverReady, so several receivers can listen. After NoData the receiver ignores MLBD. Each driver releases MLBS after its byte, and the transmitter releases MLBD at the end of the physical channel unless it also owns the next one.

The Controller sends FRAMESYNC (0x01FE) once per MOST frame on MLBS, and the link layer keeps the pattern unique on the bus. Every Device aligns its byte and physical channel boundaries to it; four bytes after its end comes PC0, the System Channel. The number of physical channels depends on the MediaLB clock speed. PC0 can carry Controller broadcasts of system control and status, such as MLBReset, MLBScan, MOSTLock and MOSTUnlock. Physical channels can be assigned statically (for example a pair of logical channels opened at power-up, through which a Device, usually the EHC, configures the rest) or dynamically through MLBScan.

At power-up the Controller may send MLBReset in the System Channel; every Device then cancels transfers and clears its buffers. Configuration is either static, decided by the system designer and passed by the EHC to the Controller over power-up logical channels or another port, or dynamic at run time through MLBScan and scSetCA, which lets one board design support several build options. The Controller keeps MLBC running while the MOST Network is unlocked, and may stop MLBC when the bus is idle to save power; ChannelAddress assignments survive and the same paths exist when MLBC restarts. Devices are clocked from MLBC and must find FRAMESYNC before communicating, and should keep checking each frame that they are still frame-locked.

Synchronisation: a locked Device that keeps seeing FRAMESYNC on time disregards any FRAMESYNC pattern at another place; a locked Device that misses FRAMESYNC at its expected place in two frames running declares unlock and releases both MLBS and MLBD; an unlocked Device that sees FRAMESYNC at the same place for three frames in a row, declare lock and resume. As transmitter: drive Command on MLBS at the start of the physical channel, then release it, and drive the data quadlet on MLBD for the whole physical channel, then release it; NoData is the MLBS default and need not be driven. As receiver of asynchronous, control or non-broadcast isochronous data: drive RxStatus during byte 2 of the physical channel, then release it; undriven means ReceiverReady, but driving it is recommended. As receiver of synchronous or broadcast isochronous data: drive no RxStatus.

Synchronous stream data is broadcast, with ReceiverReady (the MLBS default) as the only allowed response. Control and asynchronous data are packets with start and end commands, to one receiver at a time. Isochronous data may be broadcast if no receiver uses ReceiverBusy; otherwise it goes to a single receiver.

Control and asynchronous packets work the same way with their own commands. The transmitter sends ControlStart with the first quadlet, ControlContinue with middle quadlets and ControlEnd with the last. A receiver that sees the commands out of order replies with ReceiverProtocolError one quadlet later on that logical channel. To abort, the transmitter sends ControlBreak; a resent message starts again from the beginning. The transmitter moves through Idle, Start, Continue and End states, sending in each state's command only in physical channels of its ChannelAddress, sending NoData with zero data while it has nothing ready and resending after ReceiverBusy. A ReceiverProtocolError seen in Idle or Start belongs to the previous packet only if ControlEnd was sent in the physical channel just before; a packet counts as sent when its ControlEnd is not answered with ReceiverProtocolError in the next physical channel. Supporting application break requests other than after ReceiverBusy is optional. The receiver has Idle and Continue states: Idle waits for a start command and answers ReceiverBusy when it has no buffer; ControlEnd completes the packet and returns to Idle; a ControlBreak discards the packet; an invalid command is reported to the application, the packet discarded and ReceiverProtocolError sent. A standard receiver sends ReceiverProtocolError only in Continue; enhanced Devices may also check in Idle (for example a synchronous or isochronous command on a control channel).

Synchronous stream data is sent continuously and broadcast, with no block information; receivers leave RxStatus at ReceiverReady (logic low), held by the MLBS pull-down. Stereo 24-bit data needs two physical channels per frame, packed left-justified across the two quadlets; formats include 16-bit mono, 16-bit left and right, 24-bit mono, 24-bit left and right and 32-bit sequential, whose internal format the system designer chooses. The transmitter has one state, Transmit: once the channel is set up it always sends SyncData, with safe data such as zeros when it has nothing. Synchronous data is stopped only by removing the ChannelAddress from the bus. The receiver has one state, Continue: SyncData quadlets are stored; any other command is a protocol error reported to the application, and its data is dropped and replaced by safe data. A receiver that does not see its ChannelAddress in a frame should treat the channel as not set up or removed (for example mute its outputs).

Isochronous data streams like synchronous data, but its commands mark the start of a block (IsoSync1Byte to IsoSync4Bytes) or the middle of one (Iso1Byte to Iso4Bytes) and say how many bytes of the quadlet are valid, left-justified. IsoNoData is sent while the channel is active but has nothing for this quadlet. The transmitter starts sending at once; after ReceiverBusy it resends the same data without advancing. A receiver uses only the valid bytes. NoData means the channel is not set up yet. The only responses are ReceiverBusy and the default ReceiverReady; busy should be rare because transmitters may hold little isochronous data. If any receiver uses ReceiverBusy only one receiver is allowed; if none drives RxStatus the stream can be broadcast.

Every Device meets the physical layer for the speeds it supports and follows the synchronisation rules. For Controllers all System commands, dynamic configuration and DeviceAddresses are optional. For Devices each transport method is optional, but a supported method is supported fully, with all its Command and RxStatus values; added protocol-error checks on asynchronous and control channels must be documented. System responses and dynamic configuration are optional for Devices, but if present must follow the specification. Device documentation must state the speeds, System commands and transport methods supported, the DeviceAddress, and the Index and transport method used for each ChannelAddress.

MediaLB block (MLB PHY): physical and link layer of the 3-pin interface, serial/parallel conversion and frame synchronisation. Host Bus Interface (HBI): 16-bit parallel client access for the Host Controller (HC) to every MOST channel and data type, up to 64 independent channels, 40 ns minimum latency per word and 400 Mbps maximum bandwidth. Routing Fabric (RF): carries data to and from the HBI and the MediaLB block, with a bus arbiter and multiplexing to the Channel Table RAM (CTR) and Data Buffer RAM (DBR). Memory Interface (MIF): bridge from the I/O bus to the CTR and DBR. Interrupt Interface (INTIF): tells the HBI of changes to channel descriptors. Clocks, Power and Reset (CPR): clock and reset multiplexing and synchronisation. AHB block: links the AHB host side to the HBI client side. APB block: turns two-cycle APB accesses into single-cycle I/O accesses.

Real-time access over the 3-pin interface to every network data type: streaming, packet, control and isochronous. Single-ended 3-pin mode up to 1024xFs (49.152 MHz at Fs = 48 kHz). ChannelAddresses 0x0002 to 0x007E map to logical channels 1 to 63; 0x01FE is logical channel 0, the reserved System Channel.

The HBI gives the HC a 16-bit parallel client port to every MOST channel and data type: up to 64 channels, each set to send or receive synchronous, isochronous, asynchronous or control data, able to send or receive at the whole network bandwidth. To reach an HBI DMA channel, hardware turns its channel number into a channel allocation table (CAT) address, which yields the connection label and through it the channel descriptor.

operation.topic: MLB routing fabric and data buffer RAM
operation.text: Each RF DMA controller manages dynamic buffers in the DBR from channel descriptors kept in the CTR. The DBR is 8 bits × 16k entries and gives circular buffering between transmitters and receivers; the size and place of each buffer are set in software in the channel descriptor table (CDT) in the CTR. Receivers keep the write pointer and transmitters the read pointer, and the RF DMA prevents overflow and underflow with full and empty detection per channel type. Synchronous: hardware keeps the read pointer two sub-buffers behind the write pointer and periodically realigns both pointers to a sub-buffer boundary (for example after a FRAMESYNC). Isochronous: empty when RPTR = WPTR and BF = 0, full when WPTR = RPTR and BF = 1. Asynchronous and control: empty when RPTR = WPTR and RPC = WPC, full when (pointers equal with WPC ≠ RPC) or WPC = RPC - 1; hardware never reads an empty buffer or writes a full one.

The CTR is 128 bits × 144 entries and lets software route channels and allocate DBR buffers. It holds three tables: the channel descriptor table (CDT, 0x00–0x3F), the AHB descriptor table (ADT, 0x40–0x7F) and the channel allocation table (CAT, 0x80–0x8F). Each 16-bit CAT entry is one connection to or from a transmitter or receiver (a MediaLB or HBI channel), at a fixed index per channel, and holds a 6-bit connection label pointing into the CDT; a route is made by giving the Rx and Tx entries the same label. Each 128-bit CDT entry (channel descriptor) describes one DBR buffer (size, pointers), in a format that depends on the channel type. Reserved descriptor bits are written 0.

Direction is counted from the DBR, so the HBI CAT entry and the MediaLB CAT entry of one channel have opposite RNW. Tx channel (HC to MediaLB): HBI CAT RNW = 0, MediaLB CAT RNW = 1. Rx channel (MediaLB to HC): HBI CAT RNW = 1, MediaLB CAT RNW = 0.

Standard mode needs less buffer but has more interrupts and tighter latency: the HC moves one full frame of stream data in or out of each channel buffer every frame period. Multi-frame per sub-buffer mode needs more buffer but fewer interrupts and looser latency: the HC moves N frames per transfer. To use it: set MLB_MLBC0.FCNT[2:0] to the frames per sub-buffer, set MFE = 1 in the channel's CAT entry and set BD = 4 × m × bpf - 1 in the CDT; repeat per channel. A synchronous buffer is four sub-buffers, each holding 1 to 64 frames as set by FCNT.

The MIF gives the HC direct access to the CTR when MLB_MADR.TB = 0 and to the DBR when TB = 1. Each write to MLB_MADR starts one read or write cycle; reading MLB_MADR starts nothing, and MLB_MCTL.XCMP = 1 marks the cycle complete. CTR write: load the 128-bit entry into MLB_MDAT0–3, set bitwise write enables in MLB_MDWE0–3, then write MLB_MADR with WNR = 1, TB = 0 and ADDR[7:0]. CTR read: write MLB_MADR with WNR = 0, TB = 0 and ADDR[7:0], wait for XCMP, read MLB_MDAT0–3. The MIF moves 32 bits of an entry per access, so a 128-bit entry takes four accesses and a 16-bit CAT entry one. Example: CAT61 set up as an isochronous Tx entry, muted, flow control on, connection label 7: MLB_MDAT2 = 7B070000h, MLB_MDWE2 = FFFF0000h (MDWE0/1/3 = 00000000h), MLB_MADR = 80000087h. DBR write: put the byte in MLB_MDAT0[7:0] (MDAT1–3 and MDWE0–3 unused), then write MLB_MADR with WNR = 1, TB = 1 and ADDR[13:0]. DBR read: write MLB_MADR with WNR = 0, TB = 1 and ADDR[13:0], wait for XCMP, read MLB_MDAT0[7:0].

INTIF polls the HBI channel descriptors at low priority and alerts the HBI when an asynchronous or control channel has a packet to read or room for a requested packet write, or when an isochronous channel's valid bytes or empty bytes exceed the block size.

Moves data between the MLB's channel buffers and system memory through ping-pong buffers per channel, each channel described by a 128-bit ADT entry at a fixed CTR address; the 64 ADT entries map one to one to the 64 HBI physical channels. LE selects little endian (1) or big endian (0) on the AHB. BAn gives each page's 32-bit start in system memory and BDn its size: up to 2k entries for asynchronous and control channels, 8k for isochronous and synchronous. Synchronous and isochronous channel buffers can each be up to 8 kbytes deep; an isochronous page holds one or several whole blocks.

operation.topic: MLB asynchronous and control packets in system memory
operation.text: Every asynchronous and control packet follows the Port Message Protocol (PMP): its first two bytes are the packet length (PML, the length of what follows, excluding PML), and a packet is at most 2048 bytes. When software programs the DMA it marks each buffer ready with RDYn; hardware sets DNEn and interrupts the HC as it finishes each, and moves on to another buffer whose RDYn is set. The descriptor is set up before every DMA on the channel. Single-packet mode: at most one packet per ping or pong buffer, non-segmented or segmented across several buffers (PSn marks the buffer where a packet starts); DNEn is set when the packet ends or the buffer is full. Multiple-packet mode: several packets per buffer, fewer interrupts at the cost of more buffering and latency. For Tx, software sets PSn on every buffer (the first two bytes are the first packet's PML), must not touch PSn while the buffer is active (RDYn = 1, DNEn = 0), sizes the buffer to an exact number of whole packets, and may not segment; DNEn is set when the last byte of the last packet has been read. For Rx, PSn is ignored, software follows packets by their PML, DNEn is set when the buffer is full or a packet ends exactly one byte before its end, and packets may span several buffers.

MLB_MLBC0, HMCR0, HMCR1 and MLB_HCTL are written directly over APB. 1. Clear the CAT, CDT and ADT in the CTR and all bits of all registers. 2. Choose the MediaLB clock speed in MLB_MLBC0.MLBCLK and set MLB_MLBC0.MLBEN. 3. Set HMCR0 and HMCR1 to FFFFFFFFh to activate all channels and set MLB_HCTL.EN = 1.

The CAT and CDT are written indirectly through the MIF. Clear the CAT; for each logical channel N (0–63) program its CDT: the 14-bit BA, the 12- or 13-bit BD = buffer bytes - 1, with (BD + 1) = 4 × m × bpf for synchronous, (BD + 1) mod (BS + 1) = 0 for isochronous, (BD + 1) ≥ the largest packet for asynchronous (1024 for a MOST Data Packet, 1536 for a MOST Ethernet Packet) and (BD + 1) ≥ 64 for control; for isochronous set BS = block bytes - 1; clear all other bits. Then program the CAT entry of the inbound DMA (HBI for Tx channels, MediaLB for Rx) with RNW = 0, and of the outbound DMA (MediaLB for Tx, HBI for Rx) with RNW = 1, each with CT (010 asynchronous, 001 control, 011 isochronous, 000 synchronous), CL = N, MT = 1 if synchronous, CE = 1 and all other bits 0.

The ADT is written indirectly through the MIF. Clear it; for each logical channel N set the ping page: 32-bit BA1, BD1 = buffer bytes - 1 ((BD1 + 1) = n × m × bpf for synchronous, (BD1 + 1) mod (BS + 1) = 0 for isochronous, 5 ≤ (BD1 + 1) ≤ 4096 for asynchronous and control), PS1 on asynchronous and control Tx channels when that buffer holds a packet start, clear DNE1 and ERR1, set RDY1; set the pong page the same way with BA2, BD2, PS2, DNE2, ERR2, RDY2. Then choose LE, the active page PG (0 ping, 1 pong) and set CE on every active channel. Asynchronous and control packets always start with a PMP header whose first two bytes, PML, give the message length that follows; hardware uses PML to find the end of a packet, and packets may span pages or share a page.

Confirm MLB_MLBC1.CLKM = 0 (MediaLB clock present); if it reads 1, clear it, let one APB or I/O clock pass and test again. Then wait until MLB_MLBC0.MLBLK = 1 (locked), let four frames pass, and unmute the synchronous channels.

After set-up, channels are serviced by three independent flows. AHB DMA interrupts: enable all active channels in MLB_ACMRn; MLB_ACTL.SCE = 0 clears status on read, 1 needs a 1 written to clear; MLB_ACTL.SMX = 0 gives channels 0–31 on MediaLB IRQ0 and 32–63 on IRQ1, SMX = 1 puts all on IRQ0. On an interrupt read MLB_ACSRn (and write it back if SCE = 1), then for each channel read its ADT (PG, DNEn, ERRn, and PSn with the PML on asynchronous and control Rx), and reprogram the finished or failed pages. A channel that gets an AHB error response is disabled by hardware (CE = 0). MediaLB interrupts: choose software clearing (write 0) for the MSn channel status registers, enable protocol-error interrupts in MLB_MIEN (CTX_PE, CRX_PE, ATX_PE, ARX_PE, SYNC_PE, ISOC_PE), and on mlb_int read MSn, then RSTS/WSTS of the CDTs, and clear the errors to resume: WSTS[3] = 0 on synchronous, WSTS[2:1] = 00 on isochronous, RSTS[4]/WSTS[4] = 0 and RSTS[2]/WSTS[2] = 0 on asynchronous and control. System commands: the MLB answers MLBScan, MLBReset, MOST_Unlock and the like by itself and flags them in MLB_MSS; software polls MLB_MSS, clears the bit by writing 0 when done, and if SWSYSCMD = 1 reads the system data from MLB_MSD.

The MLB has no low-power features of its own. Before stopping its clocks: finish active transfers, clear MLBEN and MLBPEN in MLB_MLBC0, clear MLB_HCMR0 and MLB_HCMR1 and MLB_HCTL.EN, and clear MLB_ACMR0 and MLB_ACMR1. When the clocks return, configure the hardware again as at start-up.

CAN controller to ISO 11898-1:2015 and the Bosch CAN FD specification; an external transceiver connects it to the bus. An Rx handler does acceptance filtering, moves received messages from the CAN core into the message RAM and reports receive status; a Tx handler hands stored messages over to the CAN core and reports transmit status. Up to 128 filter elements, each a range, a bit mask or dedicated IDs.

CAN 2.0 A and B and ISO 11898-1; CAN FD frames carrying up to 64 bytes of data; error logging; tuned for AUTOSAR and SAE J1939; two configurable Rx FIFOs; separate signalling of high-priority messages; up to 64 dedicated Rx buffers and 32 dedicated Tx buffers; configurable Tx FIFO, Tx queue and Tx event FIFO; direct processor access to the message RAM, which several MCANs may share; loop-back test mode; maskable interrupts; CAN clock asynchronous to the system bus clock; power-down; debug on CAN.

CANTX and CANRX go to the transceiver and are PIO lines assigned in the PIO controllers. The MCAN clock is enabled in the PMC; the CAN core runs from the bus-independent clock PCK5, the interface from the peripheral clock. The system bus clock must always be at least the CAN clock. A CAN clock of 20, 40 or 80 MHz is recommended, made by PCK5 dividing UPLLCK (480 MHz) by 24, 12 or 6; PCK5 lets the bus and processor clocks change without disturbing the bit rate. Two interrupt lines, MCAN_INT0 and MCAN_INT1, go to the interrupt controller, which is set up first; each source is routed to one of them, and MCAN_ILE.EINT0 and EINT1 enable each line.

operation.topic: MCAN message RAM address and timestamp source
operation.text: Bits 15:2 of each message RAM section address are set in that section's configuration register; bits 31:16 for CAN0 and CAN1 are set in CCFG_CAN0 and CCFG_SYSIO. An external timestamp is the counter value CV of TC0 channel 0 (TC_CV0 at 0x4000C010); TC0.Ch0 can be clocked by PCK6 or PCK7, chosen by CCFG_PCCR.TC0CC and set up in PMC_PCK6 and PMC_PCK7.

MCAN_CCCR.INIT is set by software, by hardware reset, by an uncorrected message RAM bit error, or on Bus_Off. While INIT is set no frames move, CANTX is recessive (high), the error counters keep their values and no configuration register changes. Clearing INIT ends initialization; the bit stream processor then waits for 11 recessive bits in a row (Bus_Idle) before joining the bus. Configuration registers are writable only with INIT and CCE both set; CCE can be set only while INIT = 1 and clears itself when INIT = 0. Setting CCE clears MCAN_HPMS, MCAN_RXF0S, MCAN_RXF1S, MCAN_TXFQS, MCAN_TXBRP, MCAN_TXBTO, MCAN_TXBCF and MCAN_TXEFS, loads MCAN_TOCV.TOC from MCAN_TOCC.TOP, and holds the Tx and Rx handlers idle. MCAN_TXBAR and MCAN_TXBCR are writable only while CCE = 0. TEST, MON and DAR can be set only with INIT and CCE both 1; TEST and MON may be cleared any time.

With INIT cleared the MCAN synchronises to the bus. Accepted messages, with ID and DLC, go to a dedicated Rx buffer or to Rx FIFO 0 or 1. Messages are sent from dedicated Tx buffers, from a Tx FIFO or Tx queue, or from a mix. Automatic answers to remote frames are not implemented.

CAN FD frames come with or without bit rate switching; without it the data field may still exceed 8 bytes, with it the control, data and CRC fields go at a higher bit rate. The former reserved bit (first reserved bit with 29-bit IDs) becomes FDF: recessive for CAN FD, dominant for Classic CAN. In an FD frame res dominant and BRS recessive mean the bit rate switches; res recessive is reserved, and receiving it sets MCAN_PSR.PXE. With protocol exception handling on (MCAN_CCCR.PXHD = 0) the MCAN then goes from Receiver (MCAN_PSR.ACT = 2) to Integrating (ACT = 00) at the next sample point; with it off (PXHD = 1) it treats the bit as a form error and sends an error frame. CCCR.FDOE = 1 enables sending and receiving FD frames; Classic frames are always possible and FDF in each Tx buffer chooses the format. With FDOE = 0 received FD frames cause an error frame and no FD frame is sent whatever FDF says. FDOE = 1 with BRSE = 0 looks only at FDF; FDOE = 1 with BRSE = 1 sends frames with FDF and BRS set as FD with bit rate switching. FDOE and BRSE change only with INIT and CCE set.

operation.topic: MCAN changing CAN FD mode in operation
operation.text: Recommended only when: the data phase fails much more often than the arbitration phase (then stop using bit rate switching for transmission); at start-up, all nodes use ISO11898-1 frames until CAN FD is confirmed to work and then all switch; CAN Partial Networking wake-up messages, which must be Classic CAN; end-of-line programming with nodes that are not FD-capable, held in Silent mode until programming ends, after which all return to Classic CAN.

After a recessive BRS bit the bit timing switches inside the frame: the arbitration phase uses the nominal timing of MCAN_NBTP, the data phase the timing of MCAN_DBTP, and the timing returns at the CRC delimiter or on an error, whichever comes first. The fastest data-phase rate depends on the CAN core clock: at 20 MHz with the shortest bit time of 4 tq it is 5 Mbit/s. In both FD formats ESI is sent recessive if the transmitter is error passive at the start of the frame, dominant otherwise.

In the FD data phase only one node transmits, so bus length does not matter, but the transmitter hears its own bits back from the transceiver late; if the delay exceeds TSEG1 a bit error results, which would cap the data rate. With MCAN_DBTP.TDC = 1 the delayed transmit bit is compared with the received bit at a secondary sample point (SSP); a mismatch is acted on at the next regular sample point. Compensation is always off in the arbitration phase. SSP = measured CANTX-to-CANRX delay + MCAN_TDCR.TDCO, rounded down to whole CAN core clocks; TDCO places the SSP within the received bit (for example half a data bit). MCAN_PSR.TDCV shows the value in use; it is cleared when INIT is set and updated on each FD frame sent with TDC = 1. Limits: delay + TDCO must be under 6 data-phase bit times and at most 127 CAN core clocks (larger sums are clamped to 127); SSP checking ends with the data phase, at the CRC delimiter sample point.

With TDC = 1 each FD frame sent starts a counter at the falling edge from FDF to res on CANTX and stops it when that edge arrives on CANRX; resolution is one mtq. MCAN_TDCR.TDCF sets a filter window, a minimum SSP position, so a short dominant spike during the FDF bit as received cannot stop the count too soon: the measurement stops only once the SSP position is at least TDCF and CANRX is low.

The node receives data and remote frames and acknowledges valid frames, but sends no data, remote, active error or overload frames; on an error or overload it sends no dominant bits, waits for bus idle to resync, and its error counters do not count. Set by MCAN_CCCR.ASM, which the processor can set only with CCE and INIT both 1 and can clear at any time. The MCAN enters it by itself when the Tx handler could not read the message RAM in time; the processor clears ASM to leave. Useful for bit rate detection: try bit rates until a valid frame is received, then leave. Not to be combined with internal or external loop back.

Set by MCAN_CCCR.MON (ISO11898-1 10.12). The MCAN receives valid data and remote frames but starts no transmission and puts only recessive bits on the bus; dominant bits it must send (ACK, overload flag, active error flag) are looped back inside so it sees them while the bus stays recessive. MCAN_TXBRP is held in reset. Lets traffic be analysed without disturbing the bus.

Frames that lose arbitration or are hit by errors are retransmitted by default (ISO11898-1 6.3.3). MCAN_CCCR.DAR turns this off for time-triggered communication (ISO 11898-1 9.2). In DAR mode every transmission is cancelled once it starts on the bus; TXBRP.TRPx clears after success, if not started by the time of cancellation, on lost arbitration or on an error. Success: MCAN_TXBTO.TOx set, MCAN_TXBCF.CFx clear. Success despite cancellation: both set. Lost arbitration or disturbed frame: TOx clear, CFx set. A successful frame with Tx events enabled writes a Tx Event FIFO element with ET = 10 (transmission in spite of cancellation).

MCAN_CCCR.CSR = 1 asks for power-down: once pending transmissions finish the MCAN waits for bus idle, sets INIT, and sets MCAN_CCCR.CSA to say it is ready. Registers can still be accessed; writing INIT has no effect. The peripheral clock and CAN core clock may then be stopped. To leave, restart the clocks, clear CSR, wait for CSA to clear, then clear INIT to resume communication.

MCAN_CCCR.TEST = 1 makes MCAN_TEST writable. MCAN_TEST.TX gives CANTX four functions: serial data (default), the CAN sample point signal, constant dominant or constant recessive. MCAN_TEST.RX reads the CANRX pin. Clock domain synchronisation can delay both by several system bus clocks. Test modes are for production test or self test only, since software control of CANTX overrides every protocol function. External loop back (MCAN_TEST.LBCK): the MCAN stores its own frames as received if they pass filtering, ignores acknowledge errors, feeds Tx to Rx internally and disregards CANRX; frames still appear on CANTX. Internal loop back (LBCK and MCAN_CCCR.MON): a hot self test without disturbing a running bus; CANRX is disconnected and CANTX held recessive.

A 16-bit wrap-around counter clocked every 1 to 16 CAN bit times by prescaler TSCC.TCP, read in MCAN_TSCV.TSC; writing MCAN_TSCV zeroes it and a wrap sets MCAN_IR.TSW. At start of frame reception or transmission its value is stored in the RXTS field of the Rx buffer/FIFO element or the TXTS field of the Tx Event FIFO element. MCAN_TSCC.TSS selects an external 16-bit timestamp instead.

A 16-bit down counter on the same prescaler as the timestamp counter, configured in MCAN_TOCC and read in MCAN_TOCV.TOC, used to time out either Rx FIFO or the Tx Event FIFO. It runs only while INIT = 0 and stops when INIT is set (for example at Bus_Off). MCAN_TOCC.TOS chooses the mode. Continuous: starts when INIT clears; writing MCAN_TOCV reloads TOP and counting continues; at zero it reloads at once. FIFO-controlled: an empty FIFO loads TOP, counting starts with the first stored element, and writing MCAN_TOCV does nothing. Reaching zero sets MCAN_IR.TOO. The counter is clocked from the CAN core sample point, so its timing shifts with resynchronisation, and with bit rate switching it counts differently in arbitration and data fields.

Two filter lists, one for standard and one for extended identifiers, each run from element 0 and stop at the first match. An element can be a range, one or two exact IDs or a classic bit mask, set to accept or reject, and enabled individually. Registers involved: MCAN_GFC, MCAN_SIDFC, MCAN_XIDFC, MCAN_XIDAM. A match (per SFEC/EFEC) stores the frame in FIFO 0 or 1, stores it in an Rx buffer, stores it in an Rx buffer and pulses the filter event pin, rejects it, sets MCAN_IR.HPM, or sets HPM and stores in FIFO 0 or 1. Filtering starts once the full identifier has arrived; the data is then written 32 bits at a time. If the frame turns out bad (for example a CRC error) it is discarded, but the target Rx buffer may already be partly overwritten without its New Data flag set, or the FIFO element partly overwritten without the put index moving; MCAN_PSR.LEC and DLEC give the error. The stored identifier is always the received one, whatever filter matched, and the result depends strongly on the order of the elements.

Range: matches IDs from SF1ID/EF1ID to SF2ID/EF2ID; for extended IDs EFT = 00 ANDs the ID with MCAN_XIDAM first and EFT = 11 does not. Specific IDs: one or two exact IDs; for one, set ID1 = ID2. Classic bit mask: ID1 is the ID and ID2 the mask; only bits where the mask is 1 are compared, so an all-ones mask needs an exact match and an all-zeros mask matches everything.

operation.topic: MCAN standard and extended filter paths
operation.text: For a valid frame, a remote frame is rejected if MCAN_GFC.RRFS (standard) or RRFE (extended) is 1. If the list is enabled (MCAN_SIDFC.LSS or MCAN_XIDFC.LSE above 0) the elements are tried from 0; a match accepts or rejects per the element. A frame matching nothing is discarded or accepted per MCAN_GFC.ANFS[1] or ANFE[1]. An accepted frame aimed at a full FIFO in blocking mode is not stored. For extended frames the received ID is ANDed with MCAN_XIDAM before the list runs.

Rx FIFO 0 and 1 each hold up to 64 elements, configured in MCAN_RXF0C and MCAN_RXF1C. Reaching the watermark MCAN_RXFnC.FnWM sets MCAN_IR.RFnW; put index reaching get index signals full (MCAN_RXFnS.FnF and MCAN_IR.RFnF). An element is read at MCAN_RXFnC.FnSA + MCAN_RXFnS.FnGI × element size. Blocking mode (FnOM = 0, default): when full nothing more is written until one element is read and acknowledged; a message arriving meanwhile is lost and flagged in MCAN_RXFnS.RFnL and MCAN_IR.RFnL. Overwrite mode (FnOM = 1): when full the next accepted message replaces the oldest and both indexes advance; reading should then start at least at get index + 1, since the element at the get index may be overwritten while it is read, and the needed offset depends on how fast the processor reads. After reading, write the last element's number to MCAN_RXFnA.FnA; the get index moves there and FnF clears if the put index has not reached it.

Up to 64, starting at MCAN_RXBC.RBSA. Each needs a standard or extended filter element with SFEC/EFEC = 7 and SFID2/EFID2[10:9] = 0; the matching message goes to the buffer that element names, in the Rx FIFO element format, and sets MCAN_IR.DRX. After the last word is written the buffer's New Data flag in MCAN_NDAT1/NDAT2 sets and the buffer is locked against further matching frames until the processor writes 1 to the flag; while locked, a filter element pointing at it does not match and filtering goes on to later elements. Handling: clear IR.DRX, read the New Data registers, read the messages, clear their New Data flags.

Debug messages A, B and C go into three consecutive Rx buffers (for example 61, 62, 63) in the Rx element format, giving the DMA a fixed start address relative to MCAN_RXBC.RBSA. Each has its own filter element with SFEC/EFEC = 111; then SFID2/EFID2[10:9] drives the debug state machine and SFID2/EFID2[5:0] gives the buffer. Storing a debug message sets neither its New Data flag nor MCAN_IR.DRX; progress shows in RXF1S.DMS. The state machine keeps the three in order and restarts if one is missing. Only after A, B and C arrive in order does m_can_dma_req go active; the MCAN then leaves those RAM words alone, as if New Data were set, until the DMA finishes and it is ready for the next set.

The Tx handler takes requests from dedicated Tx buffers and from a Tx FIFO or queue, passes messages to the CAN core, maintains the put and get indexes, and writes Tx events. There are up to 32 Tx buffers; Classic or FD format is set per buffer element. A Tx scan for the highest-priority request (lowest message ID) runs whenever MCAN_TXBRP changes or a transmission starts.

For systems whose fixed message IDs give one node's burst priority over messages that should come first. With MCAN_CCCR.TXP = 1 the MCAN waits two CAN bit times after each successful transmission before starting the next, so other nodes' pending messages can start in the gap without arbitrating against it; after receiving a message it may start as soon as the bus is free. Default off. It breaks up bursts from one node and guards against a babbling-idiot application.

Wholly under processor control, each with its own message ID; of buffers with the same ID the lowest-numbered goes first. After the data is updated an add request (MCAN_TXBAR.ARn) queues it; it arbitrates internally with the Tx FIFO or queue and externally on the bus by ID. A buffer takes one element size of 32-bit words, at TXBC.TBSA + index (0 to 31) × element size.

MCAN_TXBC.TFQM = 0. Messages go out in order from the get index MCAN_TXFQS.TFGI, so messages with the same ID from different buffers keep the order written. MCAN_TXFQS.TFFL gives the free elements (get minus put). Software writes each new message where MCAN_TXFQS.TFQPI points; each add request advances that index, and reaching the get index sets MCAN_TXFQS.TFQF (full), after which nothing more should be written until a message has gone. One message is requested by writing 1 to the TXBAR bit of the put-index buffer; n messages go into n consecutive buffers from the put index, are requested together in MCAN_TXBAR, and the put index advances by n, which should not exceed the free level. Cancelling the get-index buffer moves the get index to the next pending buffer and recomputes the free level; cancelling any other leaves both alone. The next free element is at MCAN_TXBC.TBSA + TFQPI (0 to 31) × element size.

MCAN_TXBC.TFQM = 1. Queued messages go out lowest message ID first (lowest buffer number among equal IDs). New messages are written at the put index TFQPI, which an add request moves on cyclically to the next free buffer; when the queue is full (TFQF = 1) the put index is invalid and nothing more should be written until a message has gone or been cancelled. Software may instead use MCAN_TXBRP and place messages in any buffer without a pending request. Address of the next free buffer: MCAN_TXBC.TBSA + TFQPI (0 to 31) × element size.

The Tx buffer section can hold dedicated buffers (count MCAN_TXBC.NDTB) followed by a Tx FIFO or Tx queue (count MCAN_TXBC.TFQS; zero means dedicated buffers only). With a FIFO, the scan covers the dedicated buffers and the oldest pending FIFO buffer (at MCAN_TXFS.TFGI), and the lowest ID among them goes next. With a queue, every buffer with a request is scanned and the lowest ID goes next.

For gateway and AUTOSAR use: writing 1 to a buffer's bit in MCAN_TXBCR cancels its request from a dedicated or queue buffer; it is not meant for the Tx FIFO. Success sets the bit in MCAN_TXBCF. If the frame is already on the bus, TXBRP stays set until it ends; success then sets both MCAN_TXBTO and MCAN_TXBCF, failure sets only TXBCF and the frame is not repeated. Cancelling just before a transmission would start leaves a short window with no transmission even if another message is pending, which may let another node send a lower-priority message.

Each transmitted frame leaves a Tx Event FIFO element holding its ID and send time, with the message marker copied from its Tx buffer to link the two. Up to 32 elements. When full (IR.TEFF) nothing more is written until one is read and the get index advanced; an event arriving then is lost and sets MCAN_IR.TEFL. Reaching the watermark MCAN_TXEFC.EFWM sets MCAN_IR.TEFW. An element is read at MCAN_TXEFC.EFSA + 2 × MCAN_TXEFS.EFGI.

For both Rx FIFOs and for the Tx Event FIFO, software moves the get index by writing the acknowledge index in MCAN_RXF0A, MCAN_RXF1A and MCAN_TXEFA; the get index becomes that index + 1 and the fill level updates. After one element, write its get index; after a run of elements, write the last one's index once. When reading out of order (for example a high-priority message picked from a FIFO), do not write the acknowledge index: it would misplace the get index, change the fill level and lose older elements. The MCAN does not check the value written.

The message RAM is 32 bits wide and one MCAN can use up to 4352 words. Sections need not all be configured and may be in any order. In CAN FD mode the RAM needed depends on the element sizes set in MCAN_RXESC.F0DS, F1DS, RBDS and MCAN_TXESC.TBDS. The MCAN addresses whole 32-bit words: only bits 15:2 of each start address are used. The MCAN does not check the layout, so start addresses and element counts must be checked to avoid corrupted or lost data.

After reset the registers take their reset values, Bus_Off is cleared and CANTX is recessive (high). MCAN_CCCR = 0x0001 (INIT = 1) so software can configure; the MCAN does not touch the bus until the processor clears INIT.
A read or write to a reserved address in the MCAN register map sets MCAN_IR.ARA and, if enabled, raises the selected interrupt line.

Four TC modules, TC0 to TC3, each with three identical 16-bit channels (0, 1, 2): twelve channels in all. Each channel can measure frequency, count events, measure intervals, generate pulses, time delays, make PWM, count up and down, and generate a 2-bit Gray count for stepper motors. A channel offers 3 external and 5 internal clock inputs plus 2 general-purpose I/O lines that can act as triggers, and drives its own interrupt. Trigger and capture events can come straight from PWM signals; capture registers can be read by the DMAC; a compare event can raise a fault for the PWM; registers can be write-protected. A quadrature decoder (QDEC) in front of the counters, fed by TIOA0, TIOB0 and TIOB1, filters and decodes encoder signals for motor position and speed. Two module-wide registers act on all three channels: TC_BCR starts them together with one write, and TC_BMR picks each channel's external clock inputs so channels can be chained.

operation.topic: TC pins, clock, interrupt, PWM links
operation.text: TC pins are PIO lines assigned in the PIO controllers. Each channel's clock is enabled in the PMC. Each channel has its own interrupt line to the interrupt controller, set up first. Trigger/capture inputs are wired inside to the PWM, and the TC FAULT output goes to a PWM fault input.

All channels work independently and identically except when the QDEC is enabled. Each channel's 16-bit counter counts up on each rising edge of the selected clock; passing from 2^16-1 to 0 is an overflow and sets TC_SR.COVFS. TC_CV shows the count live. A trigger resets the counter, which reads 0 from the next active clock edge.

At module level TC_BMR connects each channel's XC0–XC2 inputs to TCLK pins or, for chaining, to another channel's TIOA (channel 0: TCLK0, TIOA1 or TIOA2 on XC0; channel 1: TCLK1, TIOA0 or TIOA2 on XC1; channel 2: TCLK2, TIOA0 or TIOA1 on XC2). Each channel then picks with TC_CMRx.TCCLKS one of XC0, XC1, XC2 or the internal clocks PCK6 or PCK7 (TC0.Ch0 only), MCK/8, MCK/32, MCK/128 and SLCK. TC_CMRx.CLKI inverts the clock to count on the other edge. TC_CMRx.BURST gates the clock with XC0, XC1 or XC2 high, or not at all. Chaining two timers in Waveform mode needs the TIOx outputs set to a known level through TC_CMRx.ASWTRG and TC_BCR.SYNC written to 1 to start them together. An external clock or the asynchronous PCK6/PCK7 must have each level longer than a peripheral clock period, so at least 2.5 times slower than the peripheral clock.

Enable/disable: TC_CCR CLKEN and CLKDIS; also disabled by an RB load in Capture mode (TC_CMRx.LDBDIS = 1) or an RC compare in Waveform mode (TC_CMRx.CPCDIS = 1); once disabled, start and stop do nothing and only CLKEN re-enables it; TC_SR.CLKSTA shows it enabled. Start/stop: any trigger (software, SYNC, external or compare) starts the clock; an RB load (LDBSTOP = 1, Capture) or RC compare (CPCSTOP = 1, Waveform) stops it; start and stop work only while the clock is enabled.

TC_CMRx.WAVE chooses Capture mode (measurement; TIOAx and TIOBx inputs) or Waveform mode (generation; TIOAx always an output, TIOBx an output unless it is the external trigger). Any trigger clears the counter and starts its clock, taking effect at the next active edge of the selected clock, so the counter may read non-zero just after a trigger when the clock is slow. Triggers common to both modes: software (TC_CCR.SWTRG), SYNC (all channels together by writing TC_BCR.SYNC) and RC compare when TC_CMRx.CPCTRG is set. An external trigger is TIOAx or TIOBx in Capture mode, or TIOBx, XC0, XC1 or XC2 in Waveform mode (enabled by TC_CMRx.ENETRG); its pulses must be longer than a peripheral clock period.

Entered with WAVE = 0, for timing pulses and measuring the frequency, period, duty cycle or phase of the signals on TIOAx and TIOBx. TC_RA and TC_RB capture the counter on the TIOAx edges chosen by TC_CMRx.LDRA and LDRB, every 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 such edges per TC_CMRx.SBSMPLR. RA takes a value only when it has not captured since the previous trigger or RB has captured since RA last did; RB takes a value only when RA has captured since the previous trigger or since RB last did. Loading before the previous value is read overwrites it and sets TC_SR.LOVRS. The external trigger is TIOAx, TIOBx or the PWM comparator output, chosen by TC_CMR.ABETRG, on the edge(s) in ETRGEDG (0 disables it).

The DMAC can move captures to memory in Capture mode only. On channel 0 the DMA source is TC_RAB, which returns the next unread value of TC_RA or TC_RB, requested each time RA or RB loads. Transfers depend on bus load, with at least 8 peripheral clocks between them.

Entered with WAVE = 1. A channel makes one or two PWM signals of the same frequency with separate duty cycles, or single or repeated pulses. TIOBx is an output unless used as the external event (TC_CMR.EEVT). RA, RB and RC all act as compare registers: RA compare drives TIOAx, RB compare drives TIOBx, RC compare drives either or both.

TC_CMR.WAVSEL sets the counting. 00: count 0 to 2^16-1, then restart from 0; RC compare cannot trigger but can stop (CPCSTOP) or disable (CPCDIS) the clock. 10: count 0 to RC, reset on RC compare, then again; RC compare can also stop or disable the clock. 01: count up to 2^16-1, down to 0, and so on; RC compare cannot trigger but can stop or disable the clock. 11: count up to RC, down to 0, and so on; RC compare can stop or disable the clock. In every case an external event or software trigger may act at any time: in 00 and 10 it resets the counter; in 01 and 11 it reverses the direction.

The external event comes from XC0, XC1, XC2 or TIOBx, chosen by TC_CMR.EEVT, on the edge(s) in EEVTEDG (0: no event). With TIOBx as the event (EEVT = 0) TIOBx is no longer an output, compare register B makes no waveform or interrupt, and only TIOAx carries a waveform. TC_CMR.ENETRG makes the event a trigger; SYNC, the software trigger and, depending on WAVSEL, RC compare remain available.

Trigger and capture can bypass TIOA/TIOB and come straight from the PWM comparator outputs OCx (the sources of PWMH/L[2:0], before dead-time insertion), selected per channel by TRIGSRCA and TRIGSRCB in TC_EMR; each TC channel can follow a different PWM channel.

Software trigger, external event and RC compare can each set, clear or toggle TIOAx and TIOBx; RA compare acts on TIOAx and RB compare on TIOBx, as programmed in TC_CMR. TIOBx is controlled only when it is an output.

The QDEC takes TIOA0 (PHA) and TIOB0 (PHB) from the encoder and optionally TIOB1 (index, not needed for decoding), and drives channels 0 and 1; channel 2 can be the time base for speed. TC_BMR.QDEN = 0 bypasses it. TC_CMRx.TCCLKS must select XC0 (0x101); TC0XC0S has no effect with the QDEC on. Either position/revolutions or speed is measured: channel 0 counts PHA/PHB edges for fine position and channel 1 counts index pulses (revolutions); together they give a precise position. In speed mode position is not available but revolutions are. Inputs can be filtered, inverted and swapped; several events raise interrupts; an RC compare on channel 0 or 1 can interrupt through TC_SRx.CPCS.

Each input can be inverted (INVA, INVB, INVIDX), PHA and PHB swapped (SWAP), and the index taken from PHB (IDXPHB). TC_BMR.MAXFILT sets a minimum pulse width: with the filter on, pulses shorter than (MAXFILT + 1) × t_peripheral clock are dropped. (MAXFILT + 1) × t_peripheral clock must not exceed 10% of the shortest PHA, PHB or index pulse at the highest encoder speed. The filter removes spikes from dirt on the encoder disk, electromagnetic interference, or vibration while the shaft rests on a bar edge.

After filtering the decoder extracts direction and phase edges. TC_QISR shows the direction at any time; its polarity follows INVA, INVB, INVIDX and SWAP. A direction change is reported in TC_QISR, and can interrupt, when two consecutive edges of one phase see the same level on the other and an edge then occurs on the other; the first condition alone is not enough, since dirt can hide bars. TC_BMR.QDTRANS disables direction-change detection, and DIR must then be ignored. TC_QISR.QERR flags a quadrature error when two PHA/PHB edges are closer than (TC_BMR.MAXFILT + 1) × t_peripheral clock, which cannot happen in normal filtered operation. MAXFILT is tuned to the peripheral clock, encoder type and speed.

TC_BMR.POSEN = 1: channel 0 counts position from PHA/PHB edges and channel 1 counts revolutions from the index on TIOB1. Without an index, channel 0 can be cleared each revolution by putting the counts per revolution in TC_RC0.RC and setting TC_CMR.CPCTRG. Channels 0 and 1 run in Capture mode (WAVE = 0) with ETRGEDG = 0x01 (rising) and ABETRG = 0x1 (TIOAx); start with TC_CCR.CLKEN and SWTRG. Position reads in TC_CV0 and revolutions in TC_CV1, which can be joined into one 32-bit value; channel 0 clears on each index count, and both count up or down with the decoded direction, shown in TC_QISR.

TC_BMR.SPEEDEN = 1 measures speed on channel 0. Channel 2 gives the time base: period in TC_RC2, Waveform mode, WAVSEL = 0x10 (clear on RC compare) and ACPC = 0x11 (toggle TIOA); with QDEN and SPEEDEN set it feeds TIOA of channel 0. Channel 0 runs in Capture mode with ABETRG = 1 (TIOA trigger), EDGTRG = 0x01 (clear on rising edge) and LDRA = 0x01 so TC_RA0 loads as the counter clears (LDRB = 0x01). Start with CLKEN and SWTRG in TC_CCR; the speed is read from TC_RA0.RA, refreshed once per time-base period. Channel 1 can still count revolutions.

operation.topic: TC QDEC missing index and contamination
operation.text: Put the nominal counts per revolution plus a margin in TC_RC0.RC (for example 1026 for 1024 counts); if an index pulse is missed the count passes RC and sets TC_SR0.CPCS, which interrupts if TC_IER0.CPCS = 1. This is valid only while TC_QISR.DIRCHG = 0. At low speed dirt may pass the filter as a long pulse; TC_SR.CPCS = 1 together with TC_QISR.DIRCHG = 1 with no intended reversal shows contamination on a phase.

With both phases counted (TC_BMR.EDGPHA = 1) and TC_BMR.AUTOC = 1, a pulse missing from one phase is detected and the count in TC_CV0/1 corrected. A defect hitting both phases at the same place is not detected, since one good phase is needed to check the other. A sound encoder gives the same count over a fixed time with and without correction, so a difference reveals contamination; this complements counting pulses between index pulses. TC_BMR.MAXCMP sets how many consecutive missing pulses raise TC_QISR.MPE (0: never), which can interrupt.

TC_SMMRx.GCEN = 1 makes a channel output a 2-bit Gray count on TIOAx and TIOBx for a stepper motor, counting up or down per TC_SMMRx.DOWN. The channel must be in Waveform mode; TC_RCx sets the period.

TC_RCx can always be compared with TC_CVx, setting CPCSx and an interrupt, but interrupt handling takes an unpredictable time. Instead the FAULT output of TIMER1 can be driven by CPCS of TC_SR0 and/or TC_SR1, each enabled in TC_FMR (ENCF0, ENCF1) and ORed, into the PWM fault input, for example to act at once on a speed or position overflow with the QDEC.

TC_WPMR.WPEN write-protects the block mode, channel mode (capture and waveform), fault mode, stepper motor mode, RA, RB, RC and extended mode registers. The first channel's clock must be enabled to reach TC_WPMR.

Each PWM controller has 4 channels, and each channel drives a complementary pair of square-wave outputs (PWMHx and PWMLx). Period, duty cycle, polarity and dead time are set per channel, and each channel picks one of the clocks made by a shared clock generator that divides the PWM peripheral clock. External trigger inputs can change the outputs in real time. Period, spread spectrum, duty cycle and dead time are double-buffered so a change never produces a stray waveform. Channels can be grouped as synchronous channels that update duty cycle or dead time together, with the duty-cycle updates fed by a DMA channel. Channel 0 has a spread-spectrum counter that keeps the period moving, to lower EMI or motor acoustic noise. Eight comparison units compare against the channel 0 counter to raise interrupts, pulse two event lines (to time ADC conversions) and request DMA transfers. Outputs can be overridden in step with the counter or at once, and eight fault inputs can force the outputs asynchronously to 0, 1 or Hi-Z. Some configuration registers can be write-protected.

Four channels; a clock generator giving 13 clocks (a modulo-n counter with 11 outputs plus two linear dividers on its outputs). Per channel: a 16-bit counter, complementary outputs with a 12-bit dead-time generator, push-pull mode, its own enable and disable, clock choice, period, duty cycle and dead time, double-buffered period, duty cycle and dead times, double-buffered output polarity, center- or left-aligned waveform, output override, an interrupt each period, and a choice of when the double-buffered polarity and duty cycle take effect. External trigger handling (for DC/DC or lighting control): external reset mode, external start mode, cycle-by-cycle duty mode and leading-edge blanking. Two 2-bit Gray up/down channels for stepper motors. Spread spectrum on channel 0. Synchronous channel mode: one shared counter, updates after a set number of periods, and one DMA channel to load duty cycles. Two event lines for ADC synchronisation with programmable delay. Eight comparison units. Eight fault inputs: 3 from PIO pins, one from the PMC when the crystal oscillator fails, and others from the ADC controller compare function, the analog comparator controller and the timer/counter compare function. Register write protection.

The PWM pins share PIO lines; the PIO controller must first assign them to the PWM function, and unused PWM lines stay available to the PIO. Not every output need be enabled: an application using four outputs gives four PIO lines to the PWM. The PWM clock is enabled in the PMC before use; it can be stopped when the PWM is idle and restarted later, and the PWM carries on from where it stopped. The PWM interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, which must be set up first.

Faults reach the PWM from PIO pins, the PMC, the ADC controllers (AFEC0, AFEC1), the analog comparator controller and the timer/counters. Fault inputs from the PIO pins have a polarity chosen by the user; those from internal peripherals are configured to polarity 1.

The PWM is a clock generator plus 4 channels. The clock generator runs from the peripheral clock and offers 13 clocks; each channel takes any one of them and makes its own waveform. A modulo-n counter gives the peripheral clock divided by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024. Two linear dividers (divide by 1 to 255) each take one of those eleven, chosen by PREA (PREB) in PWM_CLK, and divide it by DIVA (DIVB) to give clkA (clkB). After a PWM reset DIVA, DIVB, PREA and PREB are 0, so clkA and clkB are off, and every modulo-n output except the undivided peripheral clock is off; the same holds while the PMC has the PWM clock stopped. The peripheral clock must be enabled in the PMC before the PWM is used.

Each channel has six parts: a clock selector picking one generator clock; a 16-bit counter on that clock, counting up or down as configured and as comparator matches dictate; a comparator that makes the OCx waveform from either the channel's own counter or the channel 0 counter (PWM_SCM.SYNCx); a 2-bit Gray counter for stepper drive, one per pair of channels; a dead-time generator making the complementary DTOHx and DTOLx so external power switches are driven safely; an override block that can force those two outputs to set values (OOOHx, OOOLx); and asynchronous fault protection, the highest priority, that can force PWMHx and PWMLx to 0, 1 or Hi-Z when a fault is seen.

The comparator checks the counter against the period (CPRD in PWM_CPRDx) and duty cycle (CDTY in PWM_CDTYx) to make OCx. The channel clock is chosen by CPRE in PWM_CMRx (0 after reset). Left-aligned, the counter runs up to CPRD and restarts; center-aligned, it runs up to CPRD and back down to 0, so the same CPRD gives twice the period. Alignment is CALG in PWM_CMRx, left-aligned by default; center alignment suits non-overlapping waveforms. CPOL in PWM_CMRx sets the level at the start of the period (low by default). DPOLI sets the output while the channel is disabled (CHIDx = 0 in PWM_SR): 0 gives the same level as the period start, 1 the inverse.

The waveform stays at 0 when CDTY = CPRD with CPOL = 0, or CDTY = 0 with CPOL = 1. With the channel enabled it stays at 1 when CDTY = 0 with CPOL = 0, or CDTY = CPRD with CPOL = 1. In cycle-by-cycle duty mode (TRGMODE = MODE3) the CDTY = CPRD cases switch to the other level at the external trigger event. Polarity must be set before the channel is enabled, and it changes the output level at once; changing CPOL while the channel runs can upset the driven device.

Left-aligned, the channel interrupt comes at the end of each counter period. Center-aligned, CES in PWM_CMRx chooses: 0 gives the interrupt at the end of the period only, 1 at the end and at the half period.

The PWM can trigger the timer/counter for two measurements on a bridge driver. Delay measurement: with TCTS = 0 in PWM_CMRx the channel comparator output OCx is the TC trigger, routed inside to TIOB to start the TC, while the driver feedback on the TIOA pin captures the delay between OCx and the bridge response. Cumulated on-time measurement: with TCTS = 1 the channel counter event becomes the TC trigger, so the TC adds up the MOSFET on-time seen on TIOA.

A pair of channels can output a 2-bit Gray count on two outputs, with the dead-time generator and the logic after it still usable. GCEN0 = 1 drives the outputs of channels 0 and 1 from the Gray counter. The count direction is set in PWM_SMMR (DOWNx) and may be changed while running.

From OCx the dead-time generator makes complementary DTOHx and DTOLx with non-overlap times between their edges, enabled by DTE in PWM_CMRx; DTE may only change while the channel is disabled. DTH and DTL in PWM_DTx set the two delays separately and can be updated in step with the period through PWM_DTUPDx. The dead-time counter runs on the channel's selected clock; each output is held back until that counter reaches DTH or DTL. DTHI and DTLI in PWM_CMRx invert each output.

With PPM = 1 in PWM_CMRx the dead-time generator output is steered to the two lines on alternate PWM cycles; DPOLI sets the idle level of the inactive line. Push-pull is enabled per channel. It suits transformer converters such as a half bridge, where it keeps DC out of the transformer core so the core does not saturate.

OSHx and OSLx in PWM_OS replace DTOHx and DTOLx by OOVHx and OOVLx from PWM_OOV. PWM_OSS and PWM_OSSUPD set the override of one channel without touching the others; PWM_OSC and PWM_OSCUPD clear it the same way. The ...UPD registers act at the start of the next PWM period, in step with the counter, and a PWM period allows a single PWM_OSSUPD or PWM_OSCUPD action in total, across all channels. PWM_OSS and PWM_OSC act as soon as written. PWM_OS reads the present selection. The counters keep running during an override; only the outputs are forced.

Eight fault inputs can force any output pair to a programmed value, ahead of the output override. FPOL in PWM_FMR sets each input's active level: internal sources such as the ADC or timer/counter need FPOL = 1, while a GPIO pin's level is the user's choice. FMOD sets the fault mode: a peripheral without fault-clear handling needs FMOD = 1 to avoid false faults. FFIL turns on a glitch filter that rejects pulses shorter than one PWM peripheral clock. A fault becomes active when its input goes to the active level. With FMOD = 0 it stays active while the input remains at that level; with FMOD = 1 it stays active until the input has left that level and FCLR in PWM_FCR has been written. PWM_FSR gives the input levels (FIV) and the active faults (FIS).

Fault y acts on channel x when FPEx[y] is set in PWM_FPE; synchronous channels use channel 0's bits FPE0[y]. Protection triggers when the channel is enabled and any of its enabled faults is active, even with the peripheral clock stopped, but then only from an unfiltered input. When it triggers, the channel counter is reset and the outputs are forced, without waiting for the counter, to FPVHx/FPVLx in PWM_FPV and FPZHx/FPZLx in PWM_FPV2. Set FMODy, and FPEx[y], only after FPOLy holds its final value, or FSy or the protection may trigger by mistake. A fault on channel 0 stops the comparison units from matching. A fault can raise an interrupt (separate from the period interrupt) if enabled and unmasked; reading the interrupt status clears it even while the fault persists.

Faults 1 and 2 can be recoverable faults, raised internally by an external trigger event. As recoverable faults their input pins are ignored and their FFIL and FMOD bits have no effect. Fault 1 is recoverable from PWMEXTRG0 when PWM_ETRG1.RFEN = 1, PWM_ENA.CHID1 = 1 and PWM_ETRG1.TRGMODE is not 0; fault 2 likewise from PWMEXTRG1 with PWM_ETRG2.RFEN, CHID2 and PWM_ETRG2.TRGMODE. Any channel can use them through FPEx[1/2] (synchronous channels through FPE0[1/2]). Unlike a normal fault the channel counter is not cleared; the outputs are forced to FPVHx/FPVLx at once and stay forced until the end of the next PWM cycle, provided the fault has gone. A recoverable fault gives no interrupt and does not show in FSy of PWM_FSR.

On channel 0 only, a spread-spectrum counter is added to CPRD of PWM_CPRD0, so the effective period moves between CPRD - SPRD and CPRD + SPRD (SPRD in PWM_SSPR) while the duty value stays the same, giving a constantly changing duty cycle. SPRDM = 0 is triangular: the counter starts at -SPRD when channel 0 is enabled or after reset, rises by one each period, and returns to -SPRD after reaching SPRD. SPRDM = 1 is random: each period it takes a new value spread evenly between -SPRD and +SPRD.

Channels set by SYNCx in PWM_SCM share source clock, period and alignment and start together, so their counters stay aligned; only one such group exists, and channel 0 is always in it because its counter settings serve the group. A synchronous channel uses CPRE and CALG of PWM_CMR0 and CPRD of PWM_CPRD0 in place of its own, so writing those fields on higher channels changes nothing. Enabling or disabling channel 0 (CHID0 in PWM_ENA or PWM_DIS) starts or stops the whole group, though a member other than 0 can still be switched alone. SYNCx may be changed in either direction only while that channel is disabled (CHIDx = 0 in PWM_SR).

UPDM in PWM_SCM picks one of three ways to update synchronous channels. Method 1 (UPDM = 0): the processor writes period, duty cycles and dead times into PWM_CPRDUPDx, PWM_CDTYUPDx and PWM_DTUPDx, and they take effect at the next period once UPDULOCK in PWM_SCUC is set. Method 2 (UPDM = 1): as method 1 for period and dead times, but duty cycles and the update period (PWM_SCUPUPD) are applied automatically after the update period UPR in PWM_SCUP. Method 3 (UPDM = 2): as method 2 except that the DMA controller writes the duty cycles of all synchronous channels, optionally timed by a comparison match (PTRM, PTRCS in PWM_SCM). The DMA destination is only PWM_DMAR; the buffer is a repeated sequence of 16-bit duty cycles, one per synchronous channel, in rising channel order.

UPDULOCK = 1 makes the update happen at the next period of the synchronous channels; while it is not set the update is held back. It reads 1 until the update is done, then 0. Sequence: set UPDM = 0; choose the channels with SYNCx; enable them with CHID0 in PWM_ENA; write the update registers needed; set UPDULOCK; the values load at the start of the next period, and once UPDULOCK has cleared new values may be written.

Period and dead times load at the next period after UPDULOCK is set, as in method 1. Duty cycles and the update period load by themselves: the controller waits UPR + 1 periods of the synchronous channels, then applies them. WRDY in PWM_ISR2 goes to 1 when new duty cycles and a new update period can be written, and is cleared by reading PWM_ISR2; it can raise an interrupt through PWM_IMR2. Sequence: UPDM = 1; SYNCx; UPR in PWM_SCUP; enable with CHID0; for period or dead-time changes write PWM_CPRDUPDx or PWM_DTUPDx and set UPDULOCK; for duty or update-period changes wait for WRDY, then write PWM_CDTYUPDx or PWM_SCUPUPD, which load at the next period once the update period has run out.

The DMA controller writes the duty cycles, lightening the processor; period, dead times and update period are still written by the processor, and the timing is as in method 2 (UPR + 1 periods). The DMA must write duty cycles in channel order: with channels 0, 1 and 3 synchronous, channel 0 first, then 1, then 3. PWM_ISR2 flags: WRDY (ready for new duty cycles and update period; cleared on reading; it and the DMA request can be timed to a comparison match with PTRM and PTRCS) and UNRE (the update period ran out before the DMA had written all the data; cleared on reading). Sequence: UPDM = 2; SYNCx; UPR; PTRM and PTRCS (end of update period or comparison match); set up and enable the DMA transfer; enable with CHID0; period and dead-time changes through the update registers and UPDULOCK; update-period changes after WRDY through PWM_SCUPUPD; when the DMA buffer is done, set up a new transfer.

Period, spread spectrum, polarity, duty cycle, dead times, output override and the synchronous update period are double-buffered through update registers: the sync channels update period update, output selection set update, output selection clear update, spread spectrum update, channel duty cycle update, channel period update, channel dead time update and channel mode update registers. A write is held and applied at the next period boundary: left-aligned (CALG = 0) when the counter reaches CPRD, center-aligned when the counter counts down to 0. In center-aligned mode, UPDS = 1 in PWM_CMRx lets duty cycle and polarity (the channel duty cycle update and channel mode update registers) load at the next half-period boundary instead: counting up at CPRD or counting down at 0, whichever comes first after the write.

Eight comparison units compare a value with the channel 0 counter (the counter of all synchronous channels), to pulse the event lines, raise interrupts and time DMA requests for method 3. Comparison x matches when CEN in PWM_CMPMx is set and the channel 0 counter reaches CV in PWM_CMPVx. With channel 0 center-aligned, CVM in PWM_CMPVx chooses whether the match is taken counting up or down (ignored when left-aligned). An active fault on channel 0 disables the comparisons. CTR and CPR in PWM_CMPMx set how often it is tested: once every CPR + 1 periods of channel 0, when the period counter CPRCNT equals CTR; CPR is CPRCNT's top value, and CPR = CTR = 0 tests every period.

With channel 0 running, the comparison setup and value are changed through PWM_CMPMUPDx and PWM_CMPVUPDx. They load after the comparison update period CUPR in PWM_CMPMx, counted by its own counter CUPRCNT; CUPR itself can be changed through PWM_CMPMUPDx. Each PWM_CMPVUPDx write needs a PWM_CMPMUPDx write after it. A match and an update can each raise an interrupt if enabled (PWM_IER2, PWM_IDR2); reading PWM_ISR2 clears them.

Two event lines carry triggers to other peripherals such as the ADC. Each emits a one-peripheral-clock pulse when any comparison it has selected (CSEL bits in PWM_ELMRx) matches; each comparison is selected or not on its own.

Channels 1 and 2 can use an external trigger, chosen by TRGSRC in PWM_ETRGx and optionally filtered by TRGFILT. At each trigger event the channel counter value is stored in MAXCNT of PWM_ETRGx if it exceeds the value already there; reading PWM_ETRGx clears MAXCNT. TRGMODE selects external reset mode (1), external start mode (2) or cycle-by-cycle duty mode (3); 0 disables the feature. Use it only with the channel left-aligned (CALG = 0) and not synchronous (SYNCx = 0); a center-aligned or synchronous channel with TRGMODE not 0 can misbehave.

TRGMODE = 1. An edge on PWMEXTRGx, of the polarity set by TRGEDGE, clears the channel counter and starts a new cycle; if no trigger has come by the time the counter reaches CPRD, the counter clears and a new cycle starts anyway. On-time and off-time are not held constant. Example use: power factor correction, with PWMEXTRG0 regulating channel 1. CPRD of channel 1 is set long enough that TRGIN1 always arrives first. A circuit outside the device senses the inductor current; when it falls below a threshold IREF, the counter is cleared, a new period starts and the current rises again.

TRGMODE = 2. The counter can only restart after it has reached CPRD and the external trigger input is at the level set by TRGEDGE; both are needed for a new period. On-time is constant and off-time has a minimum. Example use: a buck converter. CDTY sets the fixed on-time; the minimum off-time is the difference between CDTY and CPRD. While VOUT stays above VREF the output stays inactive; below it, the mode still keeps the minimum off-time the MOSFET drive needs.

TRGMODE = 3. The PWM frequency is fixed by CPRD. A trigger event while the counter is below CDTY makes the output inactive; one while the counter is above CDTY has no effect. TRGEDGE picks the rising or falling edge. Example use: limiting the current in an LED string automatically.

Channels 1 and 2 can blank their external trigger input for a while after their own output switches, so switching transients of the power transistor are not taken as events. LEBDELAYx in the leading-edge blanking register sets the blanking time; PWMLFEN, PWMLREN, PWMHFEN and PWMHREN enable it on the falling and rising edges of PWML and PWMH. PWMEXTRGx events during the blanking time are ignored.

Before enabling channels: unlock the registers through WPCMD in PWM_WPCR; if needed program PWM_CLK (DIVA, PREA, DIVB, PREB); per channel choose clock (CPRE), alignment (CALG), counter event when center-aligned (CES) and polarity (CPOL) in PWM_CMRx; set period (PWM_CPRDx), duty cycle (PWM_CDTYx) and, if DTE is set, dead times (PWM_DTx), all writable directly only while the channel is disabled and afterwards through PWM_CPRDUPDx, PWM_CDTYUPDx and PWM_DTUPDx; choose synchronous channels (SYNCx), the WRDY/DMA request timing (PTRM, PTRCS) and the update mode (UPDM) in PWM_SCM and the update period (UPR in PWM_SCUP) if needed; set the comparisons (PWM_CMPVx, PWM_CMPMx) and event lines (PWM_ELMRx); set fault polarity (FPOL), fault protection (FMOD, FFIL in PWM_FMR, PWM_FPV, PWM_FPE); enable interrupts (CHIDx, FCHIDx in PWM_IER1; WRDY, UNRE, CMPMx, CMPUx in PWM_IER2); then enable the channels with CHIDx in PWM_ENA.

The value in PWM_CPRDx sets the resolution: the duty-cycle step can be no finer than 1/CPRD of the period, so a larger CPRD gives finer control. With CPRD = 15, PWM_CDTYx can be 1 to 14 and the step is 1/15 of the period.
