operation.topic: PWM changing duty cycle, period and dead times
operation.text: While a channel is enabled, duty cycle, period and dead times are changed through PWM_CDTYUPDx, PWM_CPRDUPDx and PWM_DTUPDx. For an asynchronous channel (SYNCx = 0) the new values load at the end of the current period. For a synchronous channel with UPDM = 0 they load at the end of the period after UPDULOCK in PWM_SCUC is written to 1. With UPDM = 1 or 2, period and dead time load the same way, but the duty cycle loads at the end of the current period once the update period has run out (UPRCNT equal to UPR in PWM_SCUP). Of several writes to one update register before it loads, the latest wins.

operation.topic: PWM changing the synchronous update period
operation.text: The update period of running synchronous channels is changed through PWM_SCUPUPD, which loads at the end of the update period (UPRCNT = UPR) and of the current PWM period. Only the last value written between updates counts. It matters only with synchronous channels present and UPDM = 1 or 2.

While channel 0 runs, comparison values and setups are changed through PWM_CMPVUPDx and PWM_CMPMUPDx; they load at the end of the comparison update period (CUPRCNT = CUPR in PWM_CMPMx) and of the current period. Write PWM_CMPVUPDx first, then PWM_CMPMUPDx. Only the last value written between updates counts.

Interrupt sources, masked by PWM_IMR1 and PWM_IMR2: end of a channel period (CHIDx in PWM_ISR1), a fault (FCHIDx in PWM_ISR1), a comparison match (CMPMx in PWM_ISR2), a comparison update (CMPUx in PWM_ISR2) and the synchronous transfer flags WRDY and UNRE in PWM_ISR2. CHIDx and FCHIDx interrupts last until PWM_ISR1 is read; WRDY, UNRE, CMPMx and CMPUx ones until PWM_ISR2 is read. Interrupts are enabled in PWM_IER1/PWM_IER2 and disabled in PWM_IDR1/PWM_IDR2.

Registers are write-protected in six groups through WPCMD and WPRGx in PWM_WPCR. Software protection can be switched on and off by software; hardware protection is switched on by software and off only by a hardware reset of the PWM. The two are applied to each group independently, and a group is protected if either is on. WPCMD = 0 removes software protection from the groups whose WPRGx is 1, WPCMD = 1 applies software protection to them, and WPCMD = 2 applies hardware protection to them. WPSWS and WPHWS in PWM_WPSR show which protection is on per group. A write to a protected register sets WPVS in PWM_WPSR and WPVSRC names the register; reading PWM_WPSR clears both.

The Analog Front-End Controller runs an analog front-end cell holding a 12-bit ADC, a programmable gain amplifier, a DAC for offset and two 6-to-1 analog multiplexers. It converts 12 analog lines one at a time with a single sample-and-hold, or 6 pairs simultaneously with both sample-and-holds (dual mode), over 0 V to VREFP. Native resolution is 12 bits, raised to as much as 16 bits by digital averaging. Each result lands in a register shared by all channels and in the channel's own register. Conversions start from software, a rising edge on the AFE_ADTRG pin, timer/counter outputs or a PWM event line. A window comparator flags results below, above, inside or outside programmable thresholds and can drive a PWM fault input through a purely combinational path, sending the PWM outputs straight to their safe state. Sleep mode, a conversion sequencer and a DMA channel lower power and processor load. Inputs are single-ended or fully differential with a 2-bit gain setting. The internal references are made from one external reference node, which may equal the analog supply and needs an external decoupling capacitor. A redundant signed digit (RSD) digital error correction reduces INL and DNL. Start-up time and tracking time are programmable.

12-bit resolution, up to 16 bits by digital averaging; a wide supply range; single-ended or differential input; single or dual sample-and-hold; programmable gain for a full-scale input range up to 0 to VDD; programmable offset per channel; automatic offset and gain error correction; up to 12 analog inputs through the internal multiplexers; each channel enabled on its own; hardware triggers (trigger pin, timer/counter TIOA outputs, PWM event line) or software trigger; drive of the PWM fault input; DMA; programmable timings; two sleep modes with a conversion sequencer (wakes on a trigger, converts every enabled channel, sleeps again; custom channel order possible); standby mode for fast wake-up, with power-down; automatic window comparison; register write protection.

AFE_ADTRG shares an I/O line with digital functions and is selected through the PIO controller. The AFE_ADx analog inputs also share I/O lines; an input is taken by the AFEC when its CHx bit is written in AFEC_CHER and no digital function is selected on it. The AFEC peripheral clock is enabled in the PMC before use and may be stopped when the AFEC is idle, but it must stay on while the AFEC is in Sleep mode. The AFEC interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, which is set up first.

operation.topic: AFEC temperature sensor, triggers and fault output
operation.text: The temperature sensor sits on AFEC channel 11 and gives a voltage VT proportional to absolute temperature (PTAT). Timer/counters and PWM event lines are optional hardware triggers; some or none may be connected. The AFEC fault output is wired to the PWM FAULT input.

The programmable gain amplifiers must be on before any conversion: set PGA0EN and PGA1EN in AFEC_ACR. Conversions run on the AFE clock. After each start of conversion the AFEC waits a transfer time of some AFE clock cycles before changing the channel selection and starting the next tracking. Each conversion has a tracking time (from channel change to start of conversion; at least 15 AFE clock periods) and a conversion time. Tracking of the next channel overlaps the current conversion; a tracking time longer than the 12-bit conversion time tCONV is stretched to the end of the previous conversion. PRESCAL in AFEC_MR sets the AFE clock from fperipheral clock/2 (PRESCAL = 1) to fperipheral clock/256 (PRESCAL = 255) and must be set to give an AFE clock within the electrical characteristics. With averaging on, conversion time is multiplied by the oversampling ratio.

Inputs convert linearly over 0 V to the voltage on VREFP. Resolution is natively 12 bits; RES = 2 or more in AFEC_EMR switches on the enhanced resolution mode. With a DMA channel attached, any resolution under 16 bits makes the transfer size 16 bits. An ADTRG asynchronous to the peripheral clock is resynchronised with up to one peripheral clock of jitter, which can lower the effective resolution.

A finished 12-bit result goes to the channel's internal register, read through AFEC_CDR (channel chosen by CSEL in AFEC_CSELR), and to AFEC_LCDR; with TAG set in AFEC_EMR, AFEC_LCDR also gives the channel number in CHNB. EOCx and DRDY are set in AFEC_ISR; a rising DRDY requests a DMA transfer, and either flag can interrupt. Reading AFEC_CDR clears EOCx, reading AFEC_LCDR clears DRDY. A channel result not read before the next one arrives sets OVREx in AFEC_OVER; a new result while DRDY is high sets GOVRE in AFEC_ISR. Reading AFEC_OVER clears OVREx and reading AFEC_ISR clears GOVRE. Disabling a channel during its conversion, or disabling and re-enabling it, leaves its data and flags undefined.

SIGNMODE in AFEC_EMR selects signed (two's complement) or unsigned results: single-ended unsigned with differential signed; single-ended signed with differential unsigned; all unsigned; or all signed. A signed result under 16 bits is sign-extended to bit 15, so a 12-bit 0xF43 reads 0xFF43 and 0x467 reads 0x0467.

Writing START = 1 in AFEC_CR is the software trigger. Hardware triggers are a timer/counter TIOA output, a PWM event line or ADTRG, chosen by TRGSEL and enabled by TRGEN in AFEC_MR. Trigger events must be spaced by more than the longest conversion sequence set by AFEC_MR, AFEC_CHSR, AFEC_SEQ1R and AFEC_SEQ2R. A hardware trigger starts conversion after a delay from its rising edge that varies between two peripheral clock periods and one AFE clock period; this jitter lowers SNR. A TIOA trigger needs its timer channel in Waveform mode. One start converts all enabled channels and then waits for the next request. AFEC_CHER and AFEC_CHDR enable and disable channels individually; with DMA only enabled channels' data are transferred.

SLEEP in AFEC_MR turns the AFE off between conversions; the sequencer then powers it on at each start request, waits for its start-up time, converts all enabled channels and turns it off until the next trigger, ignoring triggers that arrive meanwhile. It applies when triggers are further apart than the AFE start-up time. FWUP in AFEC_MR gives fast wake-up mode, in which the AFE is only partly off, saving less power but waking faster. Sequences repeat on a timer/counter output or on the PWM event line, with DMA collecting samples. USEQ in AFEC_MR with AFEC_SEQ1R and AFEC_SEQ2R gives a custom order of up to 12 conversions per sequence, in any order and with repeats; only enabled USCHx fields are converted. The reference pins stay connected in both normal and sleep modes.

CMPMODE in AFEC_EMR picks the comparison: below a low limit, above a high limit, or against both, on all channels (CMPALL) or on the one named by CMPSEL. CMPFILTER sets how many consecutive comparison hits are needed before COMPE in AFEC_ISR is set; COMPE can interrupt. Thresholds are in AFEC_CWR and must have the same signedness as the results (SIGNMODE); comparing all channels needs SIGNMODE set to ALL_UNSIGNED or ALL_SIGNED.

Each channel is single-ended (AFEC_DIFFR.DIFF = 0, the reset state) or fully differential (DIFF = 1), set per channel. Both modes use the same pins; the multiplexer maps one or two inputs to the channel.

Each channel works in single sample-and-hold (AFEC_SHMR.DUALx = 0, the reset state) or dual sample-and-hold (DUALx = 1) mode, on the same pins. Single-ended or differential and single or dual sample-and-hold can be combined.

A programmable gain amplifier with gain 1, 2 or 4 (GAIN in AFEC_CGR) works for single-ended and differential inputs, and a DAC gives a programmable offset; both are set per channel. The offset, AOFF in AFEC_COCR, works only in single-ended mode: 512 (DAC mid-scale) means no correction, and 512 + n corrects an offset of n LSB, positive or negative.

Single-ended with VVREFN = 0: gain 1 spans 0 to VVREFP, gain 2 spans (1/4)VVREFP to (3/4)VVREFP, gain 4 spans (3/8)VVREFP to (5/8)VVREFP, each centred on (1/2)VVREFP. Fully differential: VIN+ and VIN- swing about (1/2)VVREFP over the full 0 to VVREFP at gain 1, over (1/4) to (3/4)VVREFP at gain 2, and over (3/8) to (5/8)VVREFP at gain 4 (GAIN codes 10 or 11).
Each AFE has its own minimum start-up time set by STARTUP in AFEC_MR. The AFE has no input buffer amplifier to isolate the signal source.

The temperature sensor is channel 11. With AFEC_CHSR.CH11 enabled the sensor is powered and converted at the same rate as the other channels; in a user sequence it is always the last channel converted. A manual start (AFEC_CR.START, only with TRGEN off) converts it with the other enabled channels; its result is read in AFEC_CDR (with AFEC_CSELR set) and EOC11 is set. Periodic conversion puts it in AFEC_LCDR too, so it is part of the DMA buffer. The channel may be switched on or off at any time.

With AFEC_TEMPMR.RTCT set and CH11 cleared, an internal RTC trigger converts channel 11 once per second, independent of the other triggers, and the sensor is powered only for its start-up and conversion time. The result goes only to AFEC_CDR, not to AFEC_LCDR, so it stays out of the DMA buffer; EOC11 marks its end. With RTCT set and TRGEN cleared, all channels are disabled (AFEC_CHSR = 0) and channel 11 alone is converted once a second; with Sleep mode this gives low-power temperature monitoring. At each one-second trigger the sensor is switched on for 30 µs. A range or threshold in AFEC_TEMPCWR and a comparison mode in AFEC_TEMPMR make TEMPCHG in AFEC_ISR rise on a set temperature change, and it can interrupt. The latest temperature can always be read in AFEC_CDR.

RES of 13 bits or more in AFEC_EMR averages several samples, a digital low-pass filter trading speed for resolution; the resolution sets the oversampling ratio. Averaging needs one to two LSB peak-to-peak of noise on the input to work well. Free Run mode is not available with enhanced resolution. The ratio applies to every enabled channel except the temperature channel when RTC-triggered. A channel's average in AFEC_CDR is valid only with EOCx set and OVREx clear; AFEC_LCDR is valid only with DRDY set and GOVRE clear. AFEC_CDR is not buffered and changes after each sample during averaging, while overrun flags rise on the first sample of a new average, so an overrun only means the previous unread value was lost.

With USEQ cleared and STM cleared in AFEC_EMR, each trigger takes one sample per enabled channel, so RES = 2 needs four triggers for one result. With STM set (USEQ cleared) the channel sequence repeats by itself as many times as the oversampling ratio, so one trigger gives the result. With USEQ set, the sequence in AFEC_SEQxR and AFEC_CHER can repeat each channel back to back so channels are not interleaved; each end of conversion is a sample, so a channel converted four times in a row with RES = 2 gives its average at each trigger, at a quarter of the maximum sample rate. With USEQ and enhanced resolution, the number of enabled channels must be a multiple of 4 and AFEC_SEQxR must hold each channel index four times in a row.

Offset and gain correction is enabled per channel by ECORR in AFEC_CECR; the correction values are per sample-and-hold unit. AFEC_COSR selects which unit AFEC_CVR shows, for reads and writes; OFFSETCORR and GAINCORR in AFEC_CVR hold the signed correction data, worked out from two measurement points. The correction is the same in every mode and is applied after averaging, in two's complement. The data path is AFE (12-bit), averager, calibration (12 to 16-bit two's complement) and sign mode (signed or unsigned) into AFE_LCDR.

Each new value in AFEC_LCDR triggers the DMA read channel, and the same data layout repeats at each trigger, shaped by AFEC_MR, AFEC_CHSR, AFEC_SEQ1R and AFEC_SEQ2R. With TAG cleared each transfer is a 16-bit half-word holding the right-aligned result; with TAG set it is a 32-bit word with the channel number in CHNB.

The AFEC fault output goes straight to a PWM fault input and fires according to AFEC_EMR, AFEC_CWR, AFEC_TEMPMR, AFEC_TEMPCWR and the results. Two comparisons can fire it: one on AFEC_CWR for all converted channels but the last, and one on the last channel, where temperature is measured, so for example overcurrent or overtemperature can trip the PWM. A hit sends a one-peripheral-clock pulse; if that PWM fault line is enabled the PWM outputs go to their safe state at once through a combinational path. The pulse is not the COMPE bit, so the PWM must use FMOD = 1.

WPEN in AFEC_WPMR write-protects the mode, extended mode, channel sequence 1 and 2, channel enable and disable, compare window, channel gain, channel differential, channel offset compensation, temperature sensor mode, temperature compare window, analog control, sample-and-hold mode, correction select, correction values and channel error correction registers. A write to a protected register sets WPVS in AFEC_WPSR and WPVSRC names it; reading AFEC_WPSR clears WPVS.

operation.topic: AFE characteristics, reference and offset DAC
operation.text: AFE figures apply from -40°C to +105°C unless stated. VREFP is the positive reference; VREFN must be grounded. DAC0 and DAC1 give VDAC between 0 and VREFP with 10-bit accuracy; VDAC is the single-ended reference node for the sample-and-hold PGAs S/H0 and S/H1, so setting it cancels a DC offset on a single-ended input (it has no effect in fully differential operation). In differential operation the DAC is set to VREFP/2 with code 512, which does not change the output code; this is not automatic and code 512 must be written to DAC0 and DAC1 for the channel.

AFEC_ACR.IBCTL sets the ADC bias current; IBCTL = 10 is the nominal setting and is required for sampling up to 1 MHz. Below 500 kHz IBCTL = 01 may be used to save current; above 1 MHz IBCTL must be 11. The register resets to 01, so it has to be set to suit the sampling rate.
VVREFP, applied on pin VREFP, sets AFE performance: a DC change in it becomes a gain error, and noise on it becomes count noise.

The AFE first samples relative to VDAC from DAC0 or DAC1; everything after the sample-and-hold is differential about an internal common mode VCM = VVREFP/2, also in single-ended mode. In differential mode the sample-and-hold common mode is VDAC = VVREFP/2 (DAC0 and DAC1 at code 512). The AFEC_CDR code is a positive integer or two's complement of up to 16 bits, and at most 4095 with RES = 0 (12-bit, no averaging). The LSB is the quantisation step relative to VVREFP. The AFE figures cover the PGA and core together; temperature and voltage dependence are given separately.

operation.topic: AFE gain and offset error definitions
operation.text: Differential mode: the offset error EO is the code error at zero differential input; the full-scale error EFS = (EFS+) - (EFS-) in LSB, from the errors at +VVREFP/2 and -VVREFP/2; the gain error EG = 100 × EFS / 4096 in %. These errors cover the sample-and-hold and the PGA gain error. Single-ended mode: the AFE still works differentially inside, with the negative input tied internally to VVREFP/2, so the offset is taken at VVREFP/2; the offset at VINP = 0 follows from the transfer function with EG and EO. In this mode the DAC error is included as well.

The sample-and-hold input looks like a switch of resistance RON in series with a capacitance CIN to VDAC (single-ended), or two such branches from VINP and VINN to VDAC (differential). CIN is 2 to 8 pF ±20% depending on gain and mode, with negligible temperature dependence. RON is 2 kΩ typical and 8 kΩ maximum (worst process, high temperature). Typical values are used for ZIN.

operation.topic: AFE tracking time and source impedance
operation.text: During tracking the input settles through the source impedance ZSOURCE and RON into CIN. The number of time constants n needed depends on the accuracy wanted. Fifteen AFE clock periods of tracking are built into the AFEC already.

The Digital-to-Analog Converter Controller drives one differential analog output or as many as two single-ended ones, at 12-bit resolution. Modes: free-running, max speed, trigger and interpolation, plus a bypass mode for low power at low sample rates. Each channel has its own DMA channel. Features: an interpolation filter with 2×, 4×, 8×, 16× or 32× oversampling; word transfer mode to halve bus accesses; individual channel control; one hardware trigger selection per channel (external trigger pin or internal events); a FIFO per channel; register write protection.

DATRG shares an I/O line with digital functions and is chosen through the PIO controller. DAC0/DACP and DAC1/DACN also share I/O lines; enabling a DACC channel in DACC_CHER makes the DAC drive the pad and deselects the digital functions. The DACC clock is enabled in the PMC first. The DACC wakes when a conversion is asked for with at least one channel enabled and switches off when no channel is enabled. The interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, set up first.

A channel converts once DACC_CHSR.CHx is set by writing DACC_CHER.CHx; with both CHx cleared the analog cell is off. The channel is ready when DACC_CHSR.DACRDYx reads 1. The DAC clock is the peripheral clock divided down; a conversion takes 12 DAC clock periods. In max speed mode (MAXSx = 1 in DACC_MR) the conversion period is exactly 12 DAC clocks and the DAC is always clocked, using slightly more power. Otherwise (trigger or free-running) the DAC gets a clock only while converting and waits for the end of the previous conversion, so a conversion takes 12 DAC clocks plus 2 resynchronisation cycles; power and rate are lower. A channel's mode can only be changed while it is disabled. DACC_ACR.IBCTLCHx matches DAC power to its sample rate; bypass mode lowers both maximum rate and power. At the end of a conversion the output holds the new value and EOC is set in DACC_ISR; reading DACC_ISR clears it.

DIFF in DACC_MR selects the output mode. With DIFF = 0 each channel is set up on its own. With DIFF = 1, DACP is on DAC0 and DACN on DAC1; channel 0 drives everything and enabling it enables channel 1. A value sent to channel 0 is mirrored about 2048 onto channel 1: 3000 = 2048 + 952 on DAC0 gives 1096 = 2048 - 952 on DAC1.

Set by DACC_TRIGR.TRGENx. Data go to the DAC on each rising edge of the selected trigger; the trigger rate cannot exceed one per 12 DAC clock periods plus 2 resynchronisation cycles. Clearing TRGENx returns the channel to free-running or max speed mode according to DACC_MR.MAXSx.

Selected with both DACC_TRIGR.TRGENx and DACC_MR.MAXSx at 0. Conversion starts once a channel is enabled; data written to DACC_CDRx appear at the output 12 DAC clocks later, and the next value converts only after EOC of the previous one. If the FIFO runs empty no conversion happens and the output holds its value.

Selected with DACC_MR.MAXSx = 1 and DACC_TRIGR.TRGENx = 1. The controller starts a conversion every 12 DAC clocks without waiting for EOC, and the DAC clock never stops. When the FIFO empties, the last value is reconverted at that rate. DACC_ACR.IBCTLCHx must be set for 1 MSps.
Bypass turns off the DAC output buffer to save power and suits slowly changing signals. It needs free-running mode with DACC_ACR.IBCTLCHx set to bypass.

Interpolation filters with OSR 2×, 4×, 8×, 16× or 32× are available only in trigger mode with OSRx in DACC_TRIGR not 0. The input is taken once every OSR triggers and recomputed at the trigger rate by a third-order SINC filter, cutting DACC accesses and raising output SNR. The input sample rate fs is the trigger frequency divided by OSR.

Each channel has a four half-word FIFO. TXRDY in DACC_ISR active means data can be written to DACC_CDRx; data that cannot convert at once wait in the FIFO. TXRDY drops while the FIFO is full or the DACC refuses requests, and writing DACC_CDRx then corrupts the FIFO. WORD in DACC_MR allows two values per write: bits 11:0 first, bits 27:16 second, both into the selected channel's FIFO, with TXRDY counting both. Changing the access mode requires all channels off first.

WPEN in DACC_WPMR write-protects the mode, channel enable, channel disable, analog current and trigger registers. A write to a protected register sets WPVS in DACC_WPSR and WPVSRC names it; reading DACC_WPSR clears WPVS.

The Analog Comparator Controller sets up the analog comparator and raises interrupts as configured. Two 8-to-1 multiplexers choose the comparator's two inputs from the user analog inputs and the voltage references (external reference, DAC0, DAC1, temperature sensor). Hysteresis, edge detection and polarity are configurable. A compare event can drive a PWM fault.

The analog inputs share I/O lines with PIO functions; writing SELMINUS and SELPLUS in ACC_MR puts the chosen lines in analog mode. The ACC clock is enabled in the PMC, and the voltage regulator must be on for the comparator to work. The ACC interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the ACC. The ACC FAULT output is wired to the PWM FAULT input.

The ACC sets the comparator up and post-processes its output. After a settings change the comparator output may be wrong for a while, and the ACC masks it for that time. A chosen edge on the output (falling, rising or either) sets the comparison flag and raises an interrupt. Hysteresis is selectable, and the comparator has a high-speed option (shortest delay, highest current) and a low-power option (longest delay, lowest current), set in ACC_ACR.

Any write to ACC_MR or ACC_ACR, whatever the data, starts a masking period while the output settles: 8 × tperipheral clock with ISEL = 0, 128 × tperipheral clock with ISEL = 1. During it ACC_ISR reads negative (bit 31 set).

In fault mode a comparison event goes out on the ACC fault output, wired inside to a PWM fault input. The fault source is either the comparator output passed straight through (combinational) or that output resynchronised to the peripheral clock.
WPEN in ACC_WPMR write-protects ACC_MR and ACC_ACR. A write to a protected register sets WPVS in ACC_WPSR and WPVSRC names it; reading ACC_WPSR clears WPVS.

The Integrity Check Monitor is a DMA engine that hashes memory regions with SHA, following transfer descriptors kept in memory (the descriptor area). In one mode it hashes a list of regions and writes the digests to memory (the hash area); in the other it keeps monitoring memory, recomputing each digest and comparing it with the one stored in the hash area, and raises an interrupt on a mismatch. The SHA engine meets FIPS Publication 180-2. Terms: a region is a part of instruction or data memory; a region descriptor is a memory structure giving a region's attributes (start address, size, SHA mode, write-back or compare); context registers are internal, not memory-mapped, and hold the attributes of the region being processed; the main list is the list of region descriptors; a secondary list is a linked list describing the layout of a non-contiguous region; the hash area is where digests are kept.

AHB DMA host interface; up to 4 monitored memory regions, each possibly non-contiguous; block gathering through linked lists; SHA1, SHA224 and SHA256; FIPS 180-2 compliance; configurable processing period (SHA1: 85 or 209 clock cycles; SHA256 or SHA224: 72 or 194 clock cycles); programmable bus load.
The ICM clock is enabled in the PMC before use. The ICM interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the ICM.

The ICM holds a DMA interface, a monitoring state machine, an integrity scheduler, context registers, a SHA engine and configuration and status registers. Used purely as a SHA unit it needs messages padded to FIPS 180-2; for memory integrity checking padding is optional. Each block read and processing period gives an N-bit digest: 160 for SHA1, 224 for SHA224, 256 for SHA256. Once enabled, the ICM walks a circular main list of up to four region descriptors, each four words giving the region layout and its hashing setup. After a descriptor loads into the context registers, TRSIZE + 1 blocks go from memory to the SHA engine; the digest is then written to memory or compared with a stored reference, and a mismatch interrupts if unmasked. The list ends at a descriptor with WRAP or EOM set in ICM_RCFG; for continuous monitoring the last descriptor has WRAP = 1 and EOM = 0. The descriptor area is contiguous read-only memory and the hash area contiguous write-once memory.

operation.topic: ICM secondary list and bus load
operation.text: Each region descriptor can gather data through a secondary list, which cannot change the region's attributes; at its end the ICM goes back to the main list. Monitoring is a background job that needs little bandwidth; ICM_CFG.BBC limits its memory load. Each region may use its own SHA algorithm, and WRAP gives continuous monitoring.

The descriptor area is contiguous system memory reachable by the ICM and the processor. On activation the ICM fetches the descriptor at *(ICM_DSCR), and with several regions at *(ICM_DSCR) + (RID << 4), RID being the region number. A main-list descriptor has RADDR, RCFG, RCTRL and RNEXT; a secondary-list descriptor has RADDR, an unused word, RCTRL and RNEXT. ICM_RADDR is the first byte address of the region. ICM_RCTRL.TRSIZE makes the ICM transfer TRSIZE + 1 blocks of 512 bits. ICM_RNEXT.NEXT (bits 31:2) points to the next secondary-list descriptor, or is 0 for the last one.

The hash area is contiguous system memory reachable by the ICM and the processor, its start set in the hash area start address register on a 128-byte boundary. With CDWBN = 0 (write back) the digest is written at *(ICM_HASH) + (RID << 5); with CDWBN = 1 (compare) the reference digest is read from that address. Messages and digests are stored little-endian; the FIPS 180-2 one-block message 'abc' (61 62 63 80 00 … 00 18) and its two-block form are laid out in memory byte lane by byte lane with byte 0x61 in lane 0 of address 0x000.

The ICM can just compute a SHA1, SHA224 or SHA256 digest. The data start address goes in the transfer descriptor of its DMA; the descriptor is a whole number of 4 × 32-bit words, and its start address, in ICM_DSCR, is 64-byte aligned (six LSBs clear). Data already padded need one descriptor with ICM_RCFG.EOM = 1. If the padding lives elsewhere, a non-zero ICM_RNEXT.NEXT pointing at it makes the ICM join the two areas and write the digest from the start of the hash area in ICM_HASH. In either case ICM_RCFG.CDWBN and WRAP are 0, and WBDIS, EOMDIS and SLBDIS in ICM_CFG are 0. RHIEN and ECIEN are written to 1; RHC[i] and REC[i] then signal that the result is at ICM_HASH, and either can interrupt when enabled in ICM_IER.

A short processing period gives the SHA unit more bandwidth; a long one leaves more of the system bus to others. SHA1: 85 clock cycles shortest, 209 longest. SHA256 and SHA224: 72 shortest, 194 longest. Each adds 2 clock cycles to synchronise the start command.

ICM_CFG.ASCD switches it on. With ASCD set and CDWBN and EOM of ICM_RCFG at 0, the ICM first walks the main list once, computing the digests of the monitored areas; at the descriptor with WRAP = 1 it starts monitoring, setting CDWBN and clearing EOM by itself. Those bits are then ignored until monitoring ends with EOM set.

An undefined register access sets URAD in ICM_ISR if unmasked, and ICM_UASR.URAT gives its source; only the first such access is recorded. Causes: an unspecified descriptor structure member found set to one when the descriptor loads; ICM_CFG, ICM_DSCR or ICM_HASH changed during active monitoring; a read of a write-only register. Only writing 1 to ICM_CTRL.SWRST resets URAD and URAT.

The True Random Number Generator passes the NIST 800-90B test suite, NIST Special Publication 800-22 and the Diehard tests, and can serve as the entropy source seeding a NIST-approved deterministic RNG as FIPS PUB 140-2 and 140-3 require. It delivers a 32-bit random number every 84 clock cycles.

The TRNG user interface clock is enabled in the PMC; it is separate from any clock the entropy source uses, and the entropy source may be enabled before the interface clock. The TRNG interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, set up before the TRNG. After enabling, the TRNG must be given its warm-up time TRNGWUP from the AC electrical timings before its output is used.

With TRNG_CR.ENABLE = 1 a new 32-bit value is ready every 84 clock cycles: TRNG_ISR.DATRDY is set and the value is in TRNG_ODATA. The interrupt is enabled in TRNG_IER and disabled in TRNG_IDR; it is set when a value is ready and cleared by reading TRNG_ISR. Normally software checks DATRDY = 1 before reading TRNG_ODATA.

The AES block meets FIPS Publication 197. It supports the ECB, CBC, OFB, CFB and CTR modes of NIST Special Publication 800-38A and Galois/Counter Mode of NIST SP 800-38D, all usable with DMA channels so large buffers need little processor work. Software loads the key: 128, 192 or 256 bits in four, six or eight write-only 32-bit registers AES_KEYWR0–7. The 128-bit input data and, for some modes, the initialization vector go in four write-only 32-bit registers each (AES_IDATAR0–3, AES_IVR0–3). Once key, IV and input are loaded, processing can start, and the result is read from AES_ODATAR0–3 or by DMA.

FIPS 197 AES; 128, 192 or 256-bit keys; 10, 12 or 14 clock cycles of processing per block for 128, 192 or 256-bit keys; a double input buffer for speed; the modes of NIST SP 800-38A and 800-38D: ECB, CBC including CBC-MAC, CFB, OFB, CTR and GCM; data sizes of 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 bits in CFB; a last output data mode for faster MAC generation; DMA for every mode.
The AES clock is enabled in the PMC first. The AES interrupt goes to the interrupt controller, which is set up before the AES.

AES is a symmetric block cipher: encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext and decryption turns it back. CIPHER in AES_MR chooses encryption or decryption. Blocks are 128 bits; the key is 128, 192 or 256 bits in AES_KEYWRx. CBC, CFB and OFB encryption also take a 128-bit initialization vector in AES_IVRx, used in the first step of a message and of its decryption; CTR uses AES_IVRx for the counter value.

The bus and processor are little-endian and the AES registers take little-endian words, while FIPS 197 defines data big-endian. So a message starting 0xcafedeca_01234567 (big-endian) is written as AES_IDATAR0 = 0xcadefeca and AES_IDATAR1 = 0x67452301.

ECB; CBC, with CBC-MAC for CMAC acceleration; OFB; CFB with data segments of 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits (CFB8 to CFB128, chosen by AES_MR.CFBS); CTR; GCM. Pre- and post-processing and chaining are done in hardware. OPMOD in AES_MR selects the mode. In CTR mode the internal block counter is 16 bits, so it rolls over after 1 Mbyte; longer files are split into pieces of at most 1 Mbyte (the first piece shorter if the counter does not start at 0). AES_IVRx must hold the starting counter before the first piece goes into AES_IDATARx, and the right counter value before each following piece.

For computing MACs by cipher block chaining (CBC-MAC; CMAC is CBC-MAC plus one ECB block, so CBC-MAC accelerates CMAC). Normally each result appears in AES_ODATARx (manual and auto modes) or at the DMA receive buffer. AES_MR.LOD = 1 keeps only the last result of a run of operations, available only in AES_ODATARx, so no DMA read buffer is needed. Manual and auto modes, LOD = 0: DATRDY clears when an AES_ODATARx is read; if the outputs are not read between operations DATRDY stays set and the end of later operations cannot be seen. LOD = 1: DATRDY clears when an AES_IDATARx is written, and no output reads are needed between operations.

operation.topic: AES last output data mode with DMA
operation.text: LOD = 0 works for every mode except CBC-MAC, where LOD = 1 is the better choice. With LOD = 0 two DMA channels are used, one writing blocks to AES_IDATARx and one reading AES_ODATARx, and the end is the end of the output-side DMA transfer. With LOD = 1, for CBC-MAC, wait for the DMA buffer-complete flag and then for DATRDY; no receive buffer is needed and the result is only in AES_ODATARx. Reading AES_ODATARx in DMA mode ahead of the final transfer can return unpredictable data.

GCM is the AES engine in CTR mode plus a GHASH engine, a universal hash over a binary Galois field that produces an authentication tag. GHASH runs on the data after the AES step. CTR mode gives confidentiality and GHASH authenticity; GCM can also authenticate data that are not encrypted (see NIST SP 800-38D). It works with or without the DMA, on a whole message at once or on pieces over time. Data are handled in 128-bit fields with no support for unaligned data, and any supported key length can be used. AES_IVRx gives counter 0, AES_CTRR the running counter, AES_GHASHRx the hash state, AES_GCMHRx the hash subkey (optional to write), AES_AADLENR and AES_CLENR the lengths of the AAD and the text, and AES_TAGRx the tag.

Writing a new key does two things. The hash subkey H = CIPHER(Key, 128 zero bits) is generated, and nothing else may be done until AES_ISR.DATRDY (and its interrupt, if set) shows it complete; H then sits in AES_GCMHRx and may be overwritten there, after DATRDY and before data input starts, if a specific subkey is wanted. And AES_GHASHRx is cleared; an initial GHASH value, if needed, is written after the key and before the data.

Three phases: hashing the additional authenticated data (AAD), hashing and ciphering the text C, and making the tag from the AAD length, the C length and J0. The tag is made automatically when AES_MR.GTAGEN is set, or by hand through AES_GHASHRx.GHASH. AAD and C are each padded to 16-byte boundaries, with lengths AADLEN and CLEN.

operation.topic: AES GCM complete message with tag
operation.text: Only when the four LSB bytes of J0 are not 0xFFFFFFFF; otherwise, or when unknown, process without the tag and then generate it by hand. Steps: OPMOD = GCM and GTAGEN = 1; write the key and wait for DATRDY (subkey done); compute J0 per NIST (J0 = IV || 0^31 || 1 when len(IV) = 96, else J0 = GHASH_H(IV || 0^(s+64) || [len(IV)]64), which the AES can compute as an AAD-only message); set AES_IVRx.IV to inc32(J0); set AADLEN and CLEN; feed AES_IDATARx as the SMOD setting dictates (in manual or auto mode DATRDY marks each block processed, with no output during AAD); wait for TAGRDY and read the tag from AES_TAGRx.

operation.topic: AES GCM complete message without tag
operation.text: For a custom tag or a fragmented message. Steps: OPMOD = GCM, GTAGEN = 0; write the key, wait for DATRDY (the subkey can then be read or replaced in AES_GCMHRx); compute J0; AES_IVRx.IV = inc32(J0); set AADLEN and CLEN; feed AES_IDATARx; when CLEN is not 0 make sure the last output has been read, otherwise wait on DATRDY; finally AES_GHASHRx.GHASH holds the hash after the last data.

Automatic tag generation is not available. First fragment: as the untagged message, with AADLEN and CLEN set for the fragment or for the whole message (either works), the fragment aligned on 16 bytes; at the end read the last output (if it ended in C) or wait for DATRDY (if in AAD), then save AES_GHASHRx.GHASH and AES_CTR.CTR (the counter is not needed when ending in AAD). Next fragments: OPMOD and key again only if changed; AES_IVRx.IV = J0 if the fragment starts with AAD, or LSB96(J0) || saved CTR if it starts with plaintext; AADLEN and CLEN for this fragment or the remainder; restore the saved GHASH; feed the fragment; save GHASH and CTR as before. After the last fragment the GHASH value is used for manual tag generation.

Done after an untagged message has been fully processed. First S = GHASH_H(AAD || 0^v || C || 0^u || [len(AAD)]64 || [len(C)]64): OPMOD = GCM, GTAGEN = 0; key and DATRDY; AADLEN = 0x10 (16 bytes) and CLEN = 0 for a single GHASH_H on 16 bytes; write the GHASH saved at the end of the message into AES_GHASHRx; feed len(AAD)64 || len(C)64 into AES_IDATARx and wait for DATRDY; read AES_GHASHRx. Then T = GCTR_K(J0, S): OPMOD = CTR; AES_IVRx.IV = J0; feed the GHASH value just read and wait for DATRDY; read the tag from AES_ODATARx. Writing GHASH back may be skipped when it would be 0 (a zero-length packet, for example).

operation.topic: AES GCM AAD-only processing and GF128 multiplication
operation.text: With CLEN = 0 only GHASH_H runs, which serves, for example, to compute J0 when len(IV) is not 96: OPMOD = GCM, GTAGEN = 0; key and DATRDY; AADLEN = len(IV || 0^(s+64) || [len(IV)]64), CLEN = 0; feed that message (DATRDY marks each GHASH_H step); read J0 from AES_GHASHRx. GHASH can be preset at any time by writing it, before the data, to start from an initial value. A single GF(2^128) multiplication A × B: OPMOD = GCM, GTAGEN = 0; AADLEN = 0x10, CLEN = 0; B into AES_GCMHRx.H; A into AES_IDATARx; wait for DATRDY; read the product from AES_GHASHRx. Presetting GHASH to C before the data gives (A XOR C) × B.

AES_IDATARx can be double-buffered so a new block is written while the previous one is processed, shortening large jobs. This works only with DMA accesses (AES_MR.SMOD = 2) and needs AES_MR.DUALBUFF = 1.

AES_MR.SMOD selects the start mode. Manual: write AES_MR (SMOD, OPMOD and the rest); write the key in AES_KEYWRx; write the IV or counter in AES_IVRx (every mode but ECB); set DATRDY in AES_IER if an end interrupt is wanted; write the input into the allowed AES_IDATARx; set START in AES_CR. At the end DATRDY rises in AES_ISR and, if enabled, the AES interrupt line goes active. Reading any AES_ODATARx clears AES_IER.DATRDY automatically.

operation.topic: AES auto and DMA start modes
operation.text: Auto mode is like manual, but processing starts by itself as soon as the right number of AES_IDATARx have been written, with no write to AES_CR. DMA mode encrypts or decrypts a buffer with no software action meanwhile: SMOD = 2, the DMA set to non-incrementing addresses, every transfer descriptor starting at AES_IDATAR0. The writing channel fetches source data from memory, best set to word size even in CFB modes; its destination size depends on the mode, as does the source size of the reading channel that moves results to memory.

An unspecified register access raises AES_ISR.URAD and AES_ISR.URAT gives its source; only the last such access is kept. Causes: writing an input data register during processing when SMOD = IDATAR0_START; reading an output data register during processing or during subkey generation; writing the mode register during processing or during subkey generation; reading a write-only register. Only AES_CR.SWRST resets URAD and URAT.

The core brownout detector output drops when VDDCORE falls through VT- and recovers once VDDCORE has risen by the hysteresis above it, each change after a short delay (td- falling, td+ rising). The VDDCORE and VDDIO power-on reset circuits hold reset while their supply is below VT+ on the way up and assert it again when the supply drops under VT-; the VDDIO supply monitor asserts reset below its selected threshold VT- and releases it a hysteresis above.

Current is given for the low-power modes (Backup, Wait, Sleep) and for Active mode, on each supply, with the static and dynamic draw of the I/Os. The bench feeds VDDIO and VDDIN from one 3.3V source, with the on-chip regulator output VDDOUT supplying VDDCORE and VDDPLL; ammeter AMP1 reads the supply into the part in Backup mode, and in Sleep, Wait and Active mode AMP1 sits in the VDDOUT-to-VDDCORE path while AMP2 reads the total.

Backup-mode figures are taken with the slow RC oscillator on, the VDDIO supply monitor off, the RTC running, the RTT in 1 Hz mode, the BOD off and one WKUPx input enabled, read on AMP1 at ambient temperature, once with the 1 Kbyte backup SRAM powered and once with it off.

Sleep-mode figures are taken with the core clock stopped, VDDIO = VDDIN = 3.3V, MCK running from PLLA or from the fast RC oscillator at the listed frequencies, fast start-up through the WKUP0 to WKUP13 pins, every peripheral clock off and TA = 25°C. Wake-up time runs from the WKUP event to the first instruction executed.
Wait-mode figures are taken with the core and host clocks stopped, every peripheral clock off, the BOD off and the RTT on.

Active-mode figures are taken with VDDIO = VDDIN = 3.3V, VDDCORE from the internal regulator, TA = 25°C, code running from Flash in 128-bit access mode, every peripheral clock off and MCK from PLLA or the fast RC oscillator; AMP1 reads VDDCORE and AMP2 the total. The Flash wait states (FWS in EEFC_FMR) follow the core frequency.
The 4/8/12 MHz RC oscillator is calibrated during production; software reads the calibration with the EEFC Get CALIB bit command and can trim the frequency through the PMC.

With the 3 to 20 MHz oscillator the crystal sits between XIN and XOUT with a load capacitor CLEXT from each side to ground; below 8 MHz a 1 kΩ resistor goes in series between XOUT and the crystal. The oscillator contributes its own load CL across XIN and XOUT.

For either the 32768 Hz or the 3 to 20 MHz oscillator: the whole load on the crystal (oscillator internal parasitics plus board parasitics) has to equal the load the crystal is specified at, or the frequency is off. The crystal's rated drive level has to be at least the oscillator's drive level, or the crystal can be damaged. The crystal's ESR has to be no more than the oscillator's maximum ESR, and its shunt capacitance no more than the oscillator's CSHUNT, or the oscillator may fail to start.
Keep the XIN, XOUT, XIN32 and XOUT32 traces as short as possible, away from switching signals such as clocks, data and PWM, and guarded by a quiet ground.
The USB transceiver meets the voltage, power and timing requirements of the USB 2.0 specification.

The on-chip temperature sensor feeds channel 11 of AFE0 with a voltage VTEMP proportional to absolute temperature. A calibration at one temperature, removing the initial VTEMP and ADC offsets, improves its accuracy.
When code runs from the embedded Flash, the Flash access time caps the clock: the FWS field of EEFC_FMR sets how many wait states each access takes, and each setting has its own top frequency.
MediaLB reaches the 1024×Fs timings only with VDDIO = 3.3V.

operation.topic: QSPI host write and read speed
operation.text: When the QSPI only sends (to an LCD, say), its output delay QSPI2 or QSPI5 allows more than the pads can toggle, so the pad limit in the I/O characteristics sets the clock. When it reads, the clock is limited by the input setup time plus the client's output delay. A client answering in 12 ns allows 66 MHz at VDDIO = 3.3V; a Flash answering in 6 ns gives 112 MHz by the formula, but the QSPI host itself tops out at 66 MHz in the worst case, so the controller is then the limit. The timings hold for VDDIO from 3V to 3.6V with at most 40 pF on each line.

In host mode the SPI samples MISO before the edge on which MOSI shifts, using the same edge rather than the opposite one. This stretches the time allowed for the client's output delay and the board delay to more than half an SPCK period, where the usual sampling point allows less than half. A client running in mode 0 can be driven safely by the host set to mode 0.

Host write: the output delay SPI2 or SPI5 allows more than the pads can toggle, so the pad limit sets the clock. Host read: the clock is limited by the MISO setup time plus the client's output delay; a memory answering in 5 ns allows 57 MHz at VDDIO = 3.3V. Client read: the MOSI setup and hold times SPI7/SPI8 (or SPI10/SPI11) allow far more than the SPCK pad, so the pad sets the limit. Client write: the limit comes from the MISO output delay and the host's setup time. The SPI timings hold for VDDIO from 2.85V to 3.6V with at most 40 pF on each line.
The HSMCI supports MultiMedia Card specification V4.3, SD Memory Card specification V2.0, SDIO V2.0 and CE-ATA V1.1.

The SMC timings hold for VDDIO from 3V to 3.6V with at most 50 pF on the data, control and address pads; tCPMCK is one MCK period. A hold length is the whole cycle minus the setup and pulse lengths (NCS_WR_HOLD or NWE_HOLD).
In the asynchronous modes the USART reaches a baud rate of MCK2/8 with USART_MR.OVER = 1; with a 150 MHz peripheral clock that is 18.75 Mbit/s.

As SPI host, the USART drives MOSI on TXD, SCK on SCK and NSS on RTS, and reads MISO on RXD. As SPI client it reads MOSI on RXD, SCK on SCK and NSS on CTS, and drives MISO on TXD. These timings hold for VDDIO from 3V to 3.6V with at most 40 pF on each line.

The GMAC timings hold with 0 pF to 20 pF on the data and clock pads at 3.3V, and are met in MII mode at the maximum corner. For an output, the minimum access time runs from the clock edge to the first change of the signal and the maximum to the moment it is stable.

The SSC timings hold with at most 30 pF on each line at 3.3V. For the outputs TF, TD and RF the minimum access time runs from the TK or RK edge to the first change of the signal and the maximum to the moment it is stable; this applies to SSC0, SSC1, SSC4, SSC7, SSC10 and SSC13.
The ISI timings hold with at most 30 pF on each line at 3.3V.
The ISI samples DATA[7:0], VSYNC and HSYNC on the PIXCLK edge: ISI1 is the setup time before that edge, ISI2 the hold time after it, and ISI3 bounds the PIXCLK frequency.

The checklist gives the connections each pin needs and the least hardware to get the part running; it does not cover board layout. Whatever the supply scheme, the power-up and power-down sequencing rules apply.

VDDIN powers the regulator, the AFE, the DAC and the analog comparator. VDDIO powers the I/O buffers, the backup area, the 1 Kbyte backup SRAM, the 32 kHz crystal oscillator and the oscillator pads. VDDIN and VDDIO sit at the same voltage, always above VDDCORE. VDDUTMII powers the USB transceiver interface and is joined to VDDIO; it stays connected even when USB is unused, and for USB VDDUTMII and VDDIO lie between 3.0V and 3.6V. VDDPLLUSB supplies both the 3 to 20 MHz oscillator and the USB UTMI PLL; it draws little current but is noise-sensitive and is fed through an RLC filter, and for USB it lies between 3.0V and 3.6V. VDDCORE powers the core, memories and peripherals. VDDPLL powers PLLA and the fast RC oscillator; it is noise-sensitive and fed through a ferrite bead. VDDUTMIC powers the USB transceiver core and stays connected even without USB. Decoupling sits as close to the part as possible, on each supply pin, without vias.

GND is shared by VDDIN, VDDCORE and VDDIO; GNDUTMI by VDDUTMII and VDDUTMIC; GNDPLL serves VDDPLL; GNDANA serves the AFE, DAC and comparator powered from VDDIN; GNDPLLUSB serves VDDPLLUSB. Each goes to the system ground plane by the shortest path.

Every PIO line comes out of reset as an input with a 100 kOhm pull-up to VDDIO, except the lines shared with the oscillators and the debug interface, which have to be enabled as peripherals. Every input has a Schmitt trigger except XIN32/XOUT32 (PA7/PA8) and XIN/XOUT (PB8/PB9); when those oscillators are unused, those pins are set as outputs with their own trace to save current. An unused PIO draws least as an output driven low with its pull-up off. The same 100 kOhm pull-up at reset holds for the parallel-capture pins (PIODC0-7, PIODCCLK, PIODCEN1-2), the AFE, DAC and trigger pins, the bus and memory controller pins, the HSMCI, QSPI, USART, SSC, ISI, timer, PWM, SPI, TWI and FFPI pins.

VREFP is a pure analog input, 2.0V to VDDIN, fed through an LC filter with noise under 100 µVrms; the AFEC's ADC, its PGA DAC and the analog comparator all work from it. With no analog feature in use, VREFP goes to GND to save power. VREFN, the negative reference of the AFE, DAC and comparator, goes to GND or GNDANA. The AFE inputs AFEx_AD0 to AFEx_AD11 take 0 to VREFP; AFE0_AD11 is the internal temperature sensor and has no pin. The DAC outputs DAC0 and DAC1 swing 0 to VREFP; DATRG is the DAC trigger input and AFEx_ADTRG the AFE trigger input.

VBG is the USB bias reference, 0.9 V to 1.1V, set by a 5.62 kΩ ±1% resistor with 10 pF in parallel to GNDUTMI; keep the VBG trace as short as possible with a solid ground link to GNDUTMI. VBG may be left open when USB is not used. HSDM and HSDP are the high-speed data lines and are pulled down at reset.

D[15:0], A[23:0], NWAIT, NCS0 to NCS3, NRD, NWE, NWR0 and NWR1, NBS0 and NBS1, NANDOE and NANDWE are all pulled up to VDDIO at reset; the chip selects are given an external pull-up to VDDIO. The TWI lines TWDx and TWCKx take 4.7 kOhm pull-ups to VDDIO. ISI signals may need level shifting to suit the image sensor; the ISI has no dedicated master clock pin and PCK1 can serve as ISI_MCK. FFPI mode needs TST at VDDIO.

The boot paths that use USB and the PLL need a 12 MHz or 16 MHz crystal, or an external clock of that frequency in Bypass mode. The SAM-BA boot assistant talks over UART0, which needs no extra hardware, or over the USB device port, which needs that 12 MHz or 16 MHz crystal or clock; an external clock is a VDDIO square wave within 2500 ppm.
Each part carries the Atmel logo and its ordering code, then a line YYWW V (year, week of manufacture and revision) and a line with the lot number XXXXXXXXX and ARM.
144-lead LQFP, 20 x 20 mm body, 0.5 mm pitch, 1.60 mm maximum height, millimetres controlling; the gauge plane sits 0.25 mm above the seating plane.

packages.name: LQFP144
